World.title: Trump administration drops New York Times subpoenas over Air Force One reporting
World.content:
The White House had targeted journalists from The New York Times for their reporting on security concerns with a Qatari-donated Air Force One plane.

US President Donald Trump's Justice Department will withdraw subpoenas issued to reporters from The New York Times (NYT), prosecutors said at a hearing on Thursday.

The Justice Department issued the subpoenas demanding that NYT journalists disclose sources who contributed to one of the paper's reports on security concerns ‌about the president ⁠flying ⁠on a Qatari-donated Air Force One.

The report said the luxury plane lacked certain security countermeasures, including anti-missile defenses.

The Trump administration in turn said the NYT coverage posed a "substantial national security concern."

Lawyers representing the newspaper had challenged the Trump administration's requests for journalists' phone records and grand jury testimony, calling it an attempt at press intimidation.

Federal prosecutors had agreed at a hearing before District Judge Arun Subramanian to "unilaterally withdraw the subpoenas at this time," the NYT said.

Critics said the gifted plane could violate strict rules on presents for US presidents [FILE: June 2026] Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

NYT: government 'violated the 1st Amendment'

NYT lawyers said that these actions "violate the most basic First Amendment protections for newsgathering activity."

"They represent the latest salvo in an escalating series of attacks on journalists to intimidate them from engaging in reporting that the Trump Administration openly detests," the lawyers added.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) welcomed the conclusion of the case, saying it represented a victory not just for the NYT but also for "every journalist who relies on confidential sources to report in the public interest."

"The court has reaffirmed that the government cannot use its legal powers to intimidate reporters or erode the independence of the press," RSF said.

Donald Trump's new Air Force One raises security concerns To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the NYT say about the new Air Force One?

The controversial aircraft was a gift from Qatar's royal family to Trump last year.

The journalists' stories were prompted by the fact that Trump, who flew to Turkey earlier this month on the new Air Force One, departed the country on one of the older Air Force One jets, which took him to a Royal Air Force base in England.

From there, the president swapped back to the new Air Force One for the flight back to the US.

In its reports, the New York Times said the Secret Service had urged the switch in Turkey amid security concerns linked to the collapse of a shaky ceasefire with neighboring Iran.

The reports said that the new Air Force One lacks some of the sophisticated security features of the older aircraft, such as antimissile defense.

Trump has denied that security concerns were a factor in his use of the two different planes.

World.title: Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk ends hunger strike
World.content:
Sonam Wangchuk has ended his hunger strike after 26 days, saying the decision follows a "long negotiation" on various conditions and "in view of possible violence in the country."

Sonam Wangchuk has ended his hunger strike after 26 days, the Indian activist said Thursday on his X account.

The 59-year-old had been on a hunger strike since June 28 in solidarity with India's youth-led Cockroach movement.

For over a month, the student-led "Cockroach" protests have been calling for Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign over a leaked medical exam papers scandal.

But the movement has since expanded beyond students' grievances over the country's education system. It has also drawn professionals and families while channeling broader frustration against the government.

Cockroach revolution turns on India's leader To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Just now in the presence of Union Ministers JP Nadda and Dr. Jitendra Singh and the senior leaders of Apex Body of Leh Ladakh I finally broke my fast after 26 days," Wangchuk wrote.

He added that 65 members of parliament from different political parties had visited or otherwise urged him to break the fast.

Wanghuck said he had decided to end his hunger strike "after a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country."

"Meanwhile, I urge you all to stay very vigilant about not allowing violence of any kind anywhere," he added.

Days of protests, crackdowns

Earlier on Thursday, Wangchuk had offered to end his hunger strike if the government agreed not to harm student protesters.

Thursday's gathering at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in New Delhi, came in defiance of new restrictions on protest actions, after overnight clashes saw police use tear gas and batons to disperse crowds.

It was the second such confrontation between Cockroach party activists and police this week.

Announcing the end of his hunger strike, Wangchuk said he was seeking assurances from the government, including compensation for families of students who committed suicide, and the resignation of India's education minister.

India's Cockroach protests meet with batons and tear gas To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A Cockroach movement protest on Monday ended in clashes with police and dozens of arrests, after protesters defied police orders and marched toward parliament.

Following the clashes, the opposition Congress Party called for Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Home Minister Amit Shah to step down over the police crackdown.

World.title: Germany seeks energy and trading partners in Africa
World.content:
Germany wants to boost relations with Africa. During his trip, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has promoted cooperation on energy, infrastructure and the economy. He also criticized US treatment of South Africa.

In a tent in the Nigerian metropolis of Lagos, two worlds collided: Three fashionable influencers sat on cushioned stools across from Germany's 63-year-old Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul. For half an hour, the senior politician met youth from Africa's creative scene.

These young people are among the stars of Nigeria's creative industry — in a country with a population of around 240 million and a median age of just under 18. Wadephul wanted to understand what moves the younger generation. What issues are on their minds? How do they view Germany? And what do they expect from a collaboration?

After a brief hesitation, they replied: Germany and Europe listen to their music, view their art, and want to collaborate with them. But anyone who wants to travel to the German capital for Fashion Week or the Berlinale film festival can hardly get a visa, said a young man in the audience.

A conversation gets underway; everyone enjoys the exchange and subsequently uploads upbeat videos to social media platforms — to the influencers' channels as well as those of the Federal Foreign Office. This is how German diplomacy is pursuing a direct line of communication with Africa's younger generation.

Nigeria as a valuable energy supplier

There is good reason for the Foreign Minister to be promoting Germany in Nigeria. "The country is an economic powerhouse and, as Africa's largest domestic market, also a key destination for German exports," he says. Nigeria is sub-Saharan Africa's second-largest economy and already imports machinery, chemicals, and food products "Made in Germany."

However, Nigeria's raw materials account for the largest share of the trade balance. They have become even more important since the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. "In June, 25% of jet fuel shipments to Europe came from Nigeria. But we can do significantly more," emphasized Wadephul.

Vital infrastructure support

Wadephul was accompanied by a business delegation on his third trip to Africa. The group includes major corporations like Siemens as well as small and medium-sized enterprises. One of these is VIDA , a Munich-based AI company that is finalizing a multi-million-euro contract with the Nigerian government. The focus is on AI-driven infrastructure planning.

"Our solutions help identify and evaluate new locations. AI allows us to determine much more quickly the economic potential of a site, as well as the local conditions regarding security, climate trends, and other key factors," explained VIDA founder Tobias Engelmeier. His company is already implementing projects in 20 African countries.

German support for infrastructure development is in demand in many places. Since the European Union launched a €290 million ($330 mio) package as part of its Global Gateway strategy, hopes have been rising — both in Africa and among European companies — for faster progress in expanding transport, energy, and utility networks. The Nigerian government is also actively lobbying for German investment to modernize its power supply.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and President of the ECOWAS Commission Omar Touray attended the Nigerian-German business roundtable Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

Underestimated economic and political significance

Yet Germany has long underestimated Nigeria's economic and political importance. Given the potential of what is Germany's second-most important trading partner in sub-Saharan Africa, the presence of around 100 German companies is comparatively small. Siemens is involved in expanding the power grid, while Bayer is planning pharmaceutical production facilities together with regional partners. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are also increasingly entering the market, though many complain about a lack of transparency in market and decision-making structures.

"It is a challenging market with high operating costs. That is why local partners who understand the diverse structures across the 36 states are essential," says Sabine Dal'Omo, Managing Director of Siemens Sub-Saharan Africa and Chairwoman of the German-African Business Association.

Renewable energy provider Enertrag is among the companies taking a wait-and-see approach. "For us, Nigeria holds great potential — there is strong domestic demand and favorable conditions for exporting green energy. However, the overall framework remains too uncertain for us to commit to a long-term investment," said board member Anne Bendzulla.

Instead, Enertrag has been successfully investing in South Africa for several years. There, the company states it is prepared to invest around €850 million in wind energy.

Missing out by arriving late

The security situation in Nigeria is a matter of concern for German business. Consequently, the federal government has made additional funds available for cooperation with Nigeria's police authorities.

Wadephul urges the German business community not to hesitate too long. "Anyone not present in Africa today risks missing out on crucial opportunities," he told reporters. The country, with its young population, possesses immense potential and abundant resources, he added. "It would be grossly negligent of us to overlook that."

On the final day of his third trip to Africa this year, Wadephul visited South Africa, Germany's most important economic partner on the continent.



At a press conference in the capital Pretoria, South African Minister for International Relations Ronald Lamola praised the fact that "some 600 German companies operate in our country [South Africa] and employ approximately 100,000 people."

In April 2026, the two countries had elevated their relationship to a Strategic Partnership and adopted a Joint Action Plan, which focuses on strengthening cooperation in the areas of trade and investment, security and energy transition. Today, about 80% of South Africa's electricity is still generated from coal.

While in the South African capital, Wadephul criticized US President Donald Trump for not inviting South Africa, which he described as "an indispensable member of the G20," to the group's next summit.

"To exclude South Africa means sidelining an important African voice and a regional economic and political powerhouse," the German foreign minister said. "This can be in no one's interest. As — particularly at a time of growing global economic uncertainty — we need more cooperation, not less!"

He added that he was confident that "South Africa will be able to participate again as a full member of the G20 next year."

He also agreed that African states were underrepresented in the United Nations. "There can be no representative United Nations without permanent African representation on the Security Council," he said.

Wadephul's four-day diplomatic offensive in Africa is evidence of Germany's desire to engage more with democracies and middle powers around the world amid a crisis of multilateralism. As Chinese and Russian influence on the continent increase, Germany with Europe wants to offer an alternative to the Global South.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Sweden eases mining permits to cut China minerals reliance
World.content:
Sweden has declared the mining of critical minerals and rare earths a national security interest. This will ease and expedite the permit process. The government said the step was needed to counter dependence on China.

Sweden on Thursday announced plans to try to boost its mining sector, particularly when it comes to rare earths, and counter European dependence on China.

Resource-rich Sweden is already home to Europe's largest iron ore mine, and has since found considerable rare earth deposits at the same Arctic Circle site in Kiruna.

Rare earth minerals are essential for renewable energy generation, defense and electric vehicle production, modern computer manufacturing and other core industries. China accounts for roughly 70% of global mining and refining.

What did the Swedish government say about the plan?

The government in Stockholm on Thursday declared the mining of critical metals and rare earth minerals to be a national security interest.

This should ease and accelerate the permit process for new extraction projects and help attract investments, according to Energy Minister Ebba Busch, who is also deputy prime minister.

"Sweden must become a leading mining nation," she said as she outlined the new strategy, saying the government intended to "streamline authorization procedures so decisions can be taken more quickly."

Ebba Busch said that despite the country's vast mineral wealth and mining operations, only 1% of global mining investment currently found its way to Sweden Image: Viktoria Bank/TT/picture alliance

"We believe that this can contribute significantly to both Sweden's the EU's and NATO's defense capabilities," Busch said, calling European industry's dependence on China a "systemic risk."

Busch also said the move would make it easier for the state to assign land for mining projects, an area of tension with the Sami reindeer-herding indigenous people, who say the expansion of mining could spell the end for their traditional way of life.

The energy minister also said the government was looking into setting up a state-owned investment company for the mining sector.

"Today, to put it plainly, the governemnt lacks concrete tools to wisely contribute to accelerating and attracting investments in crucial strategic projects," she said.

A special train carries the Kiruna mine's minerals to a nearby port for further transit Image: Andreas Werth/imageBROKER/picture alliance

What are Sweden's existing mining credentials?

Sweden has been a European mining giant since the 10th century and the opening of the vast Falun copper mine, which at one point produced as much as two-thirds of the continent's copper. The distinctive deep red color that adorns many houses, churches and other buildings in the country is called Falun Red and hails from the disused mine. It's now a museum and UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Sweden's modern-day Falun is the vast LKAB iron ore mine in Kiruna in the Arctic Circle. Sweden holds around 60% of Europe's known iron ore deposits and, as of 2021, was responsible for around 90% of the continent's iron ore extraction, around one-third of that from Kiruna alone.

The vast frozen mining town made headlines in recent years because of the need to relocate various homes and buildings — including the church — in Kiruna because of subsidence as the giant operation literally undermines the city.

Kiruna's chuch was put on wheels and moved last summer in the more clement weather, attracting international attention Image: Fredrik Sandberg/TT/picture alliance

More than 90% of Sweden's mines operate in the sparsely populated and resource-rich Norrland region in Sapmi, the traditional territory of the Sami.

Near the Kiruna mine is the Per Geijer find, a flagship EU project seeking to reduce mineral reliance on China. This is an area where around 1.2 billion tons of mineral resources, including around 2.2 million tons of rare earth oxides, have been identified.

Mining group LKAB is examining the potential of the deposit but estimates that obtaining permits to excavate on Sami land could take 10 years.

Four of the EU's 47 strategic projects aimed at reducing mineral dependence on China are located in Sweden.

A whole city is moving — but at what cost? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: US threatens 'major military punishment' for Houthi attacks
World.content:
07/23/2026 July 23, 2026 Houthis 'snookered' into joining US-Iran conflict — Rubio

Rubio accused Iran of violating previous deals with the US, saying Tehran would "pay the price for it" Image: Brendan Smialowski/Pool AFP/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that he believed that Yemen's Houthi rebels had been tricked into joining the conflict with the United States by Tehran.

"The Houthis largely were smart and stayed out of all this throughout the conflict, but they now apparently have gotten themselves suckered into this, going after Saudi Arabia and their ships," Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of a summit of the ASEAN Southeast Asian bloc in Manila, the Philippines.

"I hope they will de-escalate, because I think the Houthis, frankly, got snookered into this thing by the Iranians," he said.

The militant group controls much of Yemen's most populous areas, including the capital, Sanaa, and is allied with Iran. It already began threatening merchant ships in the Red Sea in response to Israel's offensive in Gaza in 2023.

The Houthi rebel group is a longstanding ally of Iran Image: Khaled Abdullah/REUTERS

The top US official also accused Iran of going back on its commitments in peace talks.

"These people make deals ‌and then they break ‌it ​almost immediately or they decide, 'oh, let's change the deal'. ​That's not how deals work," he said.

"So now ⁠they're ​paying the ​price for it. And ​maybe they'll change ‌their mind here over the ​next ⁠few days as they continue to ⁠suffer ​great losses," Rubio added.

He said he believed Iran was not yet ready for a deal with Washington but said it might be soon, while also reiterating the US' position that Iran should be "denuclearized." Iran maintains its nuclear program is exclusively for civilian purposes.

Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump declared that a previous ceasefire deal with Iran was "over."

World.title: US-Saudi nuclear deal: How will it impact Middle East, US-Iran war?
World.content:
Critics say the US-Saudi deal could spark a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. It's certainly not making US allies, like Israel and the UAE, happy. And reports suggest the US may already be backtracking on the deal.

After new statements by US President Donald Trump on Thursday morning, it is still unclear whether a controversial new dealwith Saudi Arabia that allows the Middle Eastern autocracy to establish a civilian nuclear program will go ahead.

Trump said the deal could only progress if Saudi Arabia normalized diplomatic relations with Israel. In the recent past, the Saudi government has repeatedly stated it would only do this if the Israelis make genuine moves toward establishing a Palestinian state. With the current Israeli government, that is unlikely to happen.

The deal must also be voted on by the US Congress and there's been backlash already, with critics saying it could set off a nuclear arms race in the Middle East.

One of the main reasons experts are so worried is that in several years' time, the deal, as it stands now, may let the Saudis enrich their own uranium. The more uranium is enriched, the more it could potentially be diverted to make weapons. And in the past Saudi Arabian ruler Mohammed bin Salman has said that if Iran produces a nuclear bomb, then Saudi Arabia would need to have one too.

The majority of the approximately 38 countries with civilian nuclear energy programs don't enrich uranium. Instead they import it.

The US-Saudi deal also has regional implications, especially because it seems to have been formulated in a far less rigorous way than similar deals.

During the current US-Iran war, Iran has also threatened to strike the Barakah nuclear reactor in the United Arab Emirates Image: Arun Girija/Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation/WAM/AP Photo/picture alliance

United Arab Emirates: Preferential treatment for Saudis?

The less strict deal the US has made with Saudi Arabia is likely to upset the United Arab Emirates, who often compete with the Saudis for geopolitical influence.

The UAE already has a nuclear power plant, Barakah, as a result of arrangements made with the Americans back in 2009.

As with almost all of the 26 nuclear cooperation agreements the US has, the UAE's deal also included what's known as an "additional protocol" signed with the International Atomic Energy Agency, or IAEA. This means the IAEA can thoroughly inspect all nuclear facilities. The UAE also agreed to forgo uranium enrichment.

The Saudi deal is bilateral only — that is, just between the US and the Saudis and doesn't include the IAEA — and the Saudis may eventually be allowed to enrich their own uranium.

For the UAE, nuclear power was always more about the prestige of being the first Arab nation to develop it than about military ambitions, Nour Eid told DW earlier this year. Eid is an independent researcher based in Paris who has published papers on nuclear ambitions in the Middle East for a number of think tanks.

But, she pointed out, there is also a clause in the UAE agreement that stipulates that "if a regional or neighboring country has a more flexible agreement then they reserve the right to renegotiate their terms."

Israel: Not only one with nuclear bomb?

The Saudi-US nuclear deal will also worry the Israelis, especially if it leads to the development of a nuclear bomb in the Gulf state. That would make Saudi Arabia the only other country in the Middle East to have one.

Israel has never confirmed having nuclear weapons but it's generally acknowledged that it does, probably around 90 warheads plus delivery systems.

Israeli politicians see the Saudi deal as a threat and say their wishes have been ignored. "Every military nuclear program begins with a civilian one," former Israeli defense minister Avigdor Lieberman warned.

Israel is one of only four UN member states that have not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty but observers say its secret nuclear program is based in the desert near the city of Dimona Image: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP

The Saudis have lobbied for their own civilian nuclear program for years and, at one stage, possible US-Saudi cooperation on this was a seen as a foreign policy sweetener: If Saudi Arabia, often perceived as a leader of the Islamic world, agreed to normalize diplomatic relations with Israel, it would get nuclear technology from the US.

Any detachment of the nuclear issue from normalization is unlikely to please the Israelis.

"The agreement — coupled with the prospect of the US selling F-35 fighter jets to Turkey — adds to already existing differences between the US and Israel over Iran, and Israeli occupation of south Lebanon and parts of southern Syria," James Dorsey, an expert on the region at Singapore's Rajaratnam School of International Studies, wrote in his regular newsletter on Thursday.

Why the US might offend its ally

There are a number of possible reasons why the US has come up with this deal.

Paris-based researcher Eid pointed out it may have to do with American competition with China and Russia, the world's main nuclear suppliers. The Chinese and Russians have submitted bids to build nuclear plants in Saudi Arabia and these tend to come with fewer conditions, she said. Trump also previously promised to revitalize the US nuclear sector and the Saudi deal will be worth billions.

There's also the Iran war to consider. The US-Israeli war on Iran, which started late February, saw Iran target US-allied Gulf countries. That has strained American relations with Saudi Arabia, which is caught between Israel and Iran's hegemonic ambitions.

This deal binds the US and Saudi Arabia closer together, says Rosemary Kelanic, director of the Middle East program at US-based think tank, the Defense Priorities Foundation.

For example, it gives "Saudi Arabia a potent source of leverage to extract future concessions from Washington, including new security guarantees, by threatening to weaponize its program unless the US promises enhanced military protection," Kelanic argued in a Wednesday press statement .

The US might feel compelled to trade defense protection for the Saudis giving up potential nuclear weapons, as happened in West Germany and South Korea, she says.

"They made nuclear progress, we wanted to prevent them from getting the bomb, and ultimately we offered them greater US military protection so they'd abandon their programs," Kelanic explained. "Giving Riyadh uranium enrichment could functionally enmesh the US with Saudi Arabia forever."

The deal might also mean the US is forced to intervene to save the Saudi monarchy if it was threatened, she noted.

Iran: Regional rivalry

When the deal was announced, observers were quick to point out the inherent hypocrisy. The Trump administration was now prepared to give Saudi Arabia the very things they were bombing Iran for, various experts argued.

It's a blow to the Iranians because "their sworn enemy [the US] … is giving their regional rival a head start on its own nuclear program," Kelanic said on social media platform, X.

That is why the deal makes a swift end to the current conflict between Iran and the US less likely, she argued. "Iran will definitely be less trusting of the US and less willing to make any concessions," Kelanic noted online.

The deal also makes the Iranians more likely to try and weaponize their own nuclear program faster, she continued.

Other observers agree and also fear the beginning of a nuclear arms race in the Middle East.

However, as Eid pointed out, none of this is likely to happen in the near term. It will take the Saudis somewhere between 10 and 20 years to develop nuclear power, let alone nuclear weapons, she told DW.

Edited by: M. Cavanagh

World.title: Trump impone nuevos aranceles de entre el 10% y el 12,5% a más de 60 países para mantener su muro comercial
World.content:
El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, ha aprobado este jueves una orden ejecutiva para imponer aranceles de entre el 10% y el 12,5% a más de 60 países, entre los que se encuentran España y el resto de miembros de la Unión Europea, Reino Unido, China, India, Japón, Corea del Sur o México, por no haber tomado suficientes medidas para controlar las importaciones de bienes producidos mediante trabajo forzoso. Está previsto que el nuevo golpe arancelario entre en vigor esta medianoche antes de que expire el arancel universal del 10% aprobado el pasado enero por el líder estadounidense para evitar un vacío legal tras el revés del Tribunal Supremo a la principal medida sobre la que pivotaba su política comercial.

“Se trata de la acción internacional en materia de derechos laborales más trascendental que Estados Unidos haya emprendido jamás, o que haya emprendido cualquier país jamás”, declaró un alto funcionario de la Administración Trump en una llamada a un grupo de periodistas. Es decir, considera, por ejemplo, que la UE no impide de manera efectiva la compra de productos a economías donde no se respetan las normas laborales básicas.

La Casa Blanca calcula que la nueva represalia comercial, alcanzará al 99% del comercio estadounidense. Trump aprueba esta nueva ronda de gravámenes a la importación para mantener el muro arancelario. Se basa en el artículo 301 de la Ley de Comercio de 1970, que le permite establecer medidas compensatorias a países que incurran en prácticas comerciales injustificables o discriminatorias. Con esta decisión, además, reaviva la guerra comercial en uno de los momentos más complejos de su segundo mandato, cuando la guerra de Irán parece haber entrado en un callejón sin salida y las encuestas revelan el creciente descontento de los estadounidenses con sus políticas.

Cruzada comercial

Pese a todo, Trump persiste en su cruzada comercial. Fue uno de los principales argumentos de la campaña electoral que lo aupó de vuelta a la Casa Blanca. Y fue una de las medidas más controvertidas en el arranque de la legislatura. El 2 de abril de 2025, una jornada que bautizó como el Día de la Liberación, propinó un puñetazo sobre el tablero geopolítico mundial y echó por tierra años de globalización, diplomacia y relaciones comerciales. Abrió una nueva era en el comercio mundial con aranceles indiscriminados a todo el planeta. Los mercados globales entraron en pánico y, aunque el miedo a que la volatilidad derivada en una crisis les obligara a ponerlos en cuarentena y renegociarlos con sus socios comerciales, ya había cambiado las reglas del comercio mundial.

El Tribunal Supremo de Estados Unidos escribió otro capítulo de esta guerra comercial. El pasado enero declaró inconstitucionales los aranceles recíprocos porque fueron aprobados eludiendo el control del Congreso y sin armazón legal oportuno. La Corte concluyó que Trump se había extralimitado al basarse en la Ley de Poderes de Emergencia (IEEPA), una norma de 1977 aprobada para otros fines.

Para evitar la humillación y que el muro arancelario que había levantado se derrumbara, Trump anunció unos días más tarde una nueva ronda de aranceles. Invocó el capítulo 122 de la Ley de Comercio, de 1974, para establecer un arancel universal del 10%. Pero esta medida comercial tenía una vigencia de solo 150 días, salvo que fuera avalada por el Congreso, algo que no ha ocurrido en un país dividido y a cuatro meses de unas elecciones de mitad de mandato, decisivas para definir el legado y los límites del poder del presidente.

Arma de negociación

El promotor inmobiliario que se hizo famoso en programas de televisión ha esgrimido los aranceles como arma de negociación diplomática. Ha amenazado con ellos a múltiples países bajo los pretextos más peregrinos. Desde un grupo de países que se alinearon con Dinamarca para evitar las ansias expansionistas de Trump en Groenlandia, hasta Canadá por los humos de los incendios al cielo estadounidense.

Trump también amenazó a España con aranceles por no aumentar el gasto en defensa, pero Washington no puede fijar tasas individuales a países de la Unión Europea sin negociarlas antes con el ejecutivo comunitario. También advirtió que impondría un arancel del 100% a aquellos países europeos que aprobaran el impuesto sobre determinados servicios digitales, conocida como tasa Google, que perjudica a las grandes tecnológicas estadounidenses. Tampoco le resultará fácil. Tendrá que buscar otra vía alternativa a la escogida para esta última ronda de aranceles.

El capítulo 301

La Casa Blanca era consciente de que no lograría el aval del Congreso para extender el arancel universal del 10%, así que buscó otro resquicio legal para mantener el muro comercial. Recurrió al artículo 301 de la Ley de Comercio de 1970, que permite imponer aranceles a países que incurran en prácticas “desleales, injustificables o discriminatorias”.

Esta norma obliga a realizar unas investigaciones previas que justifiquen la represalia comercial, así que el secretario de Comercio estadounidense, Jamieson Greer, abrió dos expedientes. Uno a 60 socios que supuestamente no se preocuparon de tomar suficientes medidas para controlar las importaciones producidas mediante trabajo forzoso; y otro a 16 países a los que acusa de sobreproducción, una práctica que tira los precios y perjudica a los productores nacionales. La Administración estadounidense esgrime el primer expediente basado en el capítulo 301 para establecer ahora los gravámenes de entre el 10% y el 12,5% a 60 países.

Analistas y expertos ya esperaban la nueva ofensiva comercial porque se acercaba la fecha de caducidad del arancel universal. De hecho, en las últimas dos semanas, Trump ya impuso un arancel del 50% a un amplio catálogo de productos importados de Canadá, como los materiales de automoción, bebidas alcohólicas, productos lácteos, muebles y textiles, entre otros. Además, estableció un impuesto del 25% a Brasil y acusó al presidente Lula da Silva de afrontar la negociación comercial con “mala fé”.

La nueva remesa de aranceles refleja el esfuerzo de Trump por cambiar las reglas del comercio mundial. Son un símbolo de su política proteccionista y aunque el presidente alega que están destinados a corregir los desequilibrios comerciales, en realidad son una fuente de recaudación para un país que acumula déficits públicos constantes y una deuda pública desbocada.

Se producen, además, en medio de la negociación del Tratado de Libre Comercio entre Estados Unidos, México y Canadá (TMEC), firmado en 2020 y cuya revisión se inició hace unas semanas. Washington quiere remodelar el pacto comercial para lograr más ventajas sobre sus vecinos y en la negociación amenaza con los aranceles. No obstante, se espera que la nueva oleada impositiva incluya exenciones para los bienes comercializados en virtud del TMEC, algo que supondría un alivio para dos de los mayores socios comerciales de Estados Unidos.

El mandatario republicano persiste en su apuesta por los aranceles pese a que los tribunales le están tumbando casi todas sus propuestas. El pasado enero, el Supremo declaró ilegales los aranceles recíprocos. Dos meses después, el Tribunal de Comercio de Estados Unidos hizo lo propio con la tasa universal del 10%, aunque otro tribunal de apelaciones los mantuvo vigentes mientras se resolvían los recursos. Se espera que decenas de empresas también recurran a esta nueva arremetida comercial pese a los esfuerzos de la Administración Trump de vestirlos de una legalidad impoluta.

World.title: Zapatero, sobre el rescate de Plus Ultra: “No es que no influyera, es que no hablé con nadie”
World.content:
La primera entrevista de José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero —en el programa Mañaneros de TVE— desde que la Audiencia Nacional le imputó por liderar una trama de tráfico de influencias ilícitas, ha dejado escasas novedades de impacto jurídico a pesar de la enorme expectación generada desde el ámbito político, sobre todo, por la incomodidad que su silencio generaba en el PSOE. El propio expresidente del Gobierno ha admitido durante su intervención que, tras dos meses sin explicaciones públicas–más allá de un breve vídeo difundido para declarar su inocencia–, a su delicada situación con la justicia se le ha sumado “un problema paralelo”: su “necesidad” de dar explicaciones porque se lo reclaman amigos y compañeros del partido. Bajo esa premisa, se ha centrado en reiterar en público lo que ya sostuvo a puerta cerrada ante el juez José Luis Calama cuando declaró como investigado el 17 de junio: que ni intervino en el rescate de Plus Ultra, ni planeó la creación de una empresa offshore para camuflar sus ingresos, ni usó a sus hijas de testaferros.

La única novedad la ha aportado sobre las joyas halladas en su despacho, supuestamente valoradas en más de 1,3 millones y sobre las que todavía no ha declarado ante el juez. Según Zapatero, fueron un “regalo de cortesía” cuyo origen no ha querido revelar, pero con el que no persiguió un “incremento patrimonial”. Aunque sí ha reconocido que quizá fue un error aceptarlas.

El día en el que se cumplen 26 años de que su victoria contra todo pronóstico en las primarias que le llevaron a la secretaría general del PSOE, una efeméride que él mismo se ha encargado de recordar, Zapatero se ha afanado en defender su inocencia y se ha quejado en varias ocasiones de que se le están atribuyendo a él y a su familia hechos muy graves sin fundamento. “Las acusaciones hay que probarlas”, ha dicho el exmandatario, visiblemente tenso durante algunos momentos de la entrevista, en la que se ha quejado de de la filtración de sus agendas y de conversaciones personales con su secretaria, Gertrudis Alcázar. “Esto no ha pasado nunca. Se ha visto afectado mi derecho a la intimidad. Tendrá que tener consecuencias [...] No juzgo intenciones de nadie pero las reglas son las que son y todos los derechos afectados en esas filtraciones son los hiperprotegidos en la Constitución”, ha señalado.

Su intervención televisada llega 48 horas después de la declaración como investigado de su amigo Julio Martínez Martínez, administrador de la empresa epicentro de la investigación —Análisis Relevante— quien señaló al exmandatario como la persona “que marcaba los pasos a seguir” en el rescate de Plus Ultra. Zapatero lo ha negado: “No hablé con nadie ni de la SEPI ni del Gobierno, ni con ninguna autoridad pública. No es que no influyera, es que no hablé con nadie del rescate de Plus Ultra”, ha dicho el expresidente, que niega el delito de tráfico de influencias que el juez le atribuye. Para que exista este delito, según el Código Penal, no hace falta que se haya ejercido eficazmente esa influencia, basta con que alguien se haya ofrecido a influir a cambio de “dádivas, presentes o cualquier otra remuneración” o se haya aceptado ese “ofrecimiento o promesa”. Además de tráfico de influencias, el instructor considera que la trama en la que supuestamente participó Zapatero incurrió en delitos de organización criminal, apropiación indebida, falsedad documental, blanqueo de capitales, contrabando y contra la Hacienda Pública.

El expresidente no ha querido ahondar en lo declarado ante el juez por Martínez Martínez ni en el escrito que este entregó el lunes en la Audiencia Nacional, en el que situaba al expresidente del Gobierno como el cerebro de esa y todas las operaciones en las que participó Análisis Relevante. “Yo no voy a entrar en la estrategia de defensa de ningún imputado. Me defiendo y reitero las afirmaciones sobre mi nulo papel en el rescate Plus Ultra”, ha afirmado el exdirigente socialista, quien también ha negado con vehemencia que, como sostiene el juez y la Policía, él ideara la constitución de una empresa offshore para desviar el dinero obtenido por un tráfico de influencias ilícito. Esta sospecha, uno de los indicios en los que los investigadores sostienen la acusación de delito fiscal contra el expresidente, es, según Zapatero, “una invención absoluta o un error”. “Pero es un elemento de cargo que se me imputa. Los hechos son los que son y quien acusa tiene que probar”, ha lamentado de nuevo.

Zapatero ha insistido en situarse como un mero consultor externo de la empresa y ha negado haberse aprovechado de forma irregular de sus contactos políticos. “Es evidente que los clientes de esa consultora podían entender que el consultor era yo, pero todo mi trabajo fue de asesoría, de asesoramiento. Nunca ni tuve intención ni participé en ninguna sociedad, ni firmé ningún contrato con ningún cliente”, ha asegurado Zapatero, quien ha explicado que la empresa la constituyeron Martínez Martínez y otros socios (Sergio Sánchez, amigo del expresidente) y él “aceptó” ser consultor. “Me parece normal percibir retribuciones por ese trabajo”, ha señalado el expresidente, que sostiene que todos sus trabajos están declarados en el impuesto del IRPF. “Lo voy a demostrar”, ha dicho.

Tampoco es verdad,afirma, que él avisara a Martínez Martínez y a los responsables de Plus Ultra de que la SEPI iba a conceder el rescate a la compañía 11 días antes de que se aprobara la ayuda. “Lo niego. Yo no sabía lo que iba a hacer el consejo de la SEPI. No intervine en nada, no lo supe y esa es la verdad. A partir de ahí, [Martínez Martínez] en su derecho a la defensa puede esgrimir lo que quiera”, ha reiterado haciendo referencia a lo declarado por su amigo, del que no ha querido renegar después de que le haya señalado ante la justicia. “Es una amistad de hace años y no va con mi código de conducta. Hay que separar las relaciones del procedimiento judicial, no va conmigo renegar de que he tenido una amistad dilatada en el tiempo con él”.

El exmandatario sí admite que llamó al vicepresidente del Banco Santander, Juan Manuel Cendoya, para pedirle que atendiera a los directivos de la aerolínea, que buscaban acceder a un crédito ICO antes de que empezara a tramitarse el rescate público. Según Zapatero, lo que él hizo fue “simplemente facilitar un contacto”. “Llamé a ese directivo [del Santander] para ver si podía recibir a unas personas. Me llegan peticiones de ese tipo todos los días. Todavía hoy. Vamos a llegar a la locura de que llamar a alguien, reunirse con alguien, es ejercer una influencia”, ha lamentado. Esa es la única gestión a favor de la aerolínea que asegura haber hecho Zapatero, que niega haber llamado a José Luis Escrivá, cuando este era ministro de Seguridad Social, para agilizar el rescate: “Ya lo ha negado el propio señor Escrivá. Quien insinúa, quien acusa, tendrá que probarlo”, ha insistido.

Su versión sobre el origen de las joyas halladas durante el registro de su despacho sigue siendo una de las incógnitas del caso porque el expresidente reclamó ante el juez tiempo para reunir la documentación necesaria para acreditar su procedencia. Un mes después de declarar en la Audiencia Nacional, Zapatero no ha dado todavía esas explicaciones, aunque en la entrevista en TVE ha asegurado por primera vez que fueron “un regalo de cortesía personal de hace muchos años”. No obstante, no ha aclarado ni de quién ni de cuándo, con el argumento de que quiere explicárselo primero al juez Calama.

El expresidente ha intentado restar importancia a las joyas y ha asegurado que nunca tuvieron para él y su familia “ni uso ni destino”, por eso no las declaró. El exdirigente socialista admite que el hallazgo de esas joyas “ha sido una circunstancia muy negativa” para él, pero ha recalcado que no las guardó en la caja fuerte “con ningún afán patrimonial” ni de “defraudar”. “Estaban con todas las joyas de nuestra familia y algunos otros regalos”, ha explicado Zapatero, quien afirma que no está de acuerdo con la tasación de 1,3 millones incorporada al sumario y ha asegurado que entregará un contrainforme. “Lo que quiero dejar claro es que ni podíamos imaginar ese valor”, ha afirmado. “¿Fue un error aceptarlas?”, le ha preguntado el periodista Javier Ruiz. “Puede ser”, ha contestado el expresidente, antes de advertir: “No he entrado nunca en una joyería”.

Zapatero ha defendido también el trabajo para Análisis Relevante de la empresa de sus hijas, What The Fav, que recibió supuestamente 3.000 euros al mes por maquetar los informes que hacía el exdirigente socialista en su faceta de consultor. Los investigadores consideran que esos pagos eran una forma de desviar dinero hacia el expresidente del Gobierno con conceptos ficticios, una sospecha que Zapatero ha calificado de “increíble”. “Lo que me faltaba es que por mi cabeza hubiera pasado que mis hijas fueran testaferros de algo”, ha señalado el expresidente, quien ha asegurado que sus hijas van a presentar “todos los contratos y trabajos” que han hecho para Análisis Relevante.

World.title: “Si no tenemos habilidades para tolerar la frustración o para empatizar vamos a tener muchas dificultades en la vida”
World.content:
La psicóloga y conferenciante Patricia Ramírez reflexiona con su hija Carmen Rodríguez sobre la importancia de aprender desde la escuela la gestión de las emociones. Es la primera charla de ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja para debatir sobre la educación que necesitamos

Patricia Ramírez @Patri_Psicóloga Psicóloga, escritora y conferenciante Cuenta con más de 27 años de trayectoria como profesional de la salud, es doctora en Psicología por la Universidad de Granada y dirige una clínica de consultas online Además de ejercer con sus pacientes, lo divulga: tiene más de un millón de seguidores en redes sociales y ha escrito trece libros. En 2024 publicó Cómo tener tiempo para todo (Grijalbo), sobre el impacto del ritmo de vida en el bienestar psicológico Carmen Rodríguez Representante y 'community manager' Tras estudiar Derecho, abandonar unas oposiciones después de dos años y trabajar en un obrador como repostera, decidió dar un giro a su carrera para incorporarse al proyecto de divulgación de su madre, la psicóloga Patricia Ramírez, de la que hoy es representante. Sus cambios laborales le han permitido comprender las inquietudes que comparten muchos jóvenes; la presión académica, las dudas y, en definitiva, la búsqueda de un camino propio

Hay quien regula las emociones con la comida, quien lo hace con horas de scroll infinito frente a un móvil y quien es capaz de gestionarlas de manera saludable. Ese aprendizaje es, para la psicóloga Patricia Ramírez, la esencia de la educación emocional. “Nos permite una mejor tolerancia a la frustración, responsabilizarnos de nuestra vida, tener mejores vínculos con otras personas y un mayor respeto hacia nosotros mismos”. Una herramienta para conectar con la vida, con otras personas y con uno mismo, dice.

“La gente que busca el perfeccionismo nunca está satisfecha con ella misma. Y esto afecta muchísimo a la autoestima”

Para poder desarrollar la educación emocional, la apuesta de Ramírez es que se introduzca desde los primeros años, en las aulas. “Materias como Matemáticas, Física o Geografía son fundamentales, pero, si no tenemos habilidades para tolerar la frustración o empatizar con otra persona, vamos a tener muchas dificultades en la vida”, asegura. Esa es su propuesta para la educación del futuro: “educar en valores desde que los niños son chiquitos: el respeto, el esfuerzo, la justicia, la bondad, el amor, la responsabilidad, la empatía. Los valores son los superpoderes de niños y adolescentes”, cuenta.

“A un adolescente exigente le diría que tiene que crear un espacio para poder comunicar lo que siente; lo bueno y lo malo, sus decisiones, sus dudas”

A Carmen Rodríguez le costó encontrar su vocación. “¿Tú has pensado alguna vez que yo perdía el tiempo?”, le pregunta a Patricia, que le contesta desde la doble perspectiva de madre y psicóloga: “Yo he pensado que estabas explorando diferentes caminos hasta que poco a poco has ido encontrando el tuyo. Y creo que ahí los padres no podemos influiros en qué decisiones tenéis que tomar, porque tú tienes que vivir tu vida, no la vida que un padre o una madre elige para ti”. Una charla que sirve de inspiración para afrontar retos e inquietudes.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: Amsterdam police chief pledges safety ahead of WorldPride
World.content:
Amsterdam police chief Peter Holla opened the COC’s Shakespeare Club at the H’ART Museum on Wednesday, telling dozens of drag queens and drag kings that behind the high heels and the glamour lies a great deal of courage – courage which, he said, “deserves admiration” and “deserves safety”.

The performers arrived by boat from the nearby Stopera, the city hall and opera house complex, at the museum’s jetty on the Amstel, where the ceremony was led by the drag figurehead Dolly Bellefleur.

The Shakespeare Club is a temporary community space run by the LGBTQI+ rights organisation COC Amsterdam. It runs until July 31 and opened three days ahead of WorldPride, the international Pride festival which Amsterdam is hosting for the first time from July 25 to August 8.

“We are a city of tolerance, but it is hard work to actually make that true,” Holla said in his speech, according to the Amsterdam broadcaster AT5. “That affects me and it affects us as Amsterdam police.” Some groups have a harder time than others, he said, and a day like this was a chance to show the force was there for them too.

Holla also set out what the police do for the community, including giving information sessions to refugees from countries where officers are, in his words, “a source of fear”. Officers from Roze in Blauw, the national police network for LGBTIQ+ people, join the Canal Parade as well as Asian Pride, the Trans Pride Walk, and the Trans Diner, he said.

He urged anyone facing intimidation or violence to go to the police. “Reporting is not easy, and many victims are afraid or just want to get on with their lives,” Holla said. “But we really need the information.”

Bellefleur said the speech showed what an unusual country the Netherlands is, because that kind of public backing from the police is rare in other nations.

World.title: “The Dutch are still alive and floating despite all this water”
World.content:
Originally from Venezuela, Eduardo Petit has lived in the Netherlands for over two decades. He currently works as a legal counsel in Amsterdam, enjoys the city’s beer bars, and would love to have Herman van Veen sing at his wedding.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I came over to study in 2004. None of my former bosses could believe that I was making the decision to go to the Netherlands. I still remember one of them asking me, “Are you really going to study law in a non-English-speaking country?” They didn’t understand at all. The Netherlands isn’t a destination for many people from Venezuela.

I couldn’t convince them or any of the other people surrounding me at that moment in my life, but I was convinced it was the right decision. I wanted to encounter a culture that was very different from my own and very attractive to me.

But I considered the Netherlands as my entry to Europe. I had no intention of staying here. Towards the end of my master’s, I thought about moving to Switzerland. I even studied French for it, but that didn’t happen, and here I am over 21 years later.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

I guess I’m a staypat and a dreamer. A staypat is an expat who comes to another country and stays. I added dreamer because I’ve always dreamt that I’ll leave the Netherlands, but the deadline has never been clear. Perhaps there is a reason for that?

How long do you plan to stay?

I’m not planning to leave. I’ve never had a timeline, except at the beginning. Back then, I thought I would stay a few years. Now all these years later, there is no deadline. Who knows when I’ll actually leave? I guess time is wise and will indicate the path, but I don’t see myself staying here until I retire. I think I would rather go to a warmer place, which is my idea with my girlfriend.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

I do, but I think that learning Dutch, especially if you live in a big city like Amsterdam, is a never-ending story. There’s still so much to learn, even if you live here for many years, because there are so many different ways to say things. There are street words and slang. That’s been my experience.

I took courses, but my best learning method was my personal relationships. I had a long relationship with a Dutch girl. If there’s one thing I have to be thankful for from that relationship, it’s that she was patient with me and with this process of learning. Her and her family really helped; just sitting there at the table with them and listening. After one or two years, I started to understand what was going on.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

Biking. You can use a bike for everything here, even dating. You can ride a bike to the place, have the date, and then use the bike to get back. That’s pretty much my favourite Dutch thing, the ease of being able to pretty much live your whole life on a bike.

How Dutch have you become?

I’m now 46. That means I’ve spent about half of my life in this country. I tend to say 30% of me is Dutch. Why not more? Because there’s still a big portion of me that is international and that is Latin. I see and feel things differently. I see myself differently than the locals do.

As for the 30% that’s Dutch, I’m way more balanced with my views. I’m more concise and right to the point when it comes to business and virtually any other type of subject. I like to get to the point and there’s not much of that in the Latin world. In the Latin world, it’s more about storytelling. That’s what the conversations are like there.

People tell me I’m more Dutch, even my own family and Latin friends. I now really like planning. I’m not obsessed, but I like having a plan. It still eats at me sometimes because I love the spontaneous Latin way of life, but this is just how things work here, even on my weekends. Why do I have to plan everything for a weekend?

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Willem Drees. He was a politician and the prime minister of the Netherlands after World War II. The most important thing about him was the reconstruction of the country after the war and his social policies. He was a social democrat and one of his policies was to pool money and create the pension system.

He had a pragmatic view and realised that not everything was possible. He knew we could dream of a beautiful ideological society, but it could only be built slowly and step by step. I think his views and the way he went about his policies made him a very interesting man.

Herman van Veen. His voice made me believe that singing in Dutch can be beautiful. I never thought that was going to be possible, but then I heard his music. Another reason I would like to meet him is to invite him to sing at my wedding.

Johan Cruyff. He was a great footballer and a businessman. He helped build up the Barcelona club, but there’s also all the things he said. They were very simple and funny. I wish I could meet with him, have a beer, and just listen to him and laugh.

What’s your top tourist tip?

When I have friends visiting, I sometimes like to take them to the beer bars, but not the ones everyone knows about. I take them to the ones I call the hidden jewels, the small ones where there aren’t too many tourists.

I often tell people to get lost in Amsterdam or at least get out of the Red Light District. Go to Amsterdam-Noord, for example. It’s booming and there’s a lot going on there. There’s NDSM, the street art museum, and all the graffitti. It’s all amazing and different from other parts of the city. It has a contemporary landscape.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

How the Dutch are still alive despite all this water and how they’ve kept floating after so many years. That’s something I admire. It all works because, here we are, especially with the old houses. I live in one of them in the centre of Amsterdam. For me, it’s amazing that we can live here with all this water.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

I would go to the places where something interesting happened to me over these past 21 years. I would go check on the cinema I love the most, the Eye Film Museum. It’s beautiful and I could watch the sunset from there.

I would also want to go on a beer tour to all the places where I have great memories. In De Wildeman is one I would put on the list. Café In ’t Aepjen is another and it has amazing stories and history. I would also want to get some herring. I like herring, funnily enough.

Eduardo was talk to Brandon Hartley. You can learn more about Bucare Consultancy, Eduardo’s consultancy firm, on its website. You can also connect with him via his LinkedIn profile.

World.title: Rising costs force Amsterdam’s Kwaku festival to change
World.content:
Due to rising costs and regulatory pressure, this year’s Amsterdam Kwaku Summer Festival will be the last in its current form, its organizers have said.

“Kwaku is more than a festival – it is a unique social phenomenon that has traditionally meant a great deal to many people,” the organisation said in a press release, describing the move as a difficult decision.

“Stricter permit conditions, rising costs and increasing organisational complexity make it increasingly difficult to keep the festival affordable and accessible for everyone for whom it is actually intended. The organisation feels compelled to acknowledge that the balance in the current setup can no longer be maintained.”

“A shame”

“It’s a shame,” Zuidoost resident Alexandar Petrovic told DutchNews. “It’s a nice, big festival with great music and good times. There’s no money for that, but there is to buy F-35 fighter jets from the American military?”

Initially started as a football tournament in 1975 in the multicultural Bijlmer neighbourhood of the city’s Zuidoost, Kwaku grew into a festival with more than 120,000 visitors annually.

This year’s edition will go ahead as planned at Amsterdam’s Nelson Mandela Park in the weekends up until August 1 and 2. Featured acts include En Vogue, Kassav, Broederliefde and Dutch jazz legend Trijntje Oosterhuis.

Kwaku is consulting with local city officials to see if it’s possible to hold a different version of the festival in the coming years instead of closing down completely. Other festivals in the country are also struggling to stay afloat for similar reasons.

World.title: Unproven policy means less care for young women in crisis
World.content:
A growing group of young women with severe mental illness are getting stuck in the Dutch mental health system, and several clinics are responding by deliberately treating them less, an investigation by current affairs programme Nieuwsuur has found.

The women, estimated to number in the hundreds and aged between 15 and 30, have serious problems including chronic suicidal thoughts, self-harm and eating disorders, for which existing treatments are not working well enough.

Many are of average or above-average intelligence and struggle with perfectionism and a fear of failing or of not meeting social expectations, said Daan Creemers, a professor specialising in suicidality in adolescents.

When no treatment helps, several institutions turn to an approach known as Autonomie Bevorderend Beleid, or autonomy-promoting policy, under which women who ask for help do not always get it – including when they ask to be admitted. The aim is to break a cycle of repeated crises and admissions and give patients back control over their own lives.

“At a certain point you end up in a pattern in which we, as clinicians, feel held hostage,” Creemers told the programme, saying the policy is intended to return responsibility for young people’s safety to them.

There is no guideline for the approach and no scientific evidence that it works. The patients’ organisation MIND raised the alarm 18 months ago after receiving more than 100 negative accounts from people who said they felt neglected, and reported that in many cases the policy did not reduce suicidal thoughts and sometimes made them worse.

The parents of a 24-year-old woman from Eindhoven who took her own life in 2024, hours after being refused help at a clinic under the policy, have begun disciplinary proceedings. The case has not yet been decided.

MIND says it is not against the policy in principle, but that it should not be used until it is properly applied. The organisation has written to the health ministry calling for urgent research into the group. Creemers said the approach requires stable teams and the same clinicians over long periods, which staff turnover makes difficult.

If you or someone close to you is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. In the Netherlands, call 113 or 0800-0113 (free) for 24/7 support, or visit 113.nl, where the chat service is available in English.

World.title: Highly contagious impetigo infection on the rise among children
World.content:
The highly contagious skin infection impetigo is on the rise on among Dutch children, with 2026 seeing more cases than in previous years.

For every 100,000 children, there have been a reported 350 to 400 children with the infection in the past three weeks compared to below 300 cases in previous years, according to research institute Nivel and based on data from GPs.

The infection, known as krentenbaard (currant beard) in Dutch, is mostly seen around the nose and mouth of young children, who develop red spots, bumps and blisters with a puss-like fluid that forms a crust when scratched.

The national public health institute RIVM advises parents to prevent their children from scratching the itchy and burning blisters and to have them routinely wash their hands with soap and water.

Impetigo, which is more common in the warm summer months, is caused by bacteria but can be treated with an antibiotic ointment. But because many people don’t seek medical help for its mild symptoms that often heal on their own, it’s difficult to assess how often it occurs.

According to Nivel, this year’s peaks coincide with the higher temperatures reported by the national weather institute KNMI.

World.title: Summery weather until Sunday, up to 29° in the southeast
World.content:
The Netherlands is in for a run of summery weather, with temperatures climbing towards the weekend before showers arrive on Sunday, weather service Weeronline said.

Thursday will bring clouds with the odd light shower, though most places will stay dry, and the clouds should break up in the afternoon to give some sunshine. Maximum temperatures will be between 18° and 24°.

Saturday will be the warmest day, staying dry for much of the time with sunny spells. A moderate west to northwesterly wind will keep the coast cooler, at 20° to 24°, while inland reaches 25° to 28° and the southeast up to 29°. There is a chance of a shower on the northern coast in the afternoon and evening.

Showers are expected more widely on Sunday, mainly in the afternoon, with temperatures back to between 20° and 24°. Next week brings a mix of showers and dry, sunny spells, with Monday between 19° and 24°.

World.title: Ali B cancels talk amid fears of media spectacle
World.content:
Rapper and convicted rapist Ali B has pulled out of a business event where he was supposed to be speaking on Thursday in Vinkeveen. The Missing Pieces entrepreneurial event has also been postponed until a later date.

“Due to the exceptionally large number of media applications for the Missing Pieces event, the evening is in danger of becoming a media spectacle. That is at odds with what this meeting is meant for,” reads a joint statement by the rapper and Missing Pieces on the latter’s website. “Therefore, we [Missing Pieces and Ali] have jointly decided to move the event.”

Ali B, or Ali Bouali, was booked, said the website, to speak about “why most entrepreneurs do not break through, despite their talent”.

But following Ali B’s three-year sentence for two rapes in May, including the 2014 rape of Dutch singer Ellen ten Damme, the resulting media interest made the event untenable, Missing Pieces said.

“The whole point was for the evening to be about entrepreneurship, without his personal situation being up for discussion,” reads the joint statement. “Due to the scale of the media attention, it is not feasible at this time.”

The activist group Dolle Mina had also announced a protest at The Harbour Club in Vinkeveen, where the event was scheduled to take place.

The 44-year-old rapper, who has denied all the charges, has appealed to the Supreme Court against the verdict – the highest form of appeal. Ali B has remained free for the years it’s taken his case to wend its way through the courts and will remain so while his appeal is ongoing.

Ticket holders will be able to attend the rescheduled event or get their money back.

World.title: Erasmus Bridge reopens after Rotterdam tram collision
World.content:
The Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam reopened to all traffic on Wednesday evening after the two badly damaged trams which collided on it that morning were lifted clear of the tracks, broadcaster NOS reported. Trams are running over the bridge again.

Fifteen people were injured, one of them seriously, when a moving tram ran into the back of a stationary one waiting for the bridge to close, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported.

The salvage operation took most of the day, with the trams having to be cut apart, RET director Linda Boot told the broadcaster.

Three investigations are now under way. Police are examining the crash, including with a drone team, transport company RET is carrying out its own inquiry, and the Dutch Safety Board has begun a preliminary investigation to decide whether to open a full one.

RET said initial checks showed the driver of the rear tram had not been under the influence of alcohol or drugs. He was among those taken to hospital. Boot said it was too early to speculate about the cause.

Rotterdam mayor Carola Schouten visited the scene and called it “a terrible accident”. No further information has been released about the condition of those hurt.

World.title: Poland appoints new human rights commissioner

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has chosen Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram as Poland’s new human rights commissioner. She will take office after the five-year term of the incumbent, Marcin Wiącek, expires today. Gregorczyk-Abram is a prominent lawyer and activist, who is particularly well known for opposing the overhaul of the judiciary by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. PiS, which is now the main opposition party, strongly opposed her election, arguing that she is politically aligned with the current, more liberal government. Gregorczyk-Abram herself, however, has pledged to “put all my beliefs and views aside” when she takes up the new role. Senat wyraził zgodę na powołanie Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram na Rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich. pic.twitter.com/gz3rwGy3hi — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) July 22, 2026 The commissioner for human rights (widely known by its Polish initials, RPO) is appointed by a resolution of the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, with the consent of the upper-house Senate. Candidates must meet certain requirements, including not belonging to any political party and having legal expertise and relevant experience. As well as acting as a watchdog for human rights, the RPO also has the power to submit motions to the Constitutional Tribunal to assess the constitutionality of laws and to file so-called cassation appeals to the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative Court against rulings by lower courts. Poland’s human rights commissioner has written to the government expressing concern that a "temporary" ban on asylum claims by most migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus remains in place after more than a year https://t.co/9SA2TypQdK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Gregorczyk-Abram was last month nominated as a candidate to be the new RPO by the main ruling party, Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), along with one of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica). PiS proposed a rival candidate, Adam Borowski, a veteran of Poland’s anti-communist struggle in the 1980s. However, critics argued that Borowski, an activist and former PiS election candidate, does not appear to have the requisite legal knowledge and experience. In a Sejm vote last Friday, the ruling coalition supported Gregorczyk-Abram, who won 233 votes to Borowski’s 177. On Wednesday, her candidacy was also supported by the Senate, with 59 votes in favour and 25 against, confirming that she will become the new RPO. Gregorczyk-Abram is best known as one of the founders and leaders of the Free Courts (Wolne Sądy) initiative launched in 2017 amid a wave of protests against the then-PiS government’s efforts to take greater control over the judiciary. Free Courts was prominent in efforts to defend the rule of law. Many of its leading figures are now associated with the current ruling coalition: Maria Ejchart is a deputy justice minister, while Michał Wawrykiewicz is a member of the European Parliament representing KO. In April last year, Gregorczyk-Abram was made chairwoman of a commission established by the current government to look into cases of abuse of power against civil society under the former PiS administration. In September, her commission published its first findings, in which it said that public media outlets under PiS control had “carried out systematic repressive and defamatory actions against activists, non-governmental organisations, and civil society”. Poland's public media “carried out systematic repressive actions against activists, NGOs and civil society” during the rule of the former PiS government, a report commissioned by the new government has found https://t.co/S2MO9KGssC — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2025 PiS argues that Gregorczyk-Abram’s previous activity makes her unsuitable as a suitable candidate for RPO, which is meant to be a non-partisan role. They also point to claims that she was involved in a group of legal figures that discussed the Tusk government’s controversial takeover of public media in December 2023. “[She] is a discredited and extremely politicised person who should be brought to justice, and not receive the laurels of the commissioner for human rights,” former PiS justice minister Marcin Warchoł told the Do Rzeczy weekly last month. After a Sejm committee hearing on Gregorczyk-Abram’s candidacy earlier this month, former PiS deputy justice minister Sebastian Kaleta criticised her for ignoring questions over her alleged “role in the illegal takeover of public media”. Zadałem Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram serię pytań o jej działania i możliwe spotkania z Ewą Wrzosek w sprawie przejęcia TVP, w tym możliwego tworzenia dokumentów prokuratorskich w prywatnej kancelarii. Kandydatka ostentacyjnie zdecydowała się ignorować te pytania. Ma bardzo dużo do… — Sebastian Kaleta (@sjkaleta) July 15, 2026 Speaking to state broadcaster TVP on Wednesday after her appointment was confirmed by the Senate, Gregorczyk-Abram declared that, “from the moment I take the oath and assume the position of commissioner, I will be independent and sovereign”. She pledged to “put all my beliefs and views – because each of us has them – aside and become an advocate for all citizens, regardless of what they believe in, how they live, or who they vote for”. Gregorczyk-Abram said that among her priorities as RPO would be the justice system, supporting the rights of disabled people and their carers, protecting older people, and fighting hate speech. With regard to the last of these issues, she noted that certain politicians present some groups as “enemies”, pointing to how this previously happened with LGBT+ people and judges, and is now being directed towards Ukrainians. Those are all groups who have at various stages been targeted by PiS and other right-wing parties. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS.
