World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018813/China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.title: China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018813/China’s Bank Wealth Products Face Scrutiny Over Yield Displays
World.content:
One wealth management product advertised annualized returns above 3% but delivered a loss. A “stable, low-volatility” investment began declining the day after purchase. Other wealth management offerings highlighted their strongest short-term yields, making it harder for investors to assess their actual performance.

The cases were among those highlighted in a recent investigation by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, which found that some institutions continue to showcase selective short-term returns despite tighter regulatory scrutiny.

By the end of the first quarter this year, the number of bank wealth management investors in China had reached 148 million, while 48,000 products were available on the market, up 18.23% from a year earlier.

According to Xinhua, while regulators have curbed overt “ranking chasing” — the practice of inflating yields to improve performance rankings — some wealth management institutions continue to rely on selective performance displays.

The probe found that even products from the same bank may use different periods to calculate annualized returns, with some showing one-month figures and others three-month figures, making comparisons difficult for investors.

Lin Xiaoyuan told Xinhua that she bought a three-month holding-period product advertised with an annualized return above 3%. When it matured, the investment had posted a loss.

Another investor, surnamed Chen, said a bank wealth manager promoted a six-month “low-volatility” product as a “stellar performer.” But the investment began losing value on the day his purchase was confirmed and continued declining for the following month.

Xinhua also reviewed product pages on bank apps and found discrepancies between promotional displays and recent performance figures. One product page highlighted a “positive annual return since inception” and a cumulative return of 10.18%, while further data showed annualized losses over both the previous three-month and one-month periods.

An insider at a bank wealth management firm told Xinhua, “If everyone else is showing 4% or 5%, how can we sell ours if we show the real number?”

The probe also found that some banks use inconsistent metrics to display yields, with products from the same institution sometimes showing annualized returns calculated over different periods.

“This kind of selective disclosure is a key reason investors are being misled,” said Wang Pengbo, a senior analyst at market consultancy Botong Analysys. He added that banks often highlight their strongest short-term figures on homepages and pop-ups, making it difficult for ordinary investors to assess a product’s actual risk and return without digging through the fine print.

In December 2025, the National Financial Regulatory Administration issued rules aimed at curbing misleading performance disclosures, including selective reporting and inconsistent presentation of returns.

Such practices violate both net-value management requirements under China’s asset management regulations and the principle of fair market pricing, Wang added.

Regulators have also targeted wealth management products that use short-term returns to influence performance rankings and attract investors. Xinhua reported that selective yield presentation remains an issue despite the regulatory focus.

Experts advised investors to look beyond short-term rankings, examine longer-term performance, compare returns with benchmarks, and consider volatility alongside headline yields.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: TotalImage/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.title: China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018804/China’s Changing Climate May Be Why Your Garlic Is Moldy
World.content:
You may have had this experience. It’s dinnertime. You peel a clove of garlic and notice a small greenish-gray patch. Do you cut it away or toss the clove and reach for another? It’s a small annoyance that won’t derail your dinner, but, if social media posts are any indication, it’s an annoyance that is happening across the world, with users saying they are noticing it more and more.

It is also a reminder that food quality is shaped long before an ingredient reaches the cutting board. Garlic’s journey often begins in China, the world’s largest garlic producer and exporter, accounting for more than 70% of global production. When the kind of extreme or unusual weather made more common by climate change affects China’s garlic-growing regions, the consequences can travel well beyond the field, reaching processors, warehouses, supermarkets, and kitchens around the world.

In the garlic-producing provinces of Shandong and Jiangsu in the east, and Henan in central China, garlic is planted in the fall. Farmers will break up the soil to create crop rows, separate and select cloves, then press them, one by one, pointy-side up, into the soil. Then, after the cloves are covered with more dirt, watered, and mulched with plastic, they embark on several months of exposure to changing temperatures and moisture conditions.

The timing for this process needs to be exact. Plant too early, and the young sprouts might overdevelop, draining energy. Too late, and the plant doesn’t develop enough. In both cases, it might not be able to defend itself against diseases and the winter cold.

After planting, garlic must undergo a period of cold to initiate a process called vernalization. Only after prolonged exposure to low temperatures will the plants successfully develop bulbs — the cluster of garlic cloves. Vernalization typically requires a temperature range of 0 to 10 degrees Celsius for at least three weeks. Too much cold will harm the garlic; too little will disrupt the plant’s maturation.

Weather extremes can upset this process. In the fall of 2025, for example, excessive rainfall across northern China delayed garlic planting by about three to six weeks. The winter that followed was mild, and as a result, government data show, the garlic harvested in Shandong continued to grow during a period when no growth should have occurred.

Though this period of extra growth, in some ways, made up for the season’s late planting, this additional early-stage growth may have affected resource allocation within the plant. For example, it can cause the bulbs’ side buds — which later become cloves — to develop their own leaves instead of growing in size.

When the seasons change to spring and the world begins to bloom, a slender flower stalk begins to bolt from the center of the garlic plant. This flower stalk, known as a garlic scape, is a beloved vegetable in Chinese cuisine, often stir-fried with meat, eggs, or tofu. For the farmers, garlic scapes are a lifeline, as they represent the first opportunity to turn a profit in the garlic farming season. Large, high-quality garlic scapes can provide needed revenue to cover the costs of seasonal workers, farm supplies, and farm management for the rest of the season. Harvesting scapes also leaves more resources for the developing bulb.

However, the harvest window for garlic scapes is extremely short, often lasting for only one or two weeks. If the scapes are not harvested in time, they become old and lose much of their market value, and harvesting them relies heavily on human labor. Usually, different regions reach their harvesting season at different dates, allowing workers to move from one area to the next.

In many garlic-growing regions, this year’s spring was warmer than usual. When that happens, harvesting timelines start to overlap, tightening the labor market and placing additional strain on procurement and distribution. At this point, the farmers face the difficult decision of whether to pay more to harvest their garlic scapes or let them continue to grow, potentially affecting the quality of their bulb harvest later in the season. News stories about the pressures Chinese garlic farmers faced earlier this year spawned the social media meme, “Got garlic scapes, any takers?”

In early summer, the aboveground structures of the garlic plant begin to shrivel, while the belowground bulbs enter their prime harvest period. In northern China, farmers will bind harvested garlic into bunches and lay them out to dry in the sun. The dried skin encasing the bulb acts as a jacket, protecting it from damage, moisture fluctuations, and mold during sorting, storage, and shipping.

Global warming has caused China’s rain belt to shift northward, leading to record rainfall in northern China. If the main harvest period is hit by persistent rain, the garlic skin can get damaged, and both soil moisture and air humidity rise. Bulbs may not fully dry, and damaged outer skins can both cause garlic to sprout more leaves and make it more vulnerable to fungal growth. While a moldy bulb at the supermarket can also result from mistakes during storage and transport, a rainy harvest amplifies those risks.

The China Meteorological Administration’s Bluebook on Climate Change in China, published last year, states that, as warming continues, China is experiencing changes in precipitation patterns and extreme weather risks. This doesn’t mean climate change can be cited as the direct cause of every heavy rainfall event or every below-standard bulb of garlic; it means farmers, traders, and meteorological services must plan for more unstable combinations of heat, rain, humidity, drought, and winter warmth.

Given the large areas used to grow garlic, it’s not feasible to use greenhouses to shield it from the elements. The real test of adaptation will come from recognizing risks earlier, forecasting with more accuracy, and responding more quickly. Accurate and precise weather reporting is of the utmost importance. According to the China Meteorological Administration, Shandong’s garlic-growing Jinxiang County has created a specialized garlic meteorological service team to provide weather support throughout the production cycle.

The fate of a single bulb of garlic may seem inconsequential — but in reality, it is a signal of something larger. Climate change doesn’t just affect the far-off polar ice caps, and it isn’t just the stories of climate disasters filling our televisions. It may already be sitting on our dinner tables. These changes will not stop at the garlic bulb, but with each accurate forecast, each planting decision, and each decision to harvest, we are gradually building our ability to respond. Viewed in this way, this single bulb of garlic is a microcosm of the ongoing negotiations between humans and our climate.

Translator: Cynthia Lin.

(Header image: A farmer sorts garlic harvested from a field in Yongji, Shanxi province, May 24, 2026. Liu Baocheng/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.title: China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018801/China’s Summer Hit Recasts the Eight Immortals as Con Artists
World.content:
Before they were immortals, they were scammers.

That’s the irreverent premise behind “All Wishes Come True!,” a new Chinese animated comedy that has turned a band of mythological figures from Taoist legend into a summer box-office hit.

Released July 18, the film recasts the Eight Immortals — traditionally symbols of people from all walks of life — as con artists who impersonate gods and deceive worshippers before achieving immortality themselves.

In less than a week, the film has grossed more than 370 million yuan ($51 million), becoming the second highest-grossing domestic animated film of 2026 behind “Boonie Bears: The Hidden Protector.” It also holds an 8.3 rating on Chinese review site Douban, the highest among this summer’s new releases.

The film’s biggest twist unfolds in Penglai, a fairyland where gods and humans coexist under a surprisingly modern bureaucracy governed by an immortals management bureau. Deities are assigned temples, evaluated on performance targets, and ranked on giant leaderboards based on the incense offerings they receive.

Unlike traditional tales of the Eight Immortals’ journey toward enlightenment, the film gives the legendary figures a new beginning: they first appear as schemers targeting the riches of Fu, Lu, and Shou, the three deities of fortune, prosperity, and longevity.

Zhongli Quan, traditionally portrayed as a general who became a Taoist immortal, is reimagined as a con artist who leads the group in impersonating deities. Cao Guojiu, traditionally linked to the Song dynasty (960–1279) imperial court, appears as an official in the immortals management bureau.

After taking over a temple, the group finds itself responsible for granting wishes — and eventually becomes known for catching thieves. Their journey later leads to a clash with the war god Yang Jian.

Director Mu Zhengyang said he designed Penglai as a “first-tier megacity,” where gods and humans operate within a modern social system. “At first, audiences should feel that they’re entering a traditional Eastern fairyland. But once inside, it becomes much more like an amusement park,” he told domestic media.

The film’s character-driven approach also extends to its voice performances. Voice director Chen Hao, who worked on the popular “Ne Zha” films, voices Zhongli Quan, while Tieguai Li’s Chongqing dialect adds regional flavor to the character.

The film’s cultural references have also fueled online discussion. On streaming platform Bilibili, videos decoding more than 100 Easter eggs and hidden details have each attracted nearly one million views.

One widely discussed clue is the Eight Immortals’ temple number — 1350, the same number associated with Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King, in the “Book of Life and Death,” a mythical register of the underworld in “Journey to the West,” hinting at his possible appearance later in the story.

The same reinterpretation has also drawn criticism from some viewers, who argue that the film alters the identities and values associated with traditional mythology.

Yang Jian, for example, traditionally portrayed as a righteous war god who protects ordinary people, is reimagined as a figure willing to sacrifice heaven and humanity to save his mother. The film’s other redesigns have also drawn attention, including Cao Guojiu’s portrayal as an overweight, flamboyant official and Lan Caihe’s depiction as a toddler.

The debate also extends to the film’s portrayal of immortality. Through the line, “Only immortals can do good deeds,” it offers a new interpretation that some viewers praised, while others argued it differs from traditional Taoist ideas of attaining eternal life.

The production team, based in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, said the Eight Immortals offer creative space for reinterpretation because many audiences know their famous stories but are less familiar with their broader legends. The filmmakers said they hoped to introduce the figures to a new generation through a fresh retelling.

“We didn’t want to simply bring the Eight Immortals in front of young audiences and tell the same story again,” producer Ying Xujun told domestic media. “We had to create something new for a new generation.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A poster for “All Wishes Come True!” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

(Header image: A soybean field in Xingkai Lake Farm, Heilongjiang province, 2023. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018790/China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.title: China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018790/China Bans AI Romantic Partners, Virtual Relatives for Minors
World.content:
China’s first regulations on AI companion services have taken effect, setting new limits on chatbots designed to simulate emotional bonds with users and barring platforms from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors.

The rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other government departments in April, came into force July 15. They cover AI products designed to mimic human personalities, emotions, and communication styles.

The measures come after years of growing use of AI companion apps in China, where users have created virtual lovers modeled on TV characters, recreated deceased relatives through customized voices and personalities, and treated chatbots as long-term emotional confidants.

Regulators and state media have warned that such apps carry security and compliance risks, including emotional dependence, sexually suggestive content, and weak protections for minors.

As such, the new regulations prohibit AI apps from generating content for minors that may incite unsafe behavior, trigger extreme emotions, or foster habits that could harm their physical or mental health. They also should not excessively cater to users in ways that induce emotional dependence or addiction and damage their real-life relationships; manipulate users’ emotions to push them toward unreasonable decisions that harm their legitimate rights and interests; and act as virtual relatives or virtual partners to minors.

If a user is believed to be overly reliant on or addicted to a service, the platform must send them a reminder about overuse every two hours.

Zhang Linghan, dean of the Institute of Artificial Intelligence Law at China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media outlet China News Weekly that the emotional investment offered by anthropomorphic interactive services can easily lead to psychological dependence in users, resulting in a decline in real-world social skills, particularly a weakening of the ability to resolve emotional conflicts and build deep relationships.

The new regulations apply to any services deemed as designed to foster emotional connection and interaction. Other AI chatbot functions, such as intelligent customer service, knowledge-sharing tools, and workplace assistants, are not affected.

The same day the regulations went into effect, tech giants ByteDance and Alibaba discontinued their AI companion features on Doubao and Qianwen, respectively. Qianwen shut its companion service down immediately, while Doubao is offering users a three-month grace period to migrate their data to its sister app, Maoxiang, before it is permanently deleted on Oct. 15.

Tech companies had already begun increasing regulations of their chatbots and companion services, primarily due to findings of suggestive content in their chats. On June 30, Tencent removed its AI companion service from its chatbot Yuanbao.

In April 2023, leading Chinese AI model developer MiniMax removed its AI companion product, Glow, from multiple app stores due to pornographic content. Its product manager told domestic media that “80% of users would engage in suggestive or sexually explicit conversations with the AI companions they created within Glow.”

In June 2025, AI chat app Zhumengdao was summoned to appear before the Shanghai Municipal Cyberspace Administration for generating vulgar and suggestive content that harmed minors.

After the new regulations took effect, several other AI chatbots reported an influx of users migrating from Doubao and Qianwen, and began requiring ID verification before use.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Malte Mueller/Getty Creative/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018794/Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.title: Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018794/Between Two Needles: The Chinese Garment Factory Built Around Dialysis
World.content:
GUANGDONG, South China — Above a dialysis clinic in Guangzhou, southern China’s Guangdong province, 67 kidney patients sew, iron and finish garments for customers in China and overseas. Many once worked as chefs, truck drivers or machine technicians before illness pushed them out of their jobs. Three times a week, they leave the factory floor for four hours of dialysis, then return to work.

The workshop was opened in 2023 by Xie Qiang, a retired oncologist who wanted patients to earn an income without hiding their condition. It offers routine, independence and a community of people living with the same illness. But it is also a business struggling to survive. Dialysis interrupts production, inexperienced workers make costly mistakes, and delayed orders threaten already narrow margins.

In June, Sixth Tone followed the workers, managers and Xie as they tried to keep the factory running. Their daily routines show how difficult it is to meet deadlines and maintain quality while making room for dialysis, fatigue and medical complications.

Additional reporting: Jiang Xinyi; story editors: Qi Ya and Apurva; script editors: Apurva and Wu Huiyuan.

World.title: Kiyapo intensifies into tropical storm as it nears extreme Northern Luzon
World.content:
KIYAPO. Satellite image of Tropical Storm Kiyapo (Noul) as of July 24, 2026, 7 am.

Tropical Storm Kiyapo (Noul) is bringing significant rain to Northern Luzon, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms to much of Central Luzon and even Southern Luzon, on Friday, July 24

MANILA, Philippines – Kiyapo strengthened from a tropical depression into a tropical storm at 2 am on Friday, July 24, as its maximum sustained winds increased from 55 kilometers per hour to 65 km/h.

Its gustiness also increased from 70 km/h to 80 km/h, said the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA).

Following its intensification into a tropical storm, Kiyapo was assigned the international name Noul, a name contributed by North Korea which means “red sky.”

As of 7 am on Friday, Kiyapo was already 260 kilometers east of Aparri, Cagayan. It slowed down, moving west at 20 km/h from the previous 30 km/h.

PAGASA expects the tropical storm to pass close to the northeastern portion of mainland Cagayan on Friday morning or afternoon, then pass very close to or make landfall in Cagayan’s Babuyan Islands in the afternoon or evening.

Kiyapo may also strengthen further into a severe tropical storm after passing the Babuyan Islands, followed by potential rapid intensification over the West Philippine Sea, where it could become a typhoon.

Kiyapo is bringing significant rain to Northern Luzon, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms to much of Central Luzon and even Southern Luzon, including Metro Manila and Calabarzon, on Friday.

World.title: Getting the solution right: Statement of PH media orgs, journalists on pending anti-disinformation bills
World.content:
Over 50 media organizations issue a statement rejecting the two consolidated anti-disinformation bills pending in the House and Senate, saying they criminalize individual users when waht is needed is enforcing accountability of social media platforms

MANILA, Philippines – Over 50 media organizations and over 50 journalists have come together to issue a statement about the anti-disinformation bills currently being debated in the Senate and the House of Representatives. The statement was initiated by the Movement for Media Safety PH, a group advocating for the rights and protection of media practitioners in the country. Rappler, among the signatories, is publishing the statement in full, below.

The pending anti-disinformation bills confuse the symptoms with the disease. Instead of addressing the political, economic, and technological systems that manufacture and profit from coordinated information manipulation, they place the burden on individual expression and expand government authority over speech. This threatens democratic freedoms while leaving the real drivers of disinformation largely untouched.

As institutions and individuals whose work depends on verifying facts, exposing falsehoods, and informing the public, we have every reason to support effective measures against disinformation. Journalists are among those who experience firsthand the damage that disinformation inflicts on democratic discourse and public trust. We therefore recognize the urgency of confronting this grave challenge.

We support decisive and effective action against disinformation.

However, we believe the pending anti-disinformation bills (HB 9465 and its equivalent in the Senate) are the wrong response to a real problem.

Rather than moving to dismantle the architecture of disinformation, these measures primarily criminalize expression, expand the State’s authority to regulate speech, and create legal mechanisms that are vulnerable to misuse against journalists, critics, and ordinary citizens. At the same time, they leave largely untouched the opaque algorithms, commercial incentives, coordinated influence operations, and platform structures that enable disinformation to flourish.

In short, the bills risk weakening the constitutional freedoms that sustain democratic accountability without meaningfully addressing the structural causes of information disorder.

Our principal concerns

1. Existing laws already address many harmful acts.

Philippine law already provides remedies for libel, fraud, identity theft, election offenses, cybercrime-related offenses, and other unlawful conduct associated with deception.

Before creating new criminal restrictions on protected expression, Congress should examine whether existing laws are being effectively implemented and how transparency and accountability mechanisms can instead be strengthened.

2. Criminalizing speech is ineffective, fails to address systemic disinformation, and focuses on the small fry

Criminalizing content is a blunt, disproportionate, and ultimately ineffective response that ignores the architectural roots of information disorder.

It functions as a legislative shortcut: while it risks criminalizing individual users – often targeting the “small fry” – it fails to reach the platforms, algorithmic systems, and coordinated networks that manufacture and amplify disinformation at scale.

Furthermore, criminal law is ill-suited to hold the true architects of manipulation accountable; it is notoriously difficult to enforce against extraterritorial entities, and it cannot effectively address the systemic nature of disinformation.

3. The bills fail to provide for meaningful mechanisms for platform accountability.

Digital platforms play a significant role in the amplification of disinformation, yet current legislative proposals focus disproportionately on content removal—a reactive approach that risks censorship while leaving the systems of manipulation untouched.

Platform accountability must move beyond merely forcing companies to suppress speech; it requires establishing clear, enforceable legal mechanisms that address the jurisdictional and operational realities of these entities within the Philippines.

Meaningful accountability demands transparency in recommendation algorithms, political advertising, and the infrastructure behind coordinated inauthentic behavior. Instead of incentivizing platforms to downgrade lawful speech to mitigate their own regulatory liability, the law should mandate independent auditing, standardized disclosure, and robust public oversight.

By shifting the focus from individual content to the technological architecture and the systemic operations that amplify falsehoods, we can address the root of the problem without eroding constitutional freedoms.

4. The bills create legal uncertainty that can easily be abused.

Broad and ambiguous definitions of prohibited speech invite inconsistent interpretation and selective enforcement.

Journalists routinely report on developing stories, disputed claims, whistleblower disclosures, leaked documents, election controversies, corruption allegations, and public health emergencies. These are precisely the situations where facts continue to evolve and public scrutiny is most necessary. Laws affecting expression must therefore be narrowly tailored and clearly defined. Otherwise, they create uncertainty that discourages legitimate journalism and public participation.

5. The bills risk making the State the arbiter of truth.

Government is frequently the subject of investigative reporting and public scrutiny. It cannot simultaneously serve as the ultimate authority on the truthfulness of speech concerning its own actions.

The antidote to falsehood is not government control over expression. It is greater transparency, timely access to public information, independent journalism, and more democratic debate.

A better way forward

Rejecting these bills does not mean accepting disinformation.

On the contrary, we believe the country urgently needs a comprehensive, rights-based strategy that addresses the structural drivers of information disorder rather than merely its visible manifestations.

Congress should instead prioritize measures that:

Strengthen government transparency and pass the Freedom of Information law;

Expose and regulate the financing of coordinated disinformation campaigns and influence-for-hire operations;

Require greater transparency and independent auditing of digital platforms, including political advertising, recommendation systems, and coordinated inauthentic behavior;

Support independent journalism, investigative reporting, and fact-checking initiatives;

Strengthen media and information literacy and digital literacy across schools and communities;

Encourage independent research into the country’s information ecosystem; and

Promote genuine multi-stakeholder collaboration among government, media organizations, civil society, academia, and technology companies while fully respecting constitutional rights.

These measures strengthen society’s resilience against disinformation while preserving the democratic freedoms that enable truth to emerge.

World.title: [ANALYSIS] What’s driving the current Philippine stock market rally?
World.content:
Curiously, foreign investors appear to have been favoring International Container Terminal Services Inc. and Century Pacific Food Inc.

Foreign fund flows often serve as a critical determinant to the stock market’s direction, for they account for over 50% of total value turnover on the average. So, when they enter, the market goes up, and when they exit, the market goes down.

This is exactly what happened in the market’s latest rally in the last two weeks. Foreign investors shifted into the net buying position. The amount they poured in overwhelmed domestic profit-taking. It also enabled the Philippine Stock Exchange Index (PSEi) to break the 6,400 milestone that stubbornly held in the last four months.

Curiously, foreign investors appear to have been favoring Enrique Razon Jr.’s International Container Terminal Services Inc. (ICTSI) and the Po family’s Century Pacific Food Inc. (CNPF), to mention two of their top picks.

ICTSI has been lately the market’s primary engine, pushing the market higher for its high-growth structural expansions. CNPF is actively sought as a defensive consumer hedge against broader macroeconomic uncertainty.

The return of foreign funds to the local market is at the moment being driven, according to analysts, by a shift from cooling US inflation pressures to proactive, hawkish local central bank policies. This combination has incidentally stabilized the local currency and boosted investors’ confidence.

There is reportedly a downward shift in the US June producer price index, which eased global anxieties regarding aggressive US Federal Reserve policy, directly driving capital back into emerging markets like the Philippines. Sentiments were further reinforced by robust international interest in local energy infrastructure, notably highlighted by the massive US$5 billion foreign acquisition proposal for the Lopez family’s Energy Development Corporation (EDC).

The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) for June also slowed significantly to 3.5%, down from 4.2% in May. This cooler-than-expected outcome immediately softened fears of an aggressive, multi-rate hike path from the US Federal Reserve.

Likewise, the US Producer Price Index (PPI) dropped by 0.3% in June. This contraction mitigated long-term policy uncertainties, sparking a global “risk-on” sentiment that redirected institutional capital away from safe-haven US assets and into emerging markets like the Philippines, again.

While global pressures are easing, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) has taken a highly aggressive stance to defend domestic economic stability. To combat stubborn commodity prices, the BSP Monetary Board raised its benchmark reverse repurchase (RRP) rate by 25 basis points to 4.75%.

BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. has explicitly stated that the robust domestic economy can absorb an additional interest rate hike if needed to anchor inflation expectations. This resolute monetary discipline reassures foreign funds that the central bank will not let domestic inflation slip out of control.

In contrast, local price pressures are showing signs of exhaustion. Philippine headline inflation slowed to 6.4% in June from 6.8% in May. While still high, this moderation proves that the BSP’s aggressive rate cycle is successfully cooling the economy, giving foreign investors a clear entry window before prices normalize further.

A primary concern for international fund managers is currency depreciation, which can erode equity gains. The BSP’s higher local interest rates, coupled with resilient overseas remittances, have successfully stabilized the Philippine peso. By creating an attractive interest-rate differential against the US dollar, foreign portfolios face less foreign-exchange risk, making the local bourse a safer location to park capital. (READ: [In This Economy] The peso is now at P60 to the dollar. Now what?)

In addition, foreign capital is actively anchoring on large-cap blue chips such as ICTSI and other conglomerate-heavyweights which are providing a vital psychological safety net as they have successfully absorbed geopolitical shocks stemming from the escalating US-Iran conflict.

Expected Q2 corporate earnings results

A double-digit growth figure is projected in the net income and revenues of ICTSI for the Q2. This builds seamlessly on its Q1 momentum, where net profits surged by 23%, equivalent to US$293.57 million.

Its core drivers for this growth are due to an 11% surge in global container volumes and aggressive, self-funded international hub expansions like the Durban Gateway Terminal in South Africa and Batu Ampar in Indonesia.

Furthermore, a long-term extension of its Melbourne port concession until 2066 reinforces a highly secure, multi-decade cash flow outlook that justifies its aggressive foreign premium buying. At the same time, it could allow ICTSI to easily absorb local macroeconomic pressures.

For CNPF, foreign investors are seeking out CNPF as both a stable and defensive stock play. The company is experiencing parallel double-digit expansions across both its domestic and export markets.

Foreigner investors are utilizing CNPF as a margin cushion. The company’s dollar-denominated export naturally acts as hedge on local input cost adjustments. Conversely, CNPF’s pricing power on grocery shelf essentials also shields its business from broader inflationary shifts.

CNPF’s earnings result for Q2 is scheduled to be reported on August 7, 2026. EPS is estimated to average at P1.82 apiece, based on analysts’ forecasts. In this regard, the company’s executive chairman Christopher Po has expressed that the company expects to sustain a double-digit growth in revenue and profit for the full year despite a challenging year due to supply chain factors.

Prognosis on the market rally

Again, the market’s rally is driven by expectations of an accommodative policy stance from the central bank, attractive valuations, and growing investors’ optimism on corporate earnings results for the second-quarter.

As mentioned earlier, the last time the market broke the 6,400 level was four months ago on February 10, when it closed at 6,474.60.

However, the market fell last Tuesday, July 21, at the 6,333.80 level, down 81.92 points or 1.28% from a market transaction of P7.39 billion, excluding cross transactions. Trading was apparently affected by the rise in oil prices by two digits that took effect within the day. Investors’ sentiments were dampened, as they were reminded of the continuing global risk caused by rising oil prices.

On Wednesday, July 22, the market opened with a strong start in the morning session – surging by as much as 1% before trimming gains – as investor sentiment cooled off by midday to sit at 6,286.55 by the noon recess.

At the end of the day, the market closed at 6,267.85, down 65.59 points or 1.04% on a smaller total value turnover of P5.78 billion, excluding cross transactions. It was apparently affected by the upcoming index methodology changes to be implemented, which would trigger portfolio repositioning.

Asked what he thinks about the current market rally, Jofer Gaite, vice president for sales of B.A. Securities, Inc., was quite straightforward in giving a not-so-encouraging assessment. In his observation, “foreign inflows and retail investors are pushing the market higher, momentarily ignoring the US-Iran noise.” But the headwinds of slower growth, tacky inflation, and elevated interest rates continue to be big challenges to company revenues and profits.

On a technical basis, “the market’s rise is not broad-based but mainly due to ICTSI’s fantastic run.” The market’s value turnover has been also anemic that foreign inflows are “tipping the balance greatly.”

Joel de la Peña, market strategist and chief trader of H.E. Bennett Securities Inc., has a better outlook. While the market is only oversold, incomes of companies are getting better. He likens the current market with what it was in 2013. Investors also started to reposition then, looking for bargain stocks. At that time, dividends were getting better as they are now.

Moreover, while the market is lingering at a low level, he believes that it may soon continue to rise as the economy grows albeit at a low pace due to high inflation.

Even with the market’s two-day consecutive decline, Andro Leo “Andoy” I. Beltran, vice president and head of the Digital Solutions & Investor Engagement Division of First Metro Securities Brokerage Corp. (FirstMetroSec) of the Metrobank Group, has an equally positive assessment about the market’s status.

Over the short term, according to him, investors are once again pricing geopolitical risk, leading to risk-off sentiment – a market environment where investors prioritize capital preservation and avoid volatility due to economic uncertainty or geopolitical fear.

Nevertheless, over the medium to long term, corporate earnings, interest rates, and economic fundamentals will have a much greater influence on where the market will be ultimately.

Stockbroker Rene de los Reyes of Abacus Securities Inc. of Abacus Capital & Investment Corporation group, feels that the market rally is both fundamentally and technically driven. For the longest time, according to their studies, the market has been “ridiculously” undervalued, even though it is at present technically lifted by foreign interest in ICTSI, which has an assigned weight of 27% in the main index.

Deliberately funny, Reuben Mark A. Angeles, first vice-president and Equity Research Division and Customer Experience head of FirstMetroSec of the Metrobank Group, sums the market’s current rally as what he calls “investors’ fatigue on the Middle East issue.”

Come to think of it, one stops being scared at some point in time. Nonetheless, being brave is not enough. He recommends to follow wisely what the foreign investors are doing at the moment: focus on blue-chip conglomerates, steady dividend payers, and resilient consumer brands with high-volume, liquid stocks driven by strong price action, near-term catalysts, or index changes.

Agreeably, the current market is primarily a “reset” driven by bargain hunting, foreign inflows, and relief as oil prices ease from previous Middle East war peaks. However, with the market trading near the 6,400 to 6,450 resistance zone, it will be ultimately sustained by developing macroeconomic triggers where fundamentals will ultimately prevail. – Rappler.com

World.title: Trump assures Marcos: PH’s South China Sea concerns to be ‘taken up’ with Xi
World.content:
TRUMP. US President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before signing two executive orders regarding quantum computing, in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, DC, US, June 22, 2026.

Manila and Beijing have been trading allegations — and protests — after China Coast Guard personnel sailed close to the BRP Sierra Madre, triggering a melee

MANILA, Philippines – US President Donald Trump has assured Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. that he will “take up the concerns of the Philippines” in his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Malacañang said on Thursday night, July 23.

Trump made the commitment to Marcos in a phone call on Thursday, where the two leaders “discussed the current global, economic and security situation,” Palace Communications Secretary Dave Gomez said in a press statement.

Trump and Xi are expected to meet when the latter goes on a US trip in September.

The phone call happened just a day after US State Secretary Marco Rubio met with Marcos and top government officials in Malacañang on July 22. Gomez said that during Rubio’s courtesy call on Marcos, the latter “updated” the US official on “recent incidents in the South China Sea.”

Gomez said the call with Trump was an “offshoot” of Rubio’s Palace call, which was part of his first visit to Manila as state secretary. Rubio was in the Philippines to participate in high-level meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which Manila chairs.

On July 20, or just as foreign ministers from ASEAN and beyond were arriving in Manila for the meetings, China Coast Guard personnel entered Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal, triggering a confrontation with Philippine soldiers posted on the grounded BRP Sierra Madre. A Filipino soldier was wounded in the head and another was also injured, as a result of the melee.

Manila has filed several protests over the incident, which Beijing claims was instigated by Manila.

Hours before his phone call with Trump, Marcos visited the two injured soldiers in Palawan and conferred to them the Order of Lapu-Lapu.

Ayungin Shoal is a low tide elevation that’s part of the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone in an area it calls the West Philippine Sea. China does not recognize the 2016 Arbitral Award, which affirmed the Philippines’ entitlements in those waters, including the validity of its EEZ. Beijing, in fact, claims almost all of the South China Sea, contrary to the award and international law.

The incident was brought up again during Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro’s meeting with China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi. Wang, in return, also protested the incident. Manila and Beijing had earlier summoned each other’s envoys to protest the incident.

The shoal is among the flashpoints of tensions between Manila and Beiing in the South China Sea. In 2024, CCG personnel harassed Filipino soldiers already moored at the base of the ship.

A Filipino soldier lost his thumb from China’s ramming. Navy equipment was also destroyed by the CCG. It was an incident many feared would trigger the Mutual Defense Treaty between the Philppines and the US. Manila then, however, did not invoke it.

The two Asian countries later settled on a provisional agreement whose details are not public. China’s envoy to Manila Jing Quan claims the agreement included the barring of construction materials in resupply missions.

Manila has denied this claim and said the agreement “does not concede the Philippines’ sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Lacson hints anew at more ‘damning evidence’ in Taguig infra projects
World.content:
Sen. Panfilo Lacson listens as National Bureau of Investigation chief Melvin Matibag takes the witness stand for the continuation of his cross-examination on Day 9 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on July 22, 2026. — Photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta | INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson on Friday hinted anew at uncovering more “damning evidence” in his investigation into alleged anomalous infrastructure projects in Taguig City, declaring that the “list lengthens” and the “case strengthens.”

Lacson’s scrutiny of infrastructure projects in Taguig, the political bailiwick of Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, emerged amid an escalating public feud between the two senators.

Cayetano, whose wife Lani Cayetano is Taguig’s mayor, has since denied the existence of ghost projects in the city and challenged Lacson to produce evidence to back his allegations and to also investigate other areas instead of singling out Taguig.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cayetano-Matibag spat revives ‘kaldero’ issue

In a post on X, Lacson appeared to tease further findings but did not provide details.

“TAGUIG GHOST INFRA PROJECTS UPDATE #3: There is too much damning (evidence). The plot thickens. The list lengthens. The case strengthens,” Lacson said.

“If there’s such a thing as ‘shooting into a bucket,’ there’s also ‘SHOOTING INTO THE COOKING POT,’” he added.

Lacson’s remark came amid renewed scrutiny of the controversial cauldron built for the Philippines’ hosting of the 2019 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games after the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said it would revisit issues that hounded the SEA Games organizing body then headed by Cayetano.

Article continues after this 

NBI Director Melvin Matibag, who also had heated public exchanges with Cayetano, earlier said it would also examine the cauldron that was dubbed the “P50-million kaldero” (cooking pot) after then-Senate Minority Leader Franklin Drilon questioned its cost during budget deliberations in 2019.

The NBI said the planned investigation was prompted by newly obtained documents and was not directed at the senator.

Article continues after this 

Lacson’s latest post also came after he flagged what he described as a possible “double appropriation” involving two P100-million allocations that appeared to cover the same slope protection project in Taguig City.

“One of the two must be ghost,” Lacson said in an earlier post.

Lacson said his team had found three additional P100-million slope protection projects under the 2025 General Appropriations Act, raising the total value of the Taguig projects being scrutinized from P2.085 billion to P2.385 billion.

He earlier said his team had documented at least two case studies involving suspected “ghost” infrastructure projects in Taguig.

READ: Senate panel to review Lacson’s findings on Taguig ‘ghost’ projects

Meanwhile, Senate blue ribbon committee chair Sen. Erwin Tulfo said the panel may examine Lacson’s allegations once the latter submits his findings.

Tulfo said the information from Lacson would first be reviewed to determine the allegations, witnesses and projects that should be covered by the Senate inquiry.

The NBI has likewise started looking into the alleged ghost infrastructure projects in Taguig based on Lacson’s claims.

The Inquirer has sought Cayetano’s comment on Lacson’s latest statements but has yet to receive a response as of posting time. /das

World.title: Wind signals raised over parts of N. Luzon due to Kiyapo
World.content:
Weather specialist Obet Badrina shows the state weather bureau’s track and intensity forecast for Tropical Storm Kiyapo on Friday, July 24, 2026. — Screengrab from DOST-Pagasa/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Tropical storm wind signals were hoisted over parts of Northern Luzon on Friday, July 24, as Kiyapo, formerly a tropical depression, further intensified into a tropical storm, the state weather bureau reported.

Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) weather specialist Obet Badrina said during a 5 a.m. weather advisory that Wind Signal No. 2 was raised over Batanes, northern portion of Mainland Cagayan, including Babuyan Islands, and the northern portion of Ilocos Norte, due to Kiyapo.

Meanwhile, Wind Signal No. 1 was placed over the following areas:

Article continues after this 

The rest of mainland Cagayan

Isabela

Nueva Vizcaya

Quirino

Apayao

Abra

Kalinga

Mountain Province

Ifugao

Benguet

The rest of Ilocos Norte

Ilocos Sur

La Union

The northern and central portions of Aurora

READ: Kiyapo to make possible landfall in Babuyan Islands on Friday

He added that Kiyapo may intensify into a severe tropical storm before it exits the Philippine area of responsibility on Saturday morning, which means chances of Wind Signal No. 3 being raised is still high.

“So, before it exits the Philippine Area of Responsibility early tomorrow morning, it could intensify into a severe tropical storm; this means the Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal raised could go up to Signal No. 3,” Badrina said.

As of 4 a.m., the center of Kiyapo was estimated 345 kilometers east of Aparri, Cagayan, moving west northwestward at 30 kilometers per hour. It packs maximum sustained winds of 65 kilometers per hour near the center and gustiness of up to 80 kilometers per hour.

According to Badrina, Kiyapo is likely to closely approach or make landfall over Babuyan Islands during its passage.

Article continues after this 

“The storm’s center could pass within the cone of probability, meaning it may make landfall on any of the islands in the Babuyan Islands. It could also pass close to the islands without making landfall,” Badrina stated.

Despite exiting on Saturday, Kiyapo may still enhance the southwest monsoon, or habagat, affecting the western sections of Northern and Southern Luzon, Badrina said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Kiyapo putting 6,947 barangays at risk of landslides, floods — OCD

“Even though Kiyapo is already outside the Philippine area of responsibility, it will continue to intensify the southwest monsoon. Consequently, cloudy skies are likely to persist over large parts of Luzon through the weekend, even after the typhoon exits tomorrow — particularly in the western sections of Northern and Southern Luzon,” he added.

Strong to gale-force winds brought by Kiyapo are affecting the northern seaboard of Northern Luzon, particularly Batanes and Babuyan Islands, causing rough to very rough sea conditions of up to 3.1 meters to 5.5 meters wave height, according to Pagasa.

Rough sea conditions of up to 2.8 meters to 5 meters wave height may be also experienced in the northern seaboards of Cagayan and Ilocos Norte due to the tropical storm.

Meanwhile, the southwest monsoon may affect Mindanao and the western sections of Southern Luzon and Visayas, bringing occasional rains over Occidental Mindoro, Palawan, Antique, Iloilo, Guimaras, and Negros Occidental on Friday.

Cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms may also prevail over the rest of the country due to the habagat, Badrina reported.

World.title: Cops nab 2 suspects in killing of Marcos supporter
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The police arrested on Thursday two suspects in the case of pro-Marcos vlogger Alicia “Mima Alicia” Lipata, who was shot dead by two men on a motorcycle in Caloocan City on July 17.

The suspects were tracked to Mabalacat City in Pampanga, Philippine National Police public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co told reporters in a briefing at Camp Crame.

Article continues after this 

Co identified the two men by their aliases: M.S., the alleged gunman who is 58 years old and a resident of Caloocan City, and J.A., 48 years old and from Cavite.

READ: Pro-Marcos vlogger shot dead, partner hurt

Prior cases

M.S. has multiple prior cases, according to Co, who did not elaborate.

Seized from the suspects were two hand grenades, a cal. .45 pistol and a 9mm pistol.

“We believe that the caliber .45 pistol is the same firearm used in the killing of the vlogger,” Co said.

Article continues after this 

READ: NBI: There’s ‘person of interest’ in Hontiveros’ online death threats

The two suspects are facing charges for murder and violation of Republic Act No. 10591, or the Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act, and RA No. 9516, which pertains to the illegal possession of explosives.

Article continues after this 

More suspects?

Co said that investigators are still trying to determine if Lipata’s killing was related to her political statements or personal life.

“We have received information that we cannot disclose yet as of now so as not to compromise our ongoing operations … But all I could say is based on that information, there are other people involved,” he added.

Co said the two men entered Lipata’s house around 15 to 20 minutes before she came home, suggesting that there were other people monitoring her movements.

World.title: Senate panel to review Lacson’s findings on Taguig ‘ghost’ projects
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The Senate blue ribbon committee may examine allegations of “ghost” infrastructure projects in Taguig City once Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson submits his findings, its chair Sen. Erwin Tulfo said on Thursday.

Tulfo said the information from Lacson would first be reviewed to determine the allegations, witnesses and projects that should be covered by the inquiry.

Article continues after this 

“If he submits it, of course, we will have to review that … We really have to look into that because it is a serious matter,” Tulfo told reporters.

The panel could resume its inquiry into alleged corruption in public works projects next week at the earliest after President Marcos’ State of the Nation Address on Monday.

READ: Lacson flags 2 suspected Taguig ‘ghost’ projects

Probe update

In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Lacson flagged a possible “double appropriation” involving two P100-million allocations that appeared to cover the same slope protection project in Taguig City.

“From P2.085B as earlier reported, we found three—P100M additional slope protection projects for a new total of P2.385B insertions under the 2025 [General Appropriations Act or GAA]. Two items appear to be double appropriations, involving two (2)-P100M for the same slope protection project. One of the two must be ghost,” he posted on Wednesday.

Other allegations

World.title: DOJ tasks prosecutors to handle bullying cases
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Justice (DOJ) will release next week an antibullying policy that will allow its prosecutors and action centers nationwide to receive and handle bullying complaints.

The move was taken by the DOJ following incidents of school violence in Tacloban City and Cavite just as classes opened last month.

Article continues after this 

Courses of action

Three students were killed, and 20 others were injured in a shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City on June 22, while eight students were hurt in two separate school stabbing incidents in Cavite.

READ: Bullying goes beyond school grounds, child rights advocates say

“They may assess, mediate, [or] refer [the complaint] to the schools that have primary jurisdiction in the incident,” Justice Undersecretary Ian Dato said in a press briefing on Thursday. “Or they may refer [it] to the women and children protection desk of the PNP (Philippine National Police), or receive and docket the complaint.”

READ: Olongapo school probes viral bullying video

These actions will be based on Department Circular No. 20, the DOJ policy on case-buildup by prosecutors, he added.

The DOJ hopes to help victims and their parents through this new policy addressing the rising cases of bullying. /cb

World.title: Students to SC: Stop tree cutting in Manila
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Five college students on Thursday asked the Supreme Court to issue a temporary environmental protection order (Tepo) to stop the mass cutting of trees on Quirino Avenue in Manila for the Southern Access Link Expressway (SALEx) project.

Led by journalism student Joaquin Bautista and sustainability and environment student Elisha Zantua, the group also filed a petition for certiorari after the Manila Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 41 rejected their first petition for a Tepo, citing a technicality.

Article continues after this 

Named as respondents in the students’ petition were the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the SMC Southern Access Link Expressway Corp. and Manila Judge Rosalyn Loja.

Irreversible damage

“Environmental destruction is distinct from other forms of legal injury because it is frequently irreversible. The cutting down of over 300 remaining mature urban trees cannot be remedied by future financial damages or by the planting of saplings elsewhere,” the students said in their 21-page petition.

READ: Tree cutting in Manila ‘paused,’ to be studied

They also challenged a provision in Section 23 of Republic Act No. 11966, or the PPP (Public-Private Partnership) Code, which states that only the high tribunal can issue a Tepo.

The Manila judge had cited the provision when she dismissed the students’ first petition in June. Under the PPP Code, a Tepo or similar temporary or provisional reliefs or remedies issued by lower courts are considered “void and of no force and effect” with judges who violate the provision facing possible suspension.

Article continues after this 

READ: DENR defends mass cutting of trees in Manila for road project

“It appends the balance of power. Why is it that they can suspend a judge, when only the Supreme Court can discipline judges,” lawyer Army Padilla-Santos, who represents the students, said in an interview after the filing.

Article continues after this 

“The PPP code itself gives a full judicial shield over a PPP project that will cause reckless ecological modifications that are irreparable,” she added.

Bautista, meanwhile, urged the DENR and the SMC to immediately halt the tree cutting activities and reminded them of the public’s right to a balanced and healthful ecology, as stipulated in the Constitution.

Aside from Bautista and Zantua, the other student-petitioners are Benjamin Luis Francia, Paul Benedict Callorina and Hannah Eliza Marie Guerra.

“We will fight for this; this is not just for us but for future generations to come,” Zantua said.

On May 27, Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna announced the temporary suspension of the tree-cutting activities on Quirino Avenue although by this time, over 200 trees out of the target of 600 had “already been processed.”

The DENR defended the tree cutting, saying that 50,700 tree seedlings would be planted as replacements.
