World.title: Armenian rights lawyer files ECHR complaint over Ruben Vardanyan’s 20-year jail sentence in Baku
World.content:
ECHR complaint over Vardanyan case

Human rights lawyer Siranush Sahakyan has filed a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) over the case of Ruben Vardanyan, the former state minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. She said she would represent Vardanyan before the court. Sahakyan has represented Armenian detainees at the ECHR for many years.

“The application sets out in detail violations of eight articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, supported by comprehensive legal and factual arguments,” Sahakyan said in a statement shared with the media and posted on social media.

Vardanyan is one of 19 Armenians still held in Azerbaijani prisons. In February 2026, a military court in Baku sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

According to Sahakyan, the defence was only recently able to obtain the court’s written judgment, which was required before an application could be submitted to the ECHR. She said Azerbaijan had withheld the ruling until then, which is why the complaint was filed only on 19 July.

The court found Vardanyan guilty of a number of serious offences, including waging war, financing terrorism and deportation.

Armenian rights groups, however, have described the trial in Baku as “political rather than legal”. Vardanyan himself called the proceedings “a farce” and “a mockery of justice”. During the hearings, he instructed his lawyer not to present arguments in his defence.

“It is impossible to protect rights in a system that fundamentally denies the right to a fair trial. That is why Ruben Vardanyan decided to continue his fight for justice through international legal mechanisms,” Sahakyan said.

Details of Vardanyan case

In her statement, Sahakyan disclosed further details of the case. She said the military court in Baku did not read out the full verdict. Now that Vardanyan’s family has passed the written judgment to his lawyers, it has become clear that he was convicted on 41 counts under 21 articles of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code.

According to Sahakyan, the judgment does not substantiate Vardanyan’s personal criminal responsibility with facts or evidence.

“Instead, the court concluded that the ‘criminal organisation’ – the leadership of the self-proclaimed Republic of Artsakh – had been operating in Nagorno-Karabakh since 1988. It also found that Vardanyan joined this ‘organisation’ in December 2020, although he was living in Moscow at the time.”

She also said the court treated Vardanyan’s appointment to a civilian administrative post as a violent seizure of power. His commercial and charitable activities were classified as illegal entrepreneurship and financing terrorism, while his entry into Nagorno-Karabakh via the Lachin Corridor was deemed an illegal crossing of Azerbaijan‘s state border.

Sahakyan said Vardanyan had not appealed against the verdict because he regarded the trial as staged and pre-planned, and considered all domestic legal remedies ineffective.

Background

On 17 February, a military court in Baku sentenced Russian-Armenian businessman, billionaire and philanthropist Ruben Vardanyan to 20 years in prison. His case was heard separately from those of the former leadership of Nagorno-Karabakh.

A month after the verdict, Vardanyan’s family said he had tried to raise concerns with Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner, Sabina Aliyeva, during a phone call with relatives, but the call was cut off.

The family has repeatedly appealed to the international community, saying that neither Vardanyan nor the other Armenian detainees in Azerbaijan have access to institutional protection. They argue that the country lacks independent human rights protection mechanisms. They have also noted that the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had facilitated contact between detainees and their families, has ceased operations in Azerbaijan.

On 5 February, two weeks before Vardanyan’s sentence was announced, an Azerbaijani court handed life sentences to several other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders, including former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, his deputy Davit Manukyan, former parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and former Foreign Minister Davit Babayan. Former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison.

All of the detainees faced a range of serious charges, including terrorism and genocide. Ghukasyan and Sahakyan received lighter sentences because they are over 65, and Azerbaijani law does not allow life imprisonment for people above that age.

Independent media and human rights observers were not allowed to attend the trials. Information about the proceedings was published by Azerbaijani state and pro-government media.

World.title: One minor killed, three injured in shooting in central Tbilisi
World.content:
Shooting in central Tbilisi

Late on July 22, four people, including two minors, were injured in a shooting on Vera, a central street in Tbilisi. All were taken to hospital. One of the minors died shortly after being admitted, Irakli Pirtskhalaishvili, a doctor at the clinic, told reporters.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry confirmed the incident, saying one person had been arrested in connection with it. The suspect has been charged with using a firearm and wounding four people.

He attempted to flee the scene but was detained after a police chase. According to the ministry, the suspect resisted arrest with a weapon and “sustained finger injuries during the arrest.”

The investigation is being conducted under Articles 19 and 109 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (attempted murder), which carry a penalty of up to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment.

Many witnesses to the shooting: what they say

The shooting took place in central Tbilisi, at the intersection of Akaki Shanidze and Akaki Khorava streets. The area was crowded at the time of the incident.

Eyewitness Elene Koridze wrote on social media that three young men sitting in a car “were shot simply because they were laughing.”

“About an hour ago, right outside my home, a man opened fire on three 17- and 18-year-old boys sitting in a car simply because they were laughing. He then also shot a woman who was nearby. He was quickly apprehended.

It was clear this was neither a premeditated attack nor an act of personal revenge. This is not just an isolated serious crime to which the police responded quickly, but a direct reflection of the reality we live in,” Koridze wrote.

Another eyewitness, Tiko Kvaliashvili, said:

“I was walking home when I saw a crowd on Shanidze Street and went over. Two patrol cars arrived, people started shouting, and someone was running. One boy was unconscious in the car, while two others were in shock. I gave them first aid as best I could. One had been shot in the arm, the other in the shoulder. I don’t know why they were shot.”

The son of journalist Eka Kvesitadze also witnessed the incident. She said it happened near their home while her son was out walking the dog.

“Someone had shot several minors. They were lying there covered in blood,” another witness wrote.

Witnesses also told reporters that a nearby parked red Alfa Romeo had around a dozen bullet holes.

As of now, Interior Ministry has not released any additional details.

World.title: Pro-EU protester Onise Okriashvili attacked in Tbilisi after disinformation campaign
World.content:
Georgia protester Onise Okriashvili beaten

Stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, an active participant in Georgia’s pro-European protests that have been ongoing for nearly two years, was brutally beaten by three people late on July 22 outside his home in Tbilisi’s Vake district.

Before the attack, Okriashvili had become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government media. Based on the context of the attack, this appears to have been the reason behind the assault.

A video of the attack, recorded by eyewitnesses, has spread on social media.

The footage shows three young men brutally beating Onise. “You insulted Nodar Dumbadze (a classic of Georgian literature), how dare you, bastard?” the attackers are heard saying to him.

Onise Okriashvili can be heard calling for help. Several people are nearby, but they do not dare approach him. The desperate screams of a woman trying to stop the attackers can also be heard.

Who is Onise Okriashvili and why did he become a target of propaganda?

Onise Okriashvili is known for his criticism of the ruling Georgian Dream party on social media. He also regularly organises solo protests aimed at drawing public attention — appearing with relevant posters in places where large numbers of people gather, including on public transport.

“Only their children study in Europe” — reads the sign held by Onise Okriashvili during one of his solo protests. Photo from the activist’s social media page

In recent days, the activist has become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government TV channels. They have repeatedly aired a fragment from a comedy show Punchline Therapy, in which he uses a vulgar expression while referring to Nodar Dumbadze, a classic of Georgian literature.

The fragment was shown without context, making it appear as if Okriashvili was directly insulting the writer.

On July 19, the comedian recorded a video in which he said:

“I apologise that in this video I am not talking about more important events in the country. Young people my age are dying every day because of drug use; there are political prisoners in the country; emigration is sharply increasing, and these emigrants have been deprived of the right to vote in elections, along with many other problems.

But for the third day now, Georgian Dream’s propaganda machine has been using all its resources to turn people against me. Here is an example of the video they are using to try to discredit me.“

The conversation in the video excerpt goes:

‘Is there someone you cannot stand?’ ‘What if I say Nodar Dumbadze? (vulgar expression) I will only name our government, no one else.’

“During a performance, we speak hypothetically and can say the most absurd thing that comes to mind at that moment.

This video clearly shows that I am, of course, not insulting (Nodar Dumbadze), but speaking only hypothetically, deliberately using the most absurd example that came to mind at that moment. Comedy often works exactly this way — it uses unexpected twists. That is why the audience laughs at that moment.”

“Just today we were discussing filing a lawsuit against the propaganda media for spreading defamatory claims, and today Onise was attacked,” his wife, Mariam Samushia, told journalists.

She said she heard shouting in the street in the evening. Since Onise had become a target of a propaganda campaign in recent days, she called him to warn him. Only later did she realise that her husband had been attacked.

“This is artificially created hatred,” she said.

The Interior Ministry said a criminal case had been opened over the attack on Onise Okriashvili under Article 126 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (violence). According to reports, one of the attackers has been taken to a police station and is being questioned.

News in Georgia

World.title: Chechnya’s recruitment machine: How Kadyrov sustains his forces by enlisting civilians
World.content:
Kadyrov’s Forces in Ukraine

An investigation by Novaya Gazeta Europe shows how the war has reshaped the system of power in Chechnya.

Ramzan Kadyrov has significantly expanded the number of armed units under his control. But his most loyal formations are largely kept away from the front lines.

Instead, combat losses are replenished with ordinary residents of the republic, who are often pressured into signing military contracts.

For the investigation, journalists interviewed 178 Chechen families who lost relatives in the war, as well as current and former servicemen. Their reporting examines how Chechnya’s recruitment system operates and reveals the true scale of its wartime losses.

Kadyrov’s forces

Over the course of the war, five new regiments and five battalions have been established in Chechnya. Formally, they are part of Russia’s Defense Ministry and the National Guard. In practice, however, Kadyrov determines key personnel appointments, where the units are deployed and how extensively they are involved in combat.

According to figures provided by Kadyrov, the number of security personnel in Chechnya has grown from 4,800 in 2003 to 36,243 today. At the start of 2022, before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, those forces numbered roughly 16,000 to 18,000. That means Chechnya’s security apparatus has approximately doubled in size over the course of the three-year war.

The human rights group Memorial argues that the expansion amounts to the strengthening of Kadyrov’s personal army. But a source in Chechnya’s regional office of the Federal Security Service offered a different explanation. According to the source, Kadyrov became trapped by the image of being “Putin’s chief foot soldier.” While he continued to create new units, he also sought to shield his most loyal security personnel from frontline combat.

At first, the authorities attracted recruits with high salaries. They then began actively recruiting people from other parts of Russia. Later, military service was opened to unemployed residents of Chechnya. As the flow of volunteers dwindled, the authorities increasingly turned to coercion.

The safe rear ended in the Kursk region

In 2023, Kadyrov secured the deployment of several Chechen units to the Russian border regions of Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod. At the time, these areas were considered relatively safe rear positions, allowing Kadyrov’s forces to be pulled back from the most intense sections of the front.

That changed on Aug. 6, 2024, when Ukrainian troops crossed into the Kursk region. The Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment, which had been guarding the border, offered little visible resistance. Its personnel abandoned their positions, and some were surrounded and taken prisoner.

The border regions subsequently became the scene of heavy fighting involving the Akhmat special forces, the West Akhmat Battalion and the Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment. One Akhmat commander claimed that Apti Alaudinov’s unit alone suffered more than 1,500 killed and wounded.

Security forces are shielded, civilians sent to the front

After the fighting in the Kursk region, Kadyrov moved to reduce the involvement of key National Guard units in the war. Much of the burden was shifted instead to formations under Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Sources interviewed by the publication say the decision was driven by the need to preserve the foundations of Kadyrov’s rule. His grip on power depends on the loyalty of the republic’s security forces. A prolonged war depletes that resource faster than the Chechen leadership can replace it.

A telling example is the National Guard’s Baysangur Benoevsky Battalion. It is overseen by Adam Kadyrov, the 18-year-old son and presumed heir of the Chechen leader. The battalion has been equipped with modern weapons, its own training ground and a well-funded infrastructure. Its personnel signed contracts that предусматривают service in the war. Yet the unit has remained almost entirely in Chechnya, where it focuses on training.

Another National Guard unit, the Sheikh Mansur Battalion, was deployed to the front in December 2023 and has been engaged in combat ever since.

According to the investigation, the Baysangur Battalion is effectively financed with federal funds allocated for the war while serving as the Kadyrov family’s personal security reserve.

Coerced recruitment

Since the autumn of 2024, the Chechen authorities have carried out a large-scale campaign of forced recruitment. Kadyrov publicly proposed sending what he called “troubled youth” to the front. District police departments were then assigned monthly recruitment quotas of between 25 and 50 people.

Those detained are taken to collection centers in Sernovodsk and at the Khankala military base. According to testimonies from recruits and their relatives, they are held under guard, given inadequate food and receive little to no military training. Some are sent without proper uniforms or equipment, receiving weapons only after they reach the front.

People can be sent to the front for reasons as minor as a street fight, a traffic violation, driving without insurance, tinted car windows or unpaid utility bills. Others are detained for subscribing to opposition channels or for political posts found on their phones. In some cases, relatives are offered the chance to pay for a detainee’s release or to find other “volunteers” to take their place.

According to the journalists’ estimates, 67 such raids were carried out across Chechnya between October 2024 and May 2025.

Hidden casualties

The Chechen authorities prohibit the publication of information about those killed in the war. Families are often instructed to bury relatives at night and to forgo the traditional multi-day mourning rituals. As a result, publicly available casualty lists capture only a fraction of the true death toll.

Officially, around 500 residents of Chechnya have been confirmed killed. But a source in the republic’s government told the investigators that more than 2,300 deaths have been verified internally. Another roughly 1,000 people are listed as missing in action.

Of the 183 fatalities documented by the journalists, 113 were sent to the war after October 2024. Of those, 97 had signed military contracts under coercion. The average time between deployment and death was about two months. Only 84 of the 178 families interviewed were able to recover and bury the bodies of their relatives.

The investigation identifies a fundamental shift in Kadyrov’s approach. At the start of the war, he deployed members of the security forces while portraying those forcibly recruited as volunteers. Now, his most loyal units are kept inside Chechnya, while civilians are openly treated as expendable manpower.

The authors argue that this marks a troubling precedent. Repressive practices first tested in Chechnya have often, over time, spread to the rest of Russia.

World.title: Norway set to file complaint over Trump's push to overturn red card
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's role in clearing Folarin Balogun from a mandatory one-game ban at the World Cup is set to provoke a formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators.

The Norway soccer federation said its board of directors will consider filing the complaint at its next meeting, likely on August 6.

"We need our leader in FIFA to say that this was an error," Norwegian federation president Lise Klaveness told The Times in an interview.

After Trump called FIFA president Gianni Infantino, a one-game ban for Balogun's red-card tackle against Bosnia-Herzegovina was deferred so he could play against Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake.

Belgium beat the US 4-1 after a chaotic 36 hours at the World Cup. The Belgium players were seemingly fired up by one of the greatest controversies in tournament history.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (left) with Crown Prince Haakon of Norway and Football Association of Norway president Lise Klaveness. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Trump called the referee's red card for Balogun after video review a "horrible" call and took credit for getting FIFA to review what should routinely have been a one-game ban.

"We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process," Klaveness said of the FIFA ruling that was unprecedented in the past 60 years at World Cups.

"When you bend a rule like this, you're on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk," said the former Women's World Cup player for Norway, who is an elected member of European soccer body UEFA's executive committee.

Klaveness is a lawyer and judge who has positioned the Norwegian federation as a conscience in world soccer since her election in 2022.

"It is a worry for the game when you compromise fundamental rules of the game," she said about not enforcing Balogun's ban.

Norway previously joined a London-based NGO's complaint to the FIFA ethics committee alleging Infantino breached a statutory duty of political neutrality, including by creating a peace prize to award to Trump at the World Cup draw in December.

EU politicians launch bid to investigate FIFA boss A group of European politicians launches a bid to begin an investigation into how and why a red card for an American football star was overturned at the World Cup.

The close personal and political ties between Trump and Infantino include the US president believing the soccer official could be a good pick as next secretary general of the United Nations, the New York Post reported this week.

The human rights NGO, FairSquare, also has filed an ethics complaint about the Balogun incident to the International Olympic Committee, where Infantino is an elected member, about breaching its rules on political neutrality.

FIFA and the IOC rarely acknowledge or provide updates on potential cases before their ethics bodies.

The independence of FIFA's process to handle complaints alleging unethical conduct has been questioned since the lead investigator and judge both were replaced in 2017, in the second year of Infantino's presidency.

FIFA has yet to publish documents explaining how its disciplinary judges reached verdicts about Balogun or other World Cup players.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: MotoGP to rev up motorcycle culture and pilgrimages to City of Churches
World.content:
The arrival of the Tour Down Under to Adelaide in 1999 inspired a significant uptick in Lycra-wearing cyclists in and around Adelaide, a trend that continued well into the late 2010s.

But with MotoGP landing in the City of Churches from 2027, and a Superbike World Championship round in Tailem Bend from 2028, it poses the question: Will this result in thousands of high-performance sport bikes whizzing around our roads?

Noah Orozgani works in sales at family business Moto Adelaide and says retailers believe the MotoGP is a major coup for the state.

"Like the time we had a big name like [MotoGP rider] Jack Miller come and ride for the Australian Superbikes," he says.

"There was big crowd there at Tailem Bend, the racetrack and people just went there to watch Jack Miller.

" Now there will be 20-something potential world champions riding through the streets of Adelaide. "

He says the MotoGP bikes and their riders are "out of this world" in terms of their performance and the excitement would rub off on spectators of all ages, which would in turn be good for dealerships and service centres.

Popular Australian MotoGP rider Jack Miller was rolled out for the SA government's February announcement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"The fan base is not like anything else. They get really riled up, like footy fans," he says.

"People will fly in to be a part of it, it will be huge, and getting to watch them for real, sales will go berserk.

"People are doing 360 kilometres per hour, and it just gives you that buzz, and they'll go: 'Oh yeah, I've got a bike at home, I'll go riding, and then the bike's not good enough, I need an upgrade, or a service.'"

Revving up hype

Motorcycle Alliance of South Australia chairman Heath Norris says it's likely a lot more motorcycles will be brought out of people's sheds.

"It always brings a bit of hype along with it, this sort of thing," he says.

He says Adelaide already has a strong motorcycle culture, with "great roads, great scenery and great destinations", as well as flagship charity events, like the Motorcycle Riders' Association of SA Toy Run.

Heath Norris during the 2025 charity toy run. (Supplied: Heath Norris)

That being said, he points out there is a difference between the high-performance sport bikes, or "crotch rockets" developed into superbikes, and cruiser bikes like Harley-Davidsons.

"But we're all bike enthusiasts at the end of the day," Mr Norris says.

The South Australian government is banking on strong interest in the MotoGP to warrant expenditure forecast by the former F1 Grand Prix track designer to be more than $100m to adapt the racecourse alone.

It is also facing strong and ongoing public criticism over the removal of Parklands trees that will be required to adjust the track for the MotoGP.

Banking on a big impact

A spokesperson says the 2025 MotoGP event at Phillip Island delivered an average of "$217 million in economic impact for local economies through "global exposure combined with tourism and hospitality".

Estimates MotoGP remodel could cost $100m Adelaide Street Circuit designer Bob Barnard estimates it could cost more than $100 million to remodel the track for the MotoGP.

"MotoGP has a global fan base of more than 639 million people, with a record 3.6 million attendees in races in 2025 and TV audiences up 9 per cent over the past year," he says.

The spokesperson says it is a "major global sporting property with an established national and international audience".

"South Australians will no doubt embrace motorcycle racing with the same enthusiasm we've embraced cycling, Supercars, golf and the arts, among many others."

A world first

While Victoria's Phillip Island Grand Prix racecourse is regarded as among the best worldwide, enthusiasts have said the location had limits when it came to accessibility.

The Adelaide MotoGP street circuit will be in the city's east parklands and Victoria Park. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

A street circuit like Adelaide, the world's first, was expected to draw significant international visitors, and its timing alongside the Supercars Championship Adelaide Grand Final would further bolster attention.

Mr Orozgani points out that every year there was a huge contingent of people who would ride bikes over to Phillip Island via the Great Ocean Road to watch the MotoGP.

"Religiously, they went to Melbourne to watch the races and come back," Mr Orozgani says.

Describing the end of that annual event as a "downside" to the MotoGP coming to SA, he adds it may mean people interstate will ride their bikes to Adelaide instead.

The Phillip Island GP track is considered among the best of its kind in the world. (Supplied: Ading Attamimi)

Raising awareness

Mr Norris hopes an increased profile through motorcycle racing will improve road awareness among other road users, pointing out that Adelaide drivers are not always willing to share the road.

Some Adelaide drivers struggle to accommodate road cyclists as well, particularly those who legally ride two abreast. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"I've ridden in Queensland, and people get out of your way when they see you coming up behind," he says.

" It's just that some people are quite arrogant here. They think that lane filtering is illegal, for example. "

Lane filtering is when a motorcycle rider edges between two lanes of stationary traffic on the same side of the road, or traffic moving at 30km/h or less in the same direction, which is a legal and practical activity to ease congestion.

"A lot of people here are oblivious to motorcycles," Mr Norris says.

Dealerships are expecting the MotoGP to boost Adelaide interest in motorcycles. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

Asked if SAPOL was expecting more high-performance sport bikes on the roads as a result of the MotoGP, Officer in Charge of Traffic Services Branch Superintendent Shane Johns says it is committed to improving road safety for all road users.

"Major events can result in increased traffic volumes, including more motorcycles on our roads," he says.

"SAPOL routinely plans for these events with an appropriate policing response, which includes targeted road safety operations where required.

"SAPOL encourages all motorcyclists to ride within the speed limit, to the conditions, and to make responsible decisions on the road."

A motorcyclist caught at 200 kilometres per hour in an 80km/h zone in the Adelaide Hills during 2015. (Supplied: SA Police)

World.title: White House will not fight Tate brothers extradition to UK
World.content:
US President Donald Trump will not stop the extradition of influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan to Britain on sex crime charges, the White House says.

Self-professed misogynist Andrew Tate and his younger sibling were detained by US authorities in Miami on Saturday, local time, in a move their lawyer called "politically motivated".

The Tates are challenging their extradition.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt was asked at a news briefing if Mr Trump or the administration planned to intervene in the extradition process, and told reporters "no".

Tate brothers fight extradition to UK Andrew and Tristan Tate's attorney says an attempt to extradite the brothers is politically motivated.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also distanced the administration from the case.

"There's no role for us to play at this moment or maybe ever in that regard," he told reporters in the Philippines earlier this week.

The Tate brothers are avid supporters of Mr Trump and were part of the hyper-masculine "manosphere" that contributed to his 2024 election victory.

Andrew Tate also tried to cultivate relationships in the past with Mr Trump's sons Don Jr and Barron, US media reported.

The Tates were arrested after British prosecutors announced new charges of rape, sex trafficking and assault.

They now face 59 charges in total — 42 against Andrew and 17 against Tristan.

Their lawyer said on Monday that they were innocent and would fight extradition.

Loading...

"It's politically motivated. There's no question about it," Joseph McBride told reporters outside a Miami court after a hearing on the case.

In Romania, where they have been based in recent years, the brothers face allegations of trafficking minors, sexual intercourse with a minor and money laundering.

In March 2025, the US state of Florida launched a criminal investigation into the pair. The status of that investigation is unclear.

Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona, called for a probe into whether Trump administration officials, congressional offices or people close to Mr Trump improperly intervened to protect the Tates.

"No individual — regardless of wealth, political party, or access to the first family and the president — is above the law or beyond the reach of justice," she wrote in a letter to House Oversight Chairman James Comer.

AFP

World.title: Australia is home to thousands of people who are citizens of nowhere
World.content:
For almost her entire life, Asma Nayim Ullah was a citizen of nowhere.

The 23-year-old was one of about 8,000 people living in Australia without holding nationality from any country.

"I don't see myself as stateless because I know where I belong," Asma said.

"I know where I am from, but I'm not accepted there."

Asma is Rohingya, a mostly Muslim ethnic minority group who represent the largest stateless population in the world due to being denied citizenship by Myanmar's military regime since 1982.

Persecution of Rohingya has intensified in the past decade, with security forces accused of mass rapes, killings and torching thousands of homes, leading to the displacement of some 1.2 million people.

A burned house in Gawdu Zara village, in Mynmar's Rakhine state, where the vast majority of the country's Rohingya lived. (AP)

Asma grew up without official identity documents and thus had limited access to education and healthcare, faced arbitrary detention and was limited to where she could travel.

"My parents couldn't really move from one place to another, you have to ask for permission," she said.

The family fled Myanmar in 2013, with Asma's parents and three siblings smuggled through Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, before being intercepted by Australian border authorities on a wooden boat with more than 100 other people in the Timor Sea.

Her family were detained in an onshore detention facility in Darwin, before having their asylum claims assessed and being resettled in Sydney.

Asma was 10 years old and her mother, Sajeda, was 26.

Darwin's Wickham Point Detention Centre ceased operations in 2016. (Supplied: Dept of Immigration and Border Protection)

Citizenship isn't just a passport

As a signatory to both major international statelessness treaties, Australia is expected to report the number of stateless people in its territory annually to the United Nations refugee agency.

Most stateless people living in Australia arrived seeking asylum more than a decade ago, according to research by Melbourne Law School's Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness.

In the 1960s, the United Nations moved to protect people who lacked a recognised nationality and prevent the creation of new stateless cases. (Supplied: United Nations)

The centre's associate director Katie Robertson said while the federal government reported 8,183 stateless people living in Australia in 2025, the number could not be considered reliable.

"We know that there are thousands of stateless people in Australia," she said.

"But we also know that those numbers can't be considered as comprehensive and accurate because we don't have a mechanism for correctly working out who actually is stateless."

Australia does not have a uniform, legislated definition of statelessness or a formal mechanism for identifying stateless people.

University of Melbourne academic Katie Robertson is calling for a federal framework to formally identify stateless people living in Australia. (Supplied: University of Melbourne)

Refugee Advice and Casework Services (RACS) director Sarah Dale agreed, citing the lack of a clear pathway in Australia's immigration system for people without official identity documents.

"That is going to make it incredibly difficult for them to access visas and to apply for pathways," she said.

Asma experienced this first-hand.

Growing up in south-west Sydney, Asma and her family relied on bridging visas for three years and temporary visas for nine years.

Asma was unable to attend university as a domestic student despite growing up in Australia. (ABC News: Rex Siu)

After graduating from high school, she was ineligible for a HECS loan and classified as an international student — for whom fees are double those for local students.

"I wasn't able to study," she said.

Are stateless people still arriving in Australia?

Ms Robertson said very few stateless people have arrived in Australia since the implementation of Operation Sovereign Borders in 2013, which involved intercepting and turning back asylum seeker boats.

She said complex long-term residency pathways meant stateless populations including the Rohingya — as well as Feyli Kurds, Bidoon from the Gulf States and Palestinian people who have lived in Australia, often for more than a decade — struggle to get an education and gain employment.

Migration experts say very few stateless people have arrived in Australia since the federal government's turn back policy was introduced in 2013. (Reuters: Dadang Tri)

"The conditions they've been subjected to over the past decade or so have actually replicated the discrimination they faced in their country of origin," she said.

" They've essentially been living in legal limbo in Australia. "

Statelessness was often misunderstood despite its legal and personal consequences, Ms Robertson said, with the online Australian citizenship application form an example of how stateless people can fall through gaps in the immigration system.

"You have to select from a drop-down box what your country of nationality is and there's simply no drop-down category for stateless, miscellaneous or other," she said.

"It's forcing people to select a nationality that's never actually recognised them."

An online Australian citizenship application form, where a drop-down menu has no option for 'stateless' applicants without a nationality. (Supplied)

Asma said this experience emulated what many Rohingya people were forced to do when identifying themselves in Myanmar.

"Sometimes the only way they can get a document is if they agree to identify differently," she said.

"It's very dehumanising because you don't have a choice."

Experts call for a national statelessness framework

Migration lawyers and refugee advocates are calling for a national framework to formally identify stateless people and provide them with a pathway to permanent residency.

Ms Robertson said Australia's relatively small stateless population meant addressing the issue was achievable.

"We're not talking about hundreds of thousands of people," she said.

University of Canberra citizenship legal scholar Kim Rubenstein explained under current legislation, a person born in Australia who has never been and is not entitled to any other nationality is eligible to become an Australian citizen.

"But it doesn't go far enough towards actually fulfilling the Statelessness Convention," she argued.

Kim Rubenstein says existing legislation could be amended to better support people who are living stateless in Australia. (ABC News: Michael Barnett)

"Amending that section to be more expansive would be a positive step for Australia's commitment for the reduction of statelessness," Professor Rubenstein said.

" [It would] also have an impact on the lives of stateless people who live, in every other respect, as Australians in Australia. "

Ms Dale of RACS agreed.

"What we would like to see is a more streamlined, coherent and definitive process for people so that their statelessness is recognised across whatever process they're going before in Australia's immigration and citizenship system," she said.

Sarah Dale is the director of Refugee Advice and Casework Services, a non-for-profit that provides free specialised legal advice to refugees. (Supplied: Sarah Dale)

The Department of Home Affairs was approached for comment.

Asma's 'golden year'

After living in Australia for 11 years, Asma and her family were granted Australian citizenship in May this year.

"I'm no longer this unknown person, unspecified stateless person, I finally have a nationality," she said.

"I finally have a document that proves that I am worth as much as anyone."

Thanks to a scholarship, she graduated from the University of Technology Sydney with dreams of entering the field of public health.

Asma's mother Sajeda described obtaining her citizenship as feeling "newborn", with her family calling 2026 their "golden year".

Asma and her mother Sajeda at a community event hosted by the Australian Rohingya Women's Development Organisation in Sydney. (ABC News: Rex Siu)

Both now identify as Australian Rohingya.

As an artist, Asma said the art she creates reflects her struggles with identity.

"I can't be Rohingya without being Australian and I can't be Australian without being Rohingya," she said.

A mural by Asma and artist Yamin Rayhaf commissioned by Doctors Without Borders. (Supplied: Asma Nayim Ullah)

The family still worry about relatives who remain displaced in Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh.

Asma is the co-founder of the Australian Rohingya Women's Development Organisation, a grassroots charity that advocates for the empowerment of Rohingya women, children and their families.

"I want to get to a position where I can make it impossible to ever make another person stateless again," she said.

World.title: Fishing ban considered as NSW South Coast abalone populations depleted
World.content:
Once the New South Wales South Coast was brimming with abalone, but today most of the populations are depleted and the state government is considering a ban on commercial fishing to allow the shellfish to repopulate.

In a draft management proposal seen by the ABC, the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) has proposed a shutdown of commercial abalone harvesting from Bundeena, south of Sydney, to Eden near the Victorian border.

The proposal cites pressure from overfishing and "resource-sharing issues" with native title holders as creating "significant sustainability challenges".

The proposal would result in about 350 kilometres of coastline being declared off-limits for commercial abalone fishers.

Abalone Association of NSW (AANSW) chair Stephen Bunney said the mood among divers was one of dismay.

"It has now got to a state where three-quarters of the fishery is probably unrecoverable," he said.

" It's certainly no longer commercially viable. "

Under the proposal, the Central Zone between Bundeena and Red Point would be closed to commercial abalone harvesting. (Supplied)

In a statement, a DPIRD spokesperson said the draft was based on a reduction in commercial abalone harvest to relieve pressure on the resource and submissions from stakeholders were being considered.

Fishing quota slashed

The latest report from the independent Total Allowable Fishing Committee (TAFC), a statutory body that reviews fishing catch limits, found there was a "severe decline" in abalone stocks across the NSW coastline in the past year to either depleting or depleted.

In response, DPIRD last month slashed the amount of abalone able to be caught in the upcoming season by more than 40 per cent.

A major issue identified by the TAFC was illegal, unreported or unregulated (IUU) fishing, which the DPIRD has previously estimated at between 25 and 35 tonnes of abalone each year.

Stephen Bunney says the fishery has "pretty much collapsed" north of Eden. (Supplied)

Mr Bunney said the rezoning and closure would not address their ongoing concerns about the government's inability to stop IUU fishing.

"Many people have just lost absolute confidence in the government to manage this," he said.

" The only thing they can do, if they're not going to pursue compliance and illegal fishing, is remove the commercial fishery because it's the only thing they've got control over. "

Abalone stocks across the NSW South Coast are depleting or depleted. (ABC South East NSW: Vanessa Milton)

Native title holders 'used as a scapegoat'

The stretch of coastline that would be closed is subject to an ongoing native title claim filed by the South Coast people in 2017.

While the native title applicants have welcomed the proposed closure, applicant and long-time advocate for Aboriginal cultural fishing rights, Wally Stewart, said the South Coast Aboriginal community was being "used as a scapegoat" for the depletion.

Wally Stewart is a lead applicant in the South Coast people's native title claim. (ABC South East NSW: Vanessa Milton)

Under Commonwealth native title law passed in 1993, Aboriginal cultural fishers are entitled to take sea resources under traditional lore and custom without restrictions under state fisheries management laws.

But Mr Stewart said it had been a protracted battle for the state government to respect the rights.

"We always knew that it was our water and our resources, and there was even a law there to back it up," he said.

" But the NSW government discriminated against that and prosecuted our people under state laws. "

The DPIRD and the TAFC includes the legally protected native title catch within the IUU take.

But native title applicants say that classification has fuelled discrimination.

Abalone is a traditional food for South Coast Indigenous people. (ABC South East NSW: Vanessa Milton)

"They've made us out to be poachers and the ones that destroyed the fishery," Mr Stewart said.

"We'd be lucky to take 2 tonnes a year between the whole mob up and down the South Coast.

"In the meantime, the commercial divers have been taking around 100 tonnes a year."

The continued prosecution of native title holders by the state government under NSW fisheries management regulations was the subject of a 2022 parliamentary inquiry and a class action that was filed in 2024.

Buyout offer rejected

The draft management framework is part of the state government's attempt to reform and reset the abalone fishery that was announced in June.

It included offering a voluntary share buyout to commercial abalone fishers at a valuation of about $4,200 a share to reduce fishing pressure.

There are currently 41 shareholders in the industry with shareholdings between 10 and 90 shares, meaning the largest shareholders would receive $378,000 under the offer.

But on July 10, the AANSW voted to reject the government's offer.

Mr Bunney said the offer was unfair and poorly formulated in light of what the industry believed was a failure to police illegal fishing.

"They've offered them less than a third of what they've paid to be in these businesses when the fishery was being properly managed," he said.

"This is people's businesses. This is people's lives."

The commercial abalone industry has rejected the government's offer of a voluntary share buyout. (ABC South East NSW: Vanessa Milton)

But Mr Stewart said the government should be focused on habitat recovery rather than compensation.

"That money should go into restoration, rather than giving these guys a golden handshake," he said.

Mr Bunney said AANSW would be asking for mediation with Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty while also pushing for an upper house inquiry.

World.title: Why Waratahs 'trust each other' to deliver in grand final against Drua
World.content:
Confidence can sometimes be mistaken for arrogance, but NSW Waratahs captain Emily Chancellor knows how to distinguish between the two.

Therefore, it is no surprise the Waratahs took pride in their 33-22 win over the Western Force in the Super Rugby Women's semifinals, but refused to get carried away with their performance.

"We got out on the field in that semifinal and there was just this air of clarity around the group," Chancellor told ABC Sport.

"It wasn't arrogance. It was just this feeling of we know what to do and we know how to do it, so let's just go out and execute."

As they prepare to face Fijian Drua in Saturday's grand final in Ba, Fiji, the Waratahs have reason to be in a confident mood.

Last Saturday against the Force in Perth, the defending champions produced arguably the best 40 minutes of rugby from any side this season.

They ran in four tries during the first half and led 26-0 before the Force were able to score their first points.

The Force, who earned hosting rights by finishing above the Waratahs on the standings, clawed back some ground on the scoreboard in the second half.

But the result was never in doubt.

"We know we've got firepower out wide. We know we've got electric backs," Chancellor said.

"We've got a really strong, physical forward pack that has been quite consistent across the last few years.

"We know the forwards are doing a really good job of going direct and then it's up to the backs to do what they do best."

Waiaria Ellis was superb for the Waratahs in their semifinal win over the Force. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

It was a return to form for the Waratahs, who entered the play-offs in third place.

They dropped their final two regular-season matches against the Force (28-21) and the Queensland Reds (26-19).

The loss to the Force was the first time they had been defeated by an Australian opponent in Super Rugby Women's history.

But sudden-death rugby has become second nature to the Waratahs, who have only missed one grand final among the seven contested in the competition.

The six-time winners were rewarded for taking a punt on an untried halves pairing, Tia Hinds and Waiaria Ellis, with the selection move proving to be a masterstroke.

Hinds, an Australian sevens star making her Waratahs debut, was a revelation at scrum half, scoring two tries when she caught the Force's ruck defence napping.

She combined brilliantly with 18-year-old Wallaroos sensation Ellis, who helped drive the Waratahs' attack in her first start at fly half this season after switching from fullback.

"They (Hinds and Ellis) backed themselves," said Chancellor, who has played almost 40 Tests for the Wallaroos.

"Tia, being an incredible reader of space, took her own opportunities, and Baba (Ellis) did a really good job of being calm and collected.

"She had a really sound knowledge of our game plan and was just able to deliver and execute what she saw in front of her."

Tahs face stern test

The Drua, who have won two Super Rugby Women's championships, were impressive in their 31-5 victory over the Reds in the first semifinal in Lautoka last Saturday.

They deservedly finished the regular season on top of the standings with a 3-1 win-loss record.

But their one defeat came at the hands of the Waratahs, who triumphed 42-29 at Leichhardt Oval in the opening round.

The Waratahs defeated the Drua when they played in the opening round of the regular season. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"Fiji would probably be disappointed that it's us in the final," Chancellor said.

"We're probably the hardest ones for them to beat, in the same way they're the hardest ones for us to beat. They've been playing some really great rugby.

"They play a style that is hard to defend against, but in the same breath it creates a lot of opportunity because they do play a high-risk, high-reward version of rugby.

"So if we can withstand some pressure and stay disciplined, I believe we have an attacking game that will be hard to contain."

Chancellor's faith in her Waratahs teammates is not misplaced, as it is built on a key trait the entire squad shares: confidence.

"We're a squad who knows how to play big games," she said.

"The Waratahs are a team that knows how to win in big moments. We know how to win; we know how to perform under these pressure moments.

"We take a lot of confidence because we trust each other to do our own jobs."

World.title: Members of a 'surreal' rescue off WA's Stirling Range reunite
World.content:
Lucy Fairweather was hiking the West Australia's Stirling Range Ridge Walk in April of this year, taking in stunning views as she ate her lunch.

Unfortunately, she broke her ankle shortly after and had to be winched off the mountain pass by helicopter.

The mountainous, multi-day hike across the Stirling Range National Park is considered one of the state's toughest.

Her rescue marked the 11,000th mission for the RAC rescue helicopter service since it was established in 2003.

Ms Fairweather said the rescue was surreal.

"To be rescued off the mountain within three hours of having actually fallen was way faster than I expected," she said.

"I think just as you get lifted off the ground and feel your weight being taken by that bag, and then you start to see the view, where you were receding — crazy experience."

Thankfully, the Perth woman is nearly off her crutches and was reunited with the helicopter crew to celebrate the milestone earlier this week.

Bluff Knoll, in the Great Southern, is one of WA's highest peaks. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

'Amazing' to see patients smiling

St John Ambulance critical care paramedic James Vine said it has been amazing to reconnect with Ms Fairweather.

"It's always wonderful to touch base with patients again, and see the actual recovery and close that loop really for us," he said.

"We get kind of a real small snapshot of patients and their injuries and their families, but to see a smiling face rather than a grimacing face is always nice."

A critical care paramedic winches a patient aboard a rescue helicopter alongside Stirling Range Ridge Walk. (Supplied: DFES)

Mr Vine said it was not often you attend the scene of a rescue and people have the right gear.

"You often get down there and find that people aren't as well prepared as maybe they should be," he said.

"It was a refreshing change for ourselves; they were in the middle of a multi-day hike, so they were well prepared.

It has been an above-average year for rescues from the Stirling Range, with six already recorded.

Lucy Fairweather had to be rescued via helicopter when she injured her foot while hiking the Stirling Range Ridge Walk. (ABC News: Jon Daly)

'We were so impressed'

Ms Fairweather said it was great to come back and see her rescuers.

"It was really cool to get the chance to come back and say hi and hear about it from their perspective," she said.

"Particularly, they said at the time that it was the 11,000th rescue."

A rescue team prepares to winch down to a stranded hiker. (Supplied: DFES)

Conducting a rescue is not a simple task: with about 25 people from different emergency services involved, it takes about eight hours from start to finish.

RAC Rescue helicopter pilot Matthew Mayne said Ms Fairweather's rescue was more efficient than usual.

"The Stirling Ranges is a challenging, difficult environment, but the weather always has the last say," he said.

"We flew over the ridge line where Lucy said she was, and she was exactly where she said, and the cloud was above us, the winds were light.

"Probably not even 10 minutes later, we came back in to extract both [Lucy and the paramedic] off the ridge line."

A RAC Rescue helicopter flying past Ellen Peak in WA's Stirling National Park. (Supplied: DFES)

Three months after Ms Fairweather was told by the doctor she had "shattered" her ankle, she is looking to make a full recovery.

World.title: Budjerah's debut album Gentleman has been a long time coming
World.content:
For the past four years, Coodjinburra singer/songwriter Budjerah has been patient.

The two-time ARIA Award-winning music artist has just released his debut album, Gentleman.

But it took a while to get there.

"I think even by music industry norms, four years is a long time to get that many songs together," Budjerah said.

"I think I've written maybe three albums in the meantime separate from just these 11 tracks, and it started in 2022; I'd won two ARIAs and I really wanted to make an album.

"I didn't feel creatively satisfied, just having these little short bursts of creativity with the EPs."

Budjerah, 24, spent a month writing "a tonne of songs" with Australian singer/songwriter Matt Corby for what would have been his debut album, but just one of those songs, titled Video Game, was released, in July 2023.

Platinum and 2x ARIA Award-winning music artist Budjerah has released his debut album Gentleman. (Supplied: Daniel Boud)

In February and March of that year, Budjerah went on tour with Ed Sheeran as the support act for the Australian leg of Sheeran's Mathematics tour.

This coincided with the release of Budjerah's hit single Therapy in February 2023.

"I think the success of Therapy at the beginning of 2023, people just wanted to hear that one song," Budjerah says.

"So, I was on tour, and I was doing two to three shows a week for a year, and then more after that, and I didn't get the time to actually finish the songs, or work on any more songs, because it was all go, go, go, go, go, we need to boost this one song."

A true Gentleman

Gentleman is produced by the Grammy Award-winner Om'Mas Keith (Frank Ocean, Jay-Z), and musically it is inspired by the songs Budjerah grew up listening to.

Gentleman is out now. (Supplied: Warner Music)

The 11 tracks have a timeless R&B/pop sound including the first single, Want You Back, which quickly caught the attention of Elton John.

"I just got a call one day, and they said listen in from here, they're going to play your song on his radio show, Rocket Hour on Apple," Budjerah said.

"And so, I stayed up till the middle of the night to listen to it."

It was a full circle (of life) moment given The Lion King is Budjerah's favourite movie.

The funky, high-energy title track takes its cue from the likes of James Brown, who Budjerah is a big fan of via his uncles and grandfather.

"I felt like it was a fun way to play up the performance aspect of what I do, because everything I do is about the performance," Budjerah says.

"When I'm in the studio, I think about how the song is going to be interpreted live."

Budjerah loves to perform live so much, he even sang at his own wedding to high school sweetheart Sophie Slabb (née Moore), according to Vogue Australia.

Budjerah married his high school sweetheart, Sophie. (Supplied: Elisha Lindsay and Ashi Hilmer courtesy of Vogue Australia)

"I'm lucky I've been able to experience love," Budjerah told the ABC.

"I don't sing nothing that I don't mean.

"I always relate it to my personal experience and my stories."

The catchy Could I Be is exactly what he's talking about.

Budjerah is going on tour to support his new album.

His official tour will kick off in Melbourne on October 31, then he'll head to Anglesea in Victoria, Sydney, and the Gold Coast, before wrapping up in Brisbane on Saturday, November 21.

Budjerah collaborated with a host of esteemed songwriters on Gentleman including the legendary Diane Warren (Celine Dion and Beyoncé) on Even at My Worst.

"She's one of my songwriting heroes," he says.

"And so, getting to meet her, and then getting to sing one of her songs was just a once-in-a-lifetime experience for me."

There were some tracks on the album, however, that felt counterintuitive to Budjerah, who was raised in church to parents who were both musicians — but also pastors.

Those songs are Hard Time and Sinner.

"I thought it was funny, being a little gospel singer from Fingal Head given the song called Sinner," Budjerah said.

"And then a song called Hard Time, a lot of Aboriginal people do a bit of a hard time.

"So, I thought it was a bit of an odd topic, but my dad said, 'do both if you have enough time'.

"My dad just said, 'those two songs are perfect'.

"They weren't the obvious picks for me, but we just had fun with them, and I really enjoyed singing both of them. They fit really well for my voice."

Keeping the faith

Speaking to ABC News from the house he grew up in, Budjerah spun around and held up his Bible when asked if he still carried one around.

"I always keep it with me," he said.

"Usually, some hotels and motels have a Bible in the drawer, but not all the time, and sometimes it's just something that I need.

"So, I carry it with me, and I read it, and my faith has been something that's been really helpful and important to me, especially when I'm on the road and travelling so much, it keeps me together."

Born Budjerah Julum Slabb, the artist is from the small coastal village of Fingal Head in the far north-eastern corner of NSW.

"I had a very fun childhood," he says.

"I enjoyed the music, a very loving family, and some people have a hard time, like, other pastor's kids that I know, but I've been very blessed that I've had super supportive parents and family.

"I got to be a kid, I got to listen to good music, I got to go surfing."

Budjerah says he wants to be a "triple threat". (Supplied: Daniel Boud)

You can still find Budjerah, the eldest of four, in church on a Sunday.

"My grandfather, he goes to a church across the river that I go to, and I try to sneak in, but … I end up singing a song almost every time.

" So, if anyone wants a free concert, you might see me in a church on a Sunday, any old Sunday, I might be singing. "

Finding his voice

Budjerah first burst out on the scene as a fresh-faced teenager on The Voice, but not a single judge (Delta Goodrem, Guy Sebastian, Boy George, Kelly Rowland) turned their chair, despite a standing ovation from the audience.

"It was a pretty wild experience, especially for a 16-year-old," he says.

"I think that that was the first time that I truly experienced heartbreak, as a young person.

"I felt like my whole dream was just crushed.

"But [I] always remember Kelly Rowland just telling me, just keep singing, just keep singing.

"And it'll work out. When it's meant to happen, it'll happen."

It's not the only audition he's failed to land.

Budjerah says he tried out for the role of Malakai in the Netflix series Heartbreak High.

"Thomas Weatherall got the role. I didn't get the role," Budjerah says.

"So, I think it's really cool that I still get to be in the show somehow, with my music in there [on the soundtrack]."

He still has ambitions to act.

"I want to be a triple threat, so singing, dancing, acting," he says.

"I write songs as well, so, I guess my personal dream is to be the ultimate entertainer, so I spend a lot of time practising my dances and singing every day, and dancing every day, and acting.

"What got me into performing was doing the school musicals and school plays.

"So, I always thought maybe one day I'd come back to acting."

Gentleman is out now and Budjerah's official album tour will kick off in Melbourne in October.

World.title: With polar travel increasing in popularity, it’s best to book years ahead
World.content:
Travel newsCruises With polar travel increasing in popularity, it’s best to book years ahead Brian Johnston July 24, 2026 — 10:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Passenger numbers in the Arctic have jumped in double-digit percentages in the last couple of years and, according to an Expedition Cruise Network survey, the Arctic and Antarctic have led the increased demand among all expedition destinations in 2025. The boom is reflective of a wider travel trend towards more remote places and increasing cruise interest from younger generations, but has also been fuelled by media attention directed at Arctic destinations such as Greenland. Part of the Arctic’s popularity lies in its easy accessibility compared to Antarctica. Aurora Expeditions New regulations introduced in 2025 aimed at protecting the Arctic’s fragile environment and wildlife reflect growing pressure from cruise ships. Svalbard limited access to ships with 200 passengers or fewer and has regulated the distance ships can approach polar bears. Unlike Antarctica, the Arctic is loosely defined. Few ships can penetrate the Arctic icepack or get near the North Pole. The main destinations are Svalbard, Canada, Iceland and Greenland. Then there’s Alaska and Norway, although their most-cruised destinations are below the Arctic Circle.



Expedition cruises might concentrate on one area, join up several, or occasionally make long intrepid journeys through the Northwest Passage, which has been traversed by fewer than 500 ships in history. 



Among the more recognisable names in cruising that offer comprehensive Arctic programs are Aurora Expeditions, HX, National Geographic-Lindblad, Scenic, Seabourn and Silversea. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips I rarely come back from a trip changed – until I went here Lee Tulloch Travel columnist Aurora Expeditions has 15 polar journeys in the 2027 season on its ships Greg Mortimer and Sylvia Earle, with dedicated solo cabins attracting no single supplement on every sailing. Among them is a photography cruise in Iceland and Greenland, and another focused on polar bears in Svalbard. Silversea is offering 20 cruises on Silver Wind and Silver Endeavour that visit more than 70 destinations across Greenland and Canada. National Geographic-Lindblad Expeditions too has an expanded season, including an itinerary between Greenland and Newfoundland, and one that concentrates on Baffin Island. Meanwhile, Scenic has rolled out several new itineraries for 2027, among them a 12-day expedition to the national parks of East Greenland and Iceland, and a 15-day journey from the Norwegian fjords as far as Svalbard.



Many boutique expedition companies also operate in the Arctic, such as Albatross, AE, Quark and Secret Atlas. Last year G Adventures returned after a six-year hiatus. This May, Aqua Expeditions launches 30-guest icebreaker-superyacht Aqua Lares, which will sail five- to 14-night expeditions through Svalbard and the Norwegian Arctic, or combine the Arctic with Scottish islands.

World.title: What a viral car crash video reveals about Nigel Farage
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK politics What a viral car crash video reveals about Nigel Farage David Crowe July 24, 2026 — 10:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A car crash video has just confirmed a basic truth of British politics: yelling at Nigel Farage does not stop him. The video showed a woman driving past the Reform UK leader while he stood on a footpath with a group of local residents near the English town of Clacton. Loading The driver then did what many critics of the right-wing populist want to do. She yelled abuse that sounded like one word: “wanker”. And then she crashed her car. She drove her small grey Vauxhall into the BMW in front of her, seeing too late that it was stopped at a traffic light. “She won’t be doing that again,” Farage said on the video, which appeared to be taken by one of his supporters on Tuesday.



He also posted the video on social media, adding: “That’s what you call instant karma.” John Lennon would no doubt wince at his song title being used by a politician who is reviled by progressive Britain for leading the country out of the European Union, declaring the country to be broken, warning against asylum seekers and vowing to slash migration. Despite his recent setbacks, YouGov data suggests Farage remains the UK’s most popular politician. Getty Images But Farage put the video to good use, laughing at his critics as his post on X reached five million people. There’s no doubt Farage has challenges ahead. He has just quit his constituency of Clacton and dared his critics to run against him in a byelection, only to discover that his main opponent will be a man who wears a rubbish bin on his head for a laugh. The big mystery about the contest is whether Count Binface can keep the joke from going stale by polling day on August 13.



And the Clacton byelection is only being forced on voters because Farage was angry about an independent inquiry into donations he received from dubious sources, not least George Cottrell, an aristocratic crypto investor known as “Posh George” and once convicted of fraud. That’s awkward. The inquiry will resume when, as is likely, he returns to the House of Commons. View post on X But yelling at Farage does not work, as the woman in the small grey car learned to her cost. The Labour government thought it could dismiss Farage but has instead crumbled in the face of his attacks and its own mistakes over the past two years. The toppling of Keir Starmer as prime minister and the urgent elevation of Andy Burnham in his place prove this point. Farage seems to gain power when pilloried – a trait he shares with One Nation’s Pauline Hanson. Most attacks on him only make him stronger by amplifying his message. This is most obvious when he is publicly flayed for the harshness of his immigration policy, such as his desire to deport asylum seekers. For many voters, the harshness is the point. Farage is unlike Hanson, however, in at least two ways. Firstly, he has a better grasp of the political spectrum. He knows that fringe figures on the far right, like protest agitator Tommy Robinson, scare the public with their sheer aggression. Farage has frozen out Robinson and others like him. Hanson, by contrast, will not admit she made a mistake when she befriended Robinson on her recent visit to England.



Fellow travellers: Pauline Hanson with Nigel Farage in London last week. Facebook Secondly, he is a far more capable advocate than Hanson. He is a good public speaker and knows how to mix humour with his dire warnings about the future. This is partly because he has a big ego and wants to entertain, even if he’s short of useful policies to fix broken Britain. When Farage spoke at the Conservative Political Action Conference in London one week ago, roaming the stage without a lectern or notes, he mocked Burnham for looking down at his notes too often during a recent speech. “I put it to you that if a political leader is incapable of standing before an audience and stringing a couple of sentences together, they might be doing the job more out of personal ambition than out of conviction and belief in the country,” said Farage. When Burnham appeared in Downing Street three days later to formally take the job of prime minister, he made a point of speaking to the media without a lectern or notes. It was a small sign of the way Burnham has to lift his game in the attempt to beat his populist rival.



The opinion polls have Farage in front, although it is too soon to measure the honeymoon period for Burnham. The latest YouGov survey, dated July 20, suggested Reform had 23 per cent support, ahead of Labour on 20 per cent and the Conservative Party on 21 per cent. The Reform vote slipped by two percentage points over the previous two weeks. Prime Minister Andy Burnham watches the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony from the royal box in Glasgow on Thursday. Getty Images The wild card in British politics is Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has the potential to demolish Farage if she can lift her party’s vote above his. Burnham should be able to see off the threat from Farage. Labour has 403 seats in the House of Commons, while Reform has seven. The next general election is not due until August 2029. A serious party of government should be able to hold its nerve. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. But he needs to heed this Aussie’s advice



So far, however, Burnham is yet to really take on Farage where it counts. The new prime minister has outlined three new policies. He has temporarily scrapped the 5 per cent consumption tax on electricity bills, capped bus fares at £2 ($3.80), and cut business taxes on pubs and clubs by 20 per cent. All three policies are practical, popular and have a symbolic impact. They are aimed at showing voters that Burnham “gets” the need to act on the cost of living. And nobody should be blamed for wanting to save British pubs. Burnham’s real challenge, however, is to come up with an economic growth plan without breaking the national budget when debt is high and the bond markets are nervous. Just as importantly, he has to respond to community anxiety about migration when 70 per cent of voters think the intake is too high. The simple fact is that Labour has not “stopped the boats”. On Wednesday, another 172 asylum seekers arrived in three boats from France, collected by UK border officials in the English Channel. Related Article UK election A man dressed as a rubbish bin emerges as Farage’s biggest rival



About 36,000 people arrived by small boat in the year to the end of May. This was down 13 per cent on the previous year, but many voters want more drastic action. Voters may rally to Burnham if the new prime minister can prove he has a growth agenda and can fix the nation’s problems. They may tire of Farage if an independent inquiry uncovers more about those dubious donations. But they are unlikely to respond to yelling in the street. Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Play on: Geelong superstar Dangerfield agrees to deal for 2027 Jake Niall July 24, 2026 — 10:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Geelong and Patrick Dangerfield have agreed to a contract for 2027, confirming that the Cats’ superstar veteran will play on into his 20th AFL season. The Cats and their skipper have reached agreement on terms for a one-year deal for 2027, meaning Dangerfield will play on as he wished and push towards the 400-game mark, according to industry sources familiar with Dangerfield’s deal, speaking anonymously to discuss player contracts. Patty Dangerfield has agreed to terms with Geelong to play on in 2027. AFL Photos via Getty Images Dangerfield, who was drafted by the Adelaide Crows in 2007, will suit up for his 12th season at Geelong, an astonishing return for a player and club who joined forces for the 2016 season and helped arrest a potential slide for the Cats. Dangerfield was due to play his 15th game of 2026 on Friday night against the Demons and the 375th of his career, having surmounted a calf injury that saw him miss games from rounds two to five this season.





Like several other Geelong greats, including the retired Joel Selwood and Tom Hawkins, Dangerfield has played well into his 30s on significantly reduced dollars in his twilight years - a situation echoed at Collingwood, where Scott Pendlebury, Steele Sidebottom and Jeremy Howe have sustained careers into their mid-30s or beyond. Geelong’s capacity to keep veterans playing on at a high level in to their 30s on moderate or reduced contracts has assisted the Cats in recruiting select players from rival clubs. They have been the leading contender for Giants’ skipper and free agent Toby Greene should he leave and have remained interested in St Kilda ruckman Rowan Marshall, whom the Saints retained despite Marshall’s bid for a trade to Geelong last October.
