World.title: Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran as oil hits $US100 a barrel again
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran as oil hits $US100 a barrel again Michael Koziol Updated July 24, 2026 — 10:22am ,first published July 24, 2026 — 6:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Oil is trading above $US100 for the first time since the last phase of the Iran war after Houthi rebels fired at two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, prompting US President Donald Trump to warn of bigger strikes against the Iranian regime and its surrogates. The price of Brent crude rose more than 8 per cent on Thursday (US time), amid widespread fears that Houthi attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait will disrupt shipping in another crucial waterway. President Donald Trump on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Trump warned that if the Iran-backed militants in Yemen fired on another ship, he would inflict “major military punishment” on Iran and the Houthis themselves – “who I am very disappointed with in that they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart”. The president also told US news site Axios that he was considering a “massive attack, bigger than ever before” against Iran, and that the military was prepared to execute.



The US launched its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran at 8.45am on Friday (AEST), with strikes “aimed to hold Iran accountable and diminish threats from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to commercial shipping”. Earlier, Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf seized on the rapidly rising oil price to declare victory. “They wanted to punish Iran. Punished themselves with triple-digit oil instead,” he wrote on X. Despite the attacks, two supertankers carrying an estimated 4 million barrels of Saudi oil exited the Red Sea through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Thursday, shipping data showed, apparently escaping the Houthis’ announced blockade. The Singapore-flagged tanker Xin Long Yang, which made a U-turn and paused in the middle of the Red Sea on Tuesday, resumed its journey south, followed by the Chinese-flagged tanker Cosnew Lake. Both exited the Red Sea later on Thursday, the data showed.



Gregory Brew, an Iran and oil analyst at the Eurasia Group consultancy, said some cargo vessels were turning around and heading north, with at least one large tanker offloading some of its load to cross the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean Sea. It was “a reminder that the Houthis can ‘disrupt’ crude flows, but they can’t stop them, Hormuz-style, from reaching their destination”, Brew said on X. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri Meanwhile, the US House of Representatives again passed a resolution calling on the president to stop the war against Iran unless it was specifically authorised by Congress, after four Republicans crossed the floor. The resolution carries no practical effect, and it stalled in the Senate. Democrats used the rising price of oil to sharpen their attacks on Trump ahead of the summer congressional recess.



“The American people are against this war,” said Chuck Schumer, leader of the Democrats in the Senate, adding that it had “no direction or purpose”. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “They’re definitely against paying over four bucks for a gallon of gas.” Speaking at an event spruiking data centres, Trump defended the ongoing war, noting it was far shorter and less deadly than American campaigns in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq. “We want to get it over with, and we want to do it right, but we have to do what we came to do,” he said.



Trump also attempted to impose a caveat on a deal signed with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that provides US companies access to the kingdom’s civilian nuclear energy program – a controversial move worth billions of dollars for those American firms. Related Article Middle East at war Houthis target Saudi ships as Trump repeats threat to hit Iran’s bridges, power plants In a TruthSocial post, the president said the deal was conditional on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, an initiative from Trump’s first term by which Arab nations normalise their relations with Israel. Riyadh has long insisted that it must see meaningful progress towards a two-state solution for Palestine before it would consider joining the Accords. The deal announced on Wednesday made no mention of Saudi Arabian policy on Israel changing, and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt provided no further information at a briefing.



“If they don’t join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off,” she said of Trump’s position. “This agreement is still being worked out. It will eventually hopefully be finalised ... with the condition that the president spoke about this morning.” The effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, on top of fresh attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, has raised concerns of a spike in oil prices. AP With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Star, humbug! Johnny Depp charms as cranky Scrooge in Comic-Con stunt
World.content:
CultureMoviesPop culture Star, humbug! Johnny Depp charms as cranky Scrooge in Comic-Con stunt Michael Idato July 24, 2026 — 10:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When you walk through the crowd at the annual San Diego Comic-Con, you run into everyone: Batman, a couple of Wonder Women, the cast of Monty Python and the Holy Grail. And even Charles Dickens’ iconic literary villain, the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge. But the crowds swarming this year’s event got a little more than they bargained for when Scrooge made a surprise appearance in the middle of the city’s Gaslamp quarter, outside the hastily assembled accounting offices of Scrooge & Marley. Johnny Depp appears as Ebenezer Scrooge at Comic-Con 2026. Behind the Victorian frock coat, top hat and prosthetic makeup was none other than actor Johnny Depp, who is playing Ebenezer Scrooge in a new film adaptation of Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, titled Ebenezer. Even the setting – San Diego’s Gaslamp quarter – has a name that comfortably evokes the chilling setting of the horror-adjacent story about a miserable old man visited by the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future. Though the fake show was a bit of a push on a summer day when the mercury pushed close to 30 degrees.



Like many such stunts at Comic-Con, there was no pre-announcement. Keen-eyed fans in the area last night would have seen contractors fitting the Victorian Gothic facade to the building, and dumping the fake snow to complete the setting. But as launches go, it was a fitting kick-off for the Ebenezer marketing campaign, and a solid start to San Diego Comic-Con’s four-day movies-toys-and-TV celebration. Welcome to crazy town … 2026 San Diego Comic-Con gets under way. AP Almost 200,000 people will swarm around the heart of San Diego for the world’s biggest annual Comic-Con. Close to 150,000 of those will push through the turnstiles; the balance will crowd the surrounding neighbourhood, where film, TV and game studios have taken over storefronts and turned them into “activations” like the Ebenezer stunt. They range from the Paramount+ Lodge, with a Star Trek-themed bar and Dutton Ranch-inspired mock cattle-runs, to immersive experiences based on the upcoming HBO series Stuart Fails to Save the Universe and Lanterns, and the Apple TV+ series Silo.



As a cultural moment, San Diego Comic-Con is the expression of a shared childhood: vintage toys tucked into boxes under the bed, costumes for dress-up, posters and action figures to create the wallpaper of fantasy micro-verses. For four and a half days a year, Comic-Con is all of those things, come out to play. But it is also an intersection of movie and TV marketing, the multibillion-dollar toy world, and the strange and vast world of comic books, once cheap, mass-produced weeklies aimed at kids, now a global business with adult wallets cleanly in its cross-hairs. Day one … the cast of Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender meet the fans at Comic-Con. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell Inside the San Diego Convention Centre, there are panels promoting projects and tackling various topics and pop culture themes. Retailers and distributors are selling toys and merchandise. And studios have created vast displays, including a crowd hit showing off the newly unveiled costumes from Avengers Doomsday, this year’s big Christmas movie ticket. There are Star Wars toys, LEGO toys, DC Comics-branded toys and, in a nod to the old school hipsters, newly minted reprints of Mad Magazine’s Issue #1 being given away. And if you thought comic books were in short supply, there is a rabbit warren of alleyways filled with vendors, selling everything from dusty old copies of the classics to brand-new editions of iconic comic lines like The Avengers and Batman.



Editor's pick Podcasts The Odyssey has called it: Guilt is good Still to come: a weekend which will feature panels for the Apple TV movie Matchbox, Amazon’s The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power and Blade Runner 2099, the new HBO DC Comics spin-off Lanterns, about the Green Lantern Corps, and Saturday’s big ticket: the Marvel panel, in which fans expect to get their first glimpse of Avengers: Doomsday. San Diego Comic-Con, the first event of its type in the world, which has since spawned an army of similar fan events dressed up as comic book conventions around the world, launched in 1970, and it is estimated the event sinks as much as $US150 million ($215 million) into the local San Diego economy. San Diego Comic-Con runs until Monday, Australian time.

World.title: Love hurts. These two novels twist the knife
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Love hurts. These two novels twist the knife Thuy On July 24, 2026 — 10:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Both Lillian Telford’s Lovesick and Laura McPhee-Browne’sWorry Doll explore not just the heady rush of love, but its accompanying less salubrious sidekicks: limerence, addiction, jealousy, self-destruction and heartbreak. Telford’s debut novel treads familiar ground, covering, as it does, the milieu of Gen Z angst not dissimilar to the works of Sally Rooney, Diana Reid and Madeleine Gray. Gabby and Gordon are in their early 20s; they met on the dance floor in Brisbane’s West End on a glittering night of pill-popping decadence. There’s an instant pull together as their bodies move to the beat, enough spark and heat to kickstart a tentative relationship, but not long after, we’re made aware that their connection has broken. They love me, they love me not. Getty Images There was already a sense of foreboding in this deviation from the usual meet-cute that picks away at the glossiness of typical romcom dramatics. On their first night together, Gabby asked him if he’d ever wondered how abrupt love is, while Gordon worried that she was “a shadow he might not be able to catch”. The narrative slowly unspools to reveal the circumstances of their rupture.



Telford shifts between the perspectives of both protagonists, but the chapters are not in chronological order, so reading Lovesick can feel a bit discombobulating. Sometimes the pair are together, and other times they are apart, with many factors that influence or contribute to their estrangement. Both are shaped by trauma. Gordon has never recovered from the loss of his mother, who left his family when he was young. Gabby’s own emotional attachment to her parents is shallow compared to her fierce but sometimes misguided loyalty to her best friend, Róisín. Photo: Gordon and Gabby’s personality flaws are brought to the fore once they fall and struggle to remain in love. They may be desperate for connection, but both suffer from crippling anxiety and a low sense of self-worth, which mitigates against a mutually satisfying relationship. A happy ending is not assured. Telford writes convincingly about the messiness of desire in contemporary times and the historical fractures that need to be healed before one can even start to think about blending one’s life with another equally flawed individual. Despite their privileged middle-class backgrounds (Gordon’s a manager for a theatre space; Gabby works part-time in a bookshop when she’s not studying literature at university), there are tropes in Lovesick reminiscent of those in the ’90s grunge literary movement. Within its “spit and alcohol” pages, there is plenty of casual sex, lust, drug use, alienation, loneliness, and disaffection. Laura McPhee Browne’s third novel, Worry Doll, also surveys the bumpy terrain of romantic and sexual obsession.



Even though Heloise and Ernie have been a couple for eight years, and while their relationship is mostly fulfilling, Heloise is wilfully prepared to sabotage it by daydreaming about her recent fling with a university student, Lacey, who at 24, is 12 years younger than her. Since their random encounter on a train, the older woman has been infatuated. Though Heloise is self-aware and admits to herself that she is “duplicitous, weak”, she can’t control her desire for Lacey. Each time the phone pings with messages from her beloved, “the words light her quickly, like a match”. Meanwhile, Ernie is described as a towel, “absorbent and reliable. He is always there to make sure those around him are comfortable”. Ernie may be a safe space, but Heloise is thrumming with boredom in their long-term routines and is desperate for novelty and excitement. Photo: Worry Doll’s narrative is split into two: the first, “Lost”, is set in inner Melbourne in summer, and is seen from Heloise’s perspective; the second, “Found”, takes place 18 months later in Wellington’s winter, and admits us into Lacey’s headspace. The wildness inside Heloise’s overheated mind as she pines for the unobtainable, and the restless confusion of Lacey as she navigates young adulthood, are presented in intimate and visceral scenes. That both women have very different ideas about the strength and viability of their connections to one another is made clear. Heloise is the one who is lovesick and lust-fuelled, while Lacey approaches their interactions with a non-committal nonchalance. It’s only later that we see how vulnerable she can be, how an ex-girlfriend can make her “lavish, and open like a sore”. The author has surveyed queer friendships and the agonies of unrequited love in her debut book, Cherry Beach, and she brings the same level of sensitivity and complexities to Worry Doll. Her sensory detail of place – from the gentrified suburbs of Melbourne to the tumultuous weather of New Zealand – is beautifully evoked.

Among them is a photography cruise in Iceland and Greenland, and another focused on polar bears in Svalbard. Silversea is offering 20 cruises on Silver Wind and Silver Endeavour that visit more than 70 destinations across Greenland and Canada. National Geographic-Lindblad Expeditions too has an expanded season, including an itinerary between Greenland and Newfoundland, and one that concentrates on Baffin Island. Meanwhile, Scenic has rolled out several new itineraries for 2027, among them a 12-day expedition to the national parks of East Greenland and Iceland, and a 15-day journey from the Norwegian fjords as far as Svalbard.



Many boutique expedition companies also operate in the Arctic, such as Albatross, AE, Quark and Secret Atlas. Last year G Adventures returned after a six-year hiatus. This May, Aqua Expeditions launches 30-guest icebreaker-superyacht Aqua Lares, which will sail five- to 14-night expeditions through Svalbard and the Norwegian Arctic, or combine the Arctic with Scottish islands.

World.title: What a viral car crash video reveals about Nigel Farage
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK politics What a viral car crash video reveals about Nigel Farage David Crowe July 24, 2026 — 10:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A car crash video has just confirmed a basic truth of British politics: yelling at Nigel Farage does not stop him. The video showed a woman driving past the Reform UK leader while he stood on a footpath with a group of local residents near the English town of Clacton. Loading The driver then did what many critics of the right-wing populist want to do. She yelled abuse that sounded like one word: “wanker”. And then she crashed her car. She drove her small grey Vauxhall into the BMW in front of her, seeing too late that it was stopped at a traffic light. “She won’t be doing that again,” Farage said on the video, which appeared to be taken by one of his supporters on Tuesday.



He also posted the video on social media, adding: “That’s what you call instant karma.” John Lennon would no doubt wince at his song title being used by a politician who is reviled by progressive Britain for leading the country out of the European Union, declaring the country to be broken, warning against asylum seekers and vowing to slash migration. Despite his recent setbacks, YouGov data suggests Farage remains the UK’s most popular politician. Getty Images But Farage put the video to good use, laughing at his critics as his post on X reached five million people. There’s no doubt Farage has challenges ahead. He has just quit his constituency of Clacton and dared his critics to run against him in a byelection, only to discover that his main opponent will be a man who wears a rubbish bin on his head for a laugh. The big mystery about the contest is whether Count Binface can keep the joke from going stale by polling day on August 13.



And the Clacton byelection is only being forced on voters because Farage was angry about an independent inquiry into donations he received from dubious sources, not least George Cottrell, an aristocratic crypto investor known as “Posh George” and once convicted of fraud. That’s awkward. The inquiry will resume when, as is likely, he returns to the House of Commons. View post on X But yelling at Farage does not work, as the woman in the small grey car learned to her cost. The Labour government thought it could dismiss Farage but has instead crumbled in the face of his attacks and its own mistakes over the past two years. The toppling of Keir Starmer as prime minister and the urgent elevation of Andy Burnham in his place prove this point. Farage seems to gain power when pilloried – a trait he shares with One Nation’s Pauline Hanson. Most attacks on him only make him stronger by amplifying his message. This is most obvious when he is publicly flayed for the harshness of his immigration policy, such as his desire to deport asylum seekers. For many voters, the harshness is the point. Farage is unlike Hanson, however, in at least two ways. Firstly, he has a better grasp of the political spectrum. He knows that fringe figures on the far right, like protest agitator Tommy Robinson, scare the public with their sheer aggression. Farage has frozen out Robinson and others like him. Hanson, by contrast, will not admit she made a mistake when she befriended Robinson on her recent visit to England.



Fellow travellers: Pauline Hanson with Nigel Farage in London last week. Facebook Secondly, he is a far more capable advocate than Hanson. He is a good public speaker and knows how to mix humour with his dire warnings about the future. This is partly because he has a big ego and wants to entertain, even if he’s short of useful policies to fix broken Britain. When Farage spoke at the Conservative Political Action Conference in London one week ago, roaming the stage without a lectern or notes, he mocked Burnham for looking down at his notes too often during a recent speech. “I put it to you that if a political leader is incapable of standing before an audience and stringing a couple of sentences together, they might be doing the job more out of personal ambition than out of conviction and belief in the country,” said Farage. When Burnham appeared in Downing Street three days later to formally take the job of prime minister, he made a point of speaking to the media without a lectern or notes. It was a small sign of the way Burnham has to lift his game in the attempt to beat his populist rival.



The opinion polls have Farage in front, although it is too soon to measure the honeymoon period for Burnham. The latest YouGov survey, dated July 20, suggested Reform had 23 per cent support, ahead of Labour on 20 per cent and the Conservative Party on 21 per cent. The Reform vote slipped by two percentage points over the previous two weeks. Prime Minister Andy Burnham watches the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony from the royal box in Glasgow on Thursday. Getty Images The wild card in British politics is Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who has the potential to demolish Farage if she can lift her party’s vote above his. Burnham should be able to see off the threat from Farage. Labour has 403 seats in the House of Commons, while Reform has seven. The next general election is not due until August 2029. A serious party of government should be able to hold its nerve. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Burnham is a devastatingly good politician. But he needs to heed this Aussie’s advice



So far, however, Burnham is yet to really take on Farage where it counts. The new prime minister has outlined three new policies. He has temporarily scrapped the 5 per cent consumption tax on electricity bills, capped bus fares at £2 ($3.80), and cut business taxes on pubs and clubs by 20 per cent. All three policies are practical, popular and have a symbolic impact. They are aimed at showing voters that Burnham “gets” the need to act on the cost of living. And nobody should be blamed for wanting to save British pubs. Burnham’s real challenge, however, is to come up with an economic growth plan without breaking the national budget when debt is high and the bond markets are nervous. Just as importantly, he has to respond to community anxiety about migration when 70 per cent of voters think the intake is too high. The simple fact is that Labour has not “stopped the boats”. On Wednesday, another 172 asylum seekers arrived in three boats from France, collected by UK border officials in the English Channel. Related Article UK election A man dressed as a rubbish bin emerges as Farage’s biggest rival



About 36,000 people arrived by small boat in the year to the end of May. This was down 13 per cent on the previous year, but many voters want more drastic action. Voters may rally to Burnham if the new prime minister can prove he has a growth agenda and can fix the nation’s problems. They may tire of Farage if an independent inquiry uncovers more about those dubious donations. But they are unlikely to respond to yelling in the street. World.title: Play on: Geelong superstar Dangerfield agrees to deal for 2027
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Play on: Geelong superstar Dangerfield agrees to deal for 2027 Jake Niall July 24, 2026 — 10:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Geelong and Patrick Dangerfield have agreed to a contract for 2027, confirming that the Cats’ superstar veteran will play on into his 20th AFL season. The Cats and their skipper have reached agreement on terms for a one-year deal for 2027, meaning Dangerfield will play on as he wished and push towards the 400-game mark, according to industry sources familiar with Dangerfield’s deal, speaking anonymously to discuss player contracts. Patty Dangerfield has agreed to terms with Geelong to play on in 2027. AFL Photos via Getty Images Dangerfield, who was drafted by the Adelaide Crows in 2007, will suit up for his 12th season at Geelong, an astonishing return for a player and club who joined forces for the 2016 season and helped arrest a potential slide for the Cats. Dangerfield was due to play his 15th game of 2026 on Friday night against the Demons and the 375th of his career, having surmounted a calf injury that saw him miss games from rounds two to five this season.





Like several other Geelong greats, including the retired Joel Selwood and Tom Hawkins, Dangerfield has played well into his 30s on significantly reduced dollars in his twilight years - a situation echoed at Collingwood, where Scott Pendlebury, Steele Sidebottom and Jeremy Howe have sustained careers into their mid-30s or beyond. Geelong’s capacity to keep veterans playing on at a high level in to their 30s on moderate or reduced contracts has assisted the Cats in recruiting select players from rival clubs. They have been the leading contender for Giants’ skipper and free agent Toby Greene should he leave and have remained interested in St Kilda ruckman Rowan Marshall, whom the Saints retained despite Marshall’s bid for a trade to Geelong last October. World.title: Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran as oil hits $US100 a barrel again
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump warns of ‘massive attack’ on Iran as oil hits $US100 a barrel again Michael Koziol Updated July 24, 2026 — 10:22am ,first published July 24, 2026 — 6:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Oil is trading above $US100 for the first time since the last phase of the Iran war after Houthi rebels fired at two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, prompting US President Donald Trump to warn of bigger strikes against the Iranian regime and its surrogates. The price of Brent crude rose more than 8 per cent on Thursday (US time), amid widespread fears that Houthi attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait will disrupt shipping in another crucial waterway. President Donald Trump on Thursday. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Trump warned that if the Iran-backed militants in Yemen fired on another ship, he would inflict “major military punishment” on Iran and the Houthis themselves – “who I am very disappointed with in that they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart”. The president also told US news site Axios that he was considering a “massive attack, bigger than ever before” against Iran, and that the military was prepared to execute.



The US launched its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran at 8.45am on Friday (AEST), with strikes “aimed to hold Iran accountable and diminish threats from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to commercial shipping”. Earlier, Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf seized on the rapidly rising oil price to declare victory. “They wanted to punish Iran. Punished themselves with triple-digit oil instead,” he wrote on X. Despite the attacks, two supertankers carrying an estimated 4 million barrels of Saudi oil exited the Red Sea through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Thursday, shipping data showed, apparently escaping the Houthis’ announced blockade. The Singapore-flagged tanker Xin Long Yang, which made a U-turn and paused in the middle of the Red Sea on Tuesday, resumed its journey south, followed by the Chinese-flagged tanker Cosnew Lake. Both exited the Red Sea later on Thursday, the data showed.



Gregory Brew, an Iran and oil analyst at the Eurasia Group consultancy, said some cargo vessels were turning around and heading north, with at least one large tanker offloading some of its load to cross the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean Sea. It was “a reminder that the Houthis can ‘disrupt’ crude flows, but they can’t stop them, Hormuz-style, from reaching their destination”, Brew said on X. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea is another crucial global shipping passage. Graphic: Nathan Perri Meanwhile, the US House of Representatives again passed a resolution calling on the president to stop the war against Iran unless it was specifically authorised by Congress, after four Republicans crossed the floor. The resolution carries no practical effect, and it stalled in the Senate. Democrats used the rising price of oil to sharpen their attacks on Trump ahead of the summer congressional recess.



“The American people are against this war,” said Chuck Schumer, leader of the Democrats in the Senate, adding that it had “no direction or purpose”. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war The real oil shock from the Iran war might be just beginning Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist “They’re definitely against paying over four bucks for a gallon of gas.” Speaking at an event spruiking data centres, Trump defended the ongoing war, noting it was far shorter and less deadly than American campaigns in Vietnam, Afghanistan and Iraq. “We want to get it over with, and we want to do it right, but we have to do what we came to do,” he said.



Trump also attempted to impose a caveat on a deal signed with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that provides US companies access to the kingdom’s civilian nuclear energy program – a controversial move worth billions of dollars for those American firms. Related Article Middle East at war Houthis target Saudi ships as Trump repeats threat to hit Iran’s bridges, power plants In a TruthSocial post, the president said the deal was conditional on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords, an initiative from Trump’s first term by which Arab nations normalise their relations with Israel. Riyadh has long insisted that it must see meaningful progress towards a two-state solution for Palestine before it would consider joining the Accords. The deal announced on Wednesday made no mention of Saudi Arabian policy on Israel changing, and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt provided no further information at a briefing.



“If they don’t join the Abraham Accords, the deal is off,” she said of Trump’s position. “This agreement is still being worked out. It will eventually hopefully be finalised ... with the condition that the president spoke about this morning.” The effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, on top of fresh attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, has raised concerns of a spike in oil prices. AP With Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Star, humbug! Johnny Depp charms as cranky Scrooge in Comic-Con stunt
World.content:
CultureMoviesPop culture Star, humbug! Johnny Depp charms as cranky Scrooge in Comic-Con stunt Michael Idato July 24, 2026 — 10:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When you walk through the crowd at the annual San Diego Comic-Con, you run into everyone: Batman, a couple of Wonder Women, the cast of Monty Python and the Holy Grail. And even Charles Dickens’ iconic literary villain, the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge. But the crowds swarming this year’s event got a little more than they bargained for when Scrooge made a surprise appearance in the middle of the city’s Gaslamp quarter, outside the hastily assembled accounting offices of Scrooge & Marley. Johnny Depp appears as Ebenezer Scrooge at Comic-Con 2026. Behind the Victorian frock coat, top hat and prosthetic makeup was none other than actor Johnny Depp, who is playing Ebenezer Scrooge in a new film adaptation of Dickens’ A Christmas Carol, titled Ebenezer. Even the setting – San Diego’s Gaslamp quarter – has a name that comfortably evokes the chilling setting of the horror-adjacent story about a miserable old man visited by the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future. Though the fake show was a bit of a push on a summer day when the mercury pushed close to 30 degrees.



Like many such stunts at Comic-Con, there was no pre-announcement. Keen-eyed fans in the area last night would have seen contractors fitting the Victorian Gothic facade to the building, and dumping the fake snow to complete the setting. But as launches go, it was a fitting kick-off for the Ebenezer marketing campaign, and a solid start to San Diego Comic-Con’s four-day movies-toys-and-TV celebration. Welcome to crazy town … 2026 San Diego Comic-Con gets under way. AP Almost 200,000 people will swarm around the heart of San Diego for the world’s biggest annual Comic-Con. Close to 150,000 of those will push through the turnstiles; the balance will crowd the surrounding neighbourhood, where film, TV and game studios have taken over storefronts and turned them into “activations” like the Ebenezer stunt. They range from the Paramount+ Lodge, with a Star Trek-themed bar and Dutton Ranch-inspired mock cattle-runs, to immersive experiences based on the upcoming HBO series Stuart Fails to Save the Universe and Lanterns, and the Apple TV+ series Silo.



As a cultural moment, San Diego Comic-Con is the expression of a shared childhood: vintage toys tucked into boxes under the bed, costumes for dress-up, posters and action figures to create the wallpaper of fantasy micro-verses. For four and a half days a year, Comic-Con is all of those things, come out to play. But it is also an intersection of movie and TV marketing, the multibillion-dollar toy world, and the strange and vast world of comic books, once cheap, mass-produced weeklies aimed at kids, now a global business with adult wallets cleanly in its cross-hairs. Day one … the cast of Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender meet the fans at Comic-Con. AP Photo/Richard Shotwell Inside the San Diego Convention Centre, there are panels promoting projects and tackling various topics and pop culture themes. Retailers and distributors are selling toys and merchandise. And studios have created vast displays, including a crowd hit showing off the newly unveiled costumes from Avengers Doomsday, this year’s big Christmas movie ticket. There are Star Wars toys, LEGO toys, DC Comics-branded toys and, in a nod to the old school hipsters, newly minted reprints of Mad Magazine’s Issue #1 being given away. And if you thought comic books were in short supply, there is a rabbit warren of alleyways filled with vendors, selling everything from dusty old copies of the classics to brand-new editions of iconic comic lines like The Avengers and Batman.



Editor's pick Podcasts The Odyssey has called it: Guilt is good Still to come: a weekend which will feature panels for the Apple TV movie Matchbox, Amazon’s The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power and Blade Runner 2099, the new HBO DC Comics spin-off Lanterns, about the Green Lantern Corps, and Saturday’s big ticket: the Marvel panel, in which fans expect to get their first glimpse of Avengers: Doomsday. San Diego Comic-Con, the first event of its type in the world, which has since spawned an army of similar fan events dressed up as comic book conventions around the world, launched in 1970, and it is estimated the event sinks as much as $US150 million ($215 million) into the local San Diego economy. San Diego Comic-Con runs until Monday, Australian time.

World.title: Love hurts. These two novels twist the knife
World.content:
CultureBooksReview Love hurts. These two novels twist the knife Thuy On July 24, 2026 — 10:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Both Lillian Telford’s Lovesick and Laura McPhee-Browne’sWorry Doll explore not just the heady rush of love, but its accompanying less salubrious sidekicks: limerence, addiction, jealousy, self-destruction and heartbreak. Telford’s debut novel treads familiar ground, covering, as it does, the milieu of Gen Z angst not dissimilar to the works of Sally Rooney, Diana Reid and Madeleine Gray. Gabby and Gordon are in their early 20s; they met on the dance floor in Brisbane’s West End on a glittering night of pill-popping decadence. There’s an instant pull together as their bodies move to the beat, enough spark and heat to kickstart a tentative relationship, but not long after, we’re made aware that their connection has broken. They love me, they love me not. Getty Images There was already a sense of foreboding in this deviation from the usual meet-cute that picks away at the glossiness of typical romcom dramatics. On their first night together, Gabby asked him if he’d ever wondered how abrupt love is, while Gordon worried that she was “a shadow he might not be able to catch”. The narrative slowly unspools to reveal the circumstances of their rupture.



Telford shifts between the perspectives of both protagonists, but the chapters are not in chronological order, so reading Lovesick can feel a bit discombobulating. Sometimes the pair are together, and other times they are apart, with many factors that influence or contribute to their estrangement. Both are shaped by trauma. Gordon has never recovered from the loss of his mother, who left his family when he was young. Gabby’s own emotional attachment to her parents is shallow compared to her fierce but sometimes misguided loyalty to her best friend, Róisín. Photo: Gordon and Gabby’s personality flaws are brought to the fore once they fall and struggle to remain in love. They may be desperate for connection, but both suffer from crippling anxiety and a low sense of self-worth, which mitigates against a mutually satisfying relationship. A happy ending is not assured. Telford writes convincingly about the messiness of desire in contemporary times and the historical fractures that need to be healed before one can even start to think about blending one’s life with another equally flawed individual. Despite their privileged middle-class backgrounds (Gordon’s a manager for a theatre space; Gabby works part-time in a bookshop when she’s not studying literature at university), there are tropes in Lovesick reminiscent of those in the ’90s grunge literary movement. Within its “spit and alcohol” pages, there is plenty of casual sex, lust, drug use, alienation, loneliness, and disaffection. Laura McPhee Browne’s third novel, Worry Doll, also surveys the bumpy terrain of romantic and sexual obsession.



Even though Heloise and Ernie have been a couple for eight years, and while their relationship is mostly fulfilling, Heloise is wilfully prepared to sabotage it by daydreaming about her recent fling with a university student, Lacey, who at 24, is 12 years younger than her. Since their random encounter on a train, the older woman has been infatuated. Though Heloise is self-aware and admits to herself that she is “duplicitous, weak”, she can’t control her desire for Lacey. Each time the phone pings with messages from her beloved, “the words light her quickly, like a match”. Meanwhile, Ernie is described as a towel, “absorbent and reliable. He is always there to make sure those around him are comfortable”. Ernie may be a safe space, but Heloise is thrumming with boredom in their long-term routines and is desperate for novelty and excitement. Photo: Worry Doll’s narrative is split into two: the first, “Lost”, is set in inner Melbourne in summer, and is seen from Heloise’s perspective; the second, “Found”, takes place 18 months later in Wellington’s winter, and admits us into Lacey’s headspace. The wildness inside Heloise’s overheated mind as she pines for the unobtainable, and the restless confusion of Lacey as she navigates young adulthood, are presented in intimate and visceral scenes. That both women have very different ideas about the strength and viability of their connections to one another is made clear. Heloise is the one who is lovesick and lust-fuelled, while Lacey approaches their interactions with a non-committal nonchalance. It’s only later that we see how vulnerable she can be, how an ex-girlfriend can make her “lavish, and open like a sore”. The author has surveyed queer friendships and the agonies of unrequited love in her debut book, Cherry Beach, and she brings the same level of sensitivity and complexities to Worry Doll. Her sensory detail of place – from the gentrified suburbs of Melbourne to the tumultuous weather of New Zealand – is beautifully evoked.

World.title: Fijian Drua primed to make history in first-ever Super Rugby Women's home final
World.content:
Fijian Drua v NSW Waratahs

Kick-off: 1:05pm NZT, Saturday 25 July

Venue: Four R Stadium, Ba, Fiji

The Fijian Drua women are ready to re-write their own history when they host their first-ever Super Rugby Women's (Super Rugby W) final at home in Ba on Saturday.

Head coach Mike Legge, who has been part of the set-up since the team's inception in 2022, is confident the team can beat the defending champion NSW Waratahs.

Should the Fijian women defeat the visitors, it will secure them their third Super W title.

A win will also see them battle the winner of the Super Rugby Aupiki final between the Matatū and Blues.

Legge told reporters at news conference on Wednesday that playing a home final is massive for the team, the country and women's sports.

And having seen the team transformed after their first round loss to the Waratahs in Sydney, he is confident his side will match up and be in the running for the title come Saturday.

He said a healthy team environment has also helped in the team's turnaround and winning run since the round one loss.

"The girls have worked really hard and they deserve to be in the final," he said.

"One of the biggest keys to the success is just being enjoying each other's company, making sure while it's been an environment of hard work, it's been a light and fun environment that we've tried to create with the coaches and all the management and the Drua staff here.

"I think with most teams, if the environment's good, you're going to get success. So that's what we've we've built here."

The Drua women's side defeated the Reds 50-17 in the round-robin competition at Ballymore Stadium, Brisbane, on 27 June 2026. Facebook / Fijian Drua

Respect

Legge said the team understood what Waratahs would bring to the game as defending champs and they have respect for the side.

But, at the same time, the players have confidence in themselves as a team and are not awe-struck by the fact that their opponents are laced with Wallaroos.

"We respect the Waratahs. They have been the benchmark pretty much every year," Legge said.

"But for us, it's more about it's more about what we do on Saturday and ensuring that we stick to our process and we feel if we can do that, then then we'll we'll go a long way to getting a victory.

"We expect them to come out as the defending champ, so they're not coming here just to enjoy the scenery. They're coming here to defend their title.

"They probably haven't had the season that they wanted, so, I think they also got a point to prove and we expect nothing less from a a team that's stacked with Wallaroos, and and it's going to be a tough game."

Legge said in the past the Drua women's players would have been in awe of of the opposition, "but now for them, it's just another game, and it's whoever's in front of them, and they'll attack it how they see it".

"With the Waratahs we expect it's going to be a real grand final, and it's going to be a really good game.

"But for us, again, it's just worrying about what our process, where we feel we can attack the Tahs and making sure that we align with it, and then you know hopefully off the back of that we we can get a positive result."

Own game

Legge said they will just focus on their own game, adding they have worked out ways to try and defuse the Waratahs strong points, which is centred in winning the forward pack battles and using their speed along the backline.

He revealed the week has been focused also on ensuring the players are not complacent, which he believes becomes a problem for local sides at critical times.

"Our training yesterday (Tuesday) was quite a nervous one, so you can tell the girls are really switched on for this for this match," he said.

"The biggest message from me is just to stick to their process, you know, stick to what's worked. We're not going to change anything. We're not going to change how we play, and and just let them go out and express themselves in front of a what we hope is a packed out stadium.

"We continue to focus on our collision, and I've been consistent again with my messaging around that. The collisions are where the game is won, and if we can't win that, then you know we're going to struggle."

Legge said the Waratahs have threats all over the field, use their set piece and their lineouts as their strengths and have good playmakers who dictate the game for them.

"We've got to do what we can to nullify those, we've got some plans in place to nullify the threats, but it's going to have to be for the full 80 minutes," he said.

"It just can't be for fits and bursts."

He also pointed at discipline as a key area they will need to be consistent with, after they gave away some uncalled for penalties against the Reds last weekend.

"The Waratah will punish us if if we do the same, so it's pretty much business as usual for us in terms of our work ons."

Legge also pointed to starting off well in the final and being consistent for the full 80 minutes.

"If we can get a good start, that first 20 minutes is really important to us. We believe if we can get set the momentum we can build from that," he said.

"So, against the Waratahs, we've learnt in the past that if we start slow, we're playing catch up. It's massively important for us to to get off to a fly this weekend, and then we'll build build on top of that."

Leadership

Legge was full of praise with the team's leadership group, which features Kolora Tamani, Bitila Tawake and Alfred Fisher.

Tamani will lead the team out against the Waratahs, having been retained at halfback, while both Tawake and Fisher are on the bench as covers for the forward pack.

Legge said the trio have worked together as leaders and with the team in building a bond that makes them stand together especially under pressure during matches.

"Having a good leadership group in place is important, where everyone supports everyone," he said.

"It's just about keeping calm, especially under pressure, walking towards the pressure. I think that is the biggest key for not just our leaders, but also our whole team.

"If we can absorb the pressure, you know, walk towards it, it's gonna go a long way to us winning this competition."

Fans

Legge and the team are hoping that the 4R Electric Stadium in Ba will be packed to the brim on Saturday.

They believe the 8th man has always boosted their performances, especially at home.

"It's hugely important and I think a packed-out Ba stadium is going to make it really uncomfortable for the Waratahs, and that's what we want.

"We want our fans to come out in numbers, come out in force, and just continue to lift and uplift the girls, especially during those down times during games.

"The crowd play a massive part in actually bringing them back up to you know the level we need them. It's a massive occasion, and we just calling out to all the fans to pack out the stadium."

The team

Legge has kept the same lineup that defeated the Reds last weekend in Lautoka for the final.

That will see Karalaini Naisewa running out for her 31st Drua game at loosehead prop, with Tiana Robanakadavu at tighthead and Keleni Marawa at hooker to complete the front row.

Mereoni Nakesa and Carletta Yee pair off at locks, while Nunia Daunimoala, Salaseini Railumu and powerhouse Sulita Waisega at number eight forming the loose trio.

Captain Lomani leads the backline, which will also feature In Varanisese Qoro at 10, wingers Aqela Raitubu (11) Atelaite Buna (14), with the midfield combination of Josivini Naihamu at inside centre and Merewairita Neivoha at outside centre.

Litiana Vueti will run at fullback.

Fijiana Sevens team captain Verenaisi Ditavutu will cover the backline from the bench.

Waratahs expect 'great atmosphere'

The Waratahs have named Wallaroos fullback Caitlyn Halse in their starting lineup for her first start since the opening round of the season.

Her return sees Desiree Miller, playing in her 25th game, move to the wing, whilst Waratahs Player of the Year Amelia Whitaker will come off the bench.

Wallaroos scrumhalf Piper Simons has been cleared to return from a knee injury via the bench and she is joined by flanker Taj Heald as part of a 6-2 bench split.

"The team is extremely excited about the opportunity we have this week to compete for another Super W title," Waratahs coach Mike Ruthven said.

"We have drawn a huge amount of confidence over the last few weeks from training and the way the players performed last weekend in Perth.

"We are expecting a great atmosphere over in Fiji and we can't wait to get over there."
