World.title: Beehive bunker laptops malfunctioned during destructive storm
World.content:
This article has been updated on 24 July to clarify the timeline for NEMA to transition into DIA.

Documents show with a destructive storm bearing down on the South Island last October, some laptops in the Beehive bunker could not access the emergency management system.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) says now that there was no impact, that staff had other devices that did work.

The problem has come to light in a Department of Internal Affairs review released under the Official Information Act of how NEMA was shifted from the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet to the DIA late last year.

The reshuffle, costing just over its $2 million budget, was effective but done hastily over three months and a host of difficulties were underestimated.

"The transfer was framed as a 'lift and shift of NEMA' ... The reality was substantially different to 'lift and shift'," said the review done last November.

"The post-transfer technology support and project structure was underestimated."

In one case this meant that a vendor company failed to fully finish a job leading to the problem with new DIA laptops staff had been issued.

This was not apparent till states of emergency were declared in late October in Canterbury, Southland and parts of Otago.

"It became apparent in the lead-up to an emergency activation that some aspects of the transfer had not been adequately completed by the vendor, meaning NEMA staff were unable to access the emergency environment in the bunker through their DIA devices," said the short review.

But other laptops linked to the National Crisis Management Centre (the bunker under the Beehive) did work.

"Our response activities weren't impacted, which is a good thing," NEMA told RNZ.

"Staff had full access to all applications and tools required to support response activities, and there were no impacts to response operations, support to [Civil Defence] groups or access to systems."

The National Crisis Management Centre and its Auckland centre (NCMC and aNCMC) bunkers (and devices) were still Treasury laptops and in the Treasury NCMC until February 2026.

Emergency Management Minister Mark Mitchell at Kaikōura District Council during a storm earlier this month. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

DIA said it was accountable for making sure the tech worked. Since then it had got Datacom to make technical changes to allow access.

NEMA made the shift between departments in just 10 weeks when it had a lot on its plate.

It had recently embarked on a five-year overhaul of old, fragmented disaster response technologies and introducing new ones, such as a new national warning system, in response to Cyclone Gabrielle. An internal report suggested alongside the tech it must also helm a really big and uncertain cultural shift to be sure of lasting change in the previously fragmented sector.

Last week the agency's fledgling tech failed under pressure, with the civil defence website crashing during a tsunami alert near Te Anau, and its just-launched emergency mobile alert map not quickly updating about either the tsunami or flooding the previous week in Wairoa.

Emergency Management Minister Mark Mitchell said he would be meeting NEMA this week to make sure the website was fixed.

Last year's shift demanded that four agencies cooperated, including Treasury.

Cabinet agreed in April 2025 on the shift and wanted it done fast, starting in June and done by September 25.

"Agencies successfully completed a significant level of work to transfer people, data, and

information," said the 10-page review.

"The overwhelming feedback from NEMA staff is the transfer was well communicated, the

products and services are of a high standard, and the project was delivered by DIA in a

very tight timeframe with minimal disruption to NEMA's core business."

However, there was a very big "but" - the review's section on what went well had seven bullet points and what did not go well had 28 bullet points, for instance:

"As the project progressed, major issues arose relating to information technology and

"Outgoing host agencies [primarily DPMC] were unprepared for the level of work required to transfer NEMA's data out of their agencies and were slow to provide data necessary for a transfer, had not checked data for accuracy, prevented access to trusted vendors to assist with the work, and were critical of DIA for creating more work on limited resources."

"When DIA took over the project leadership, very little of the detailed discovery had been undertaken, requirements were not gathered and a clear scope had not been documented or agreed. This left insufficient time to determine the best transfer approach."

"The budgets did not fully capture the scale of the work."

World.title: Ballooning burial costs spurs call for government to increase funeral subsidy
World.content:
Skyrocketting burial costs in Tauranga has spurred a call for the government to increase its funeral subsidy.

The Funeral Directors Association this week released its latest review of council burial and cremation costs, with most council's having increased their costs between two and four percent this year.

An extreme exception was Tauranga, where burial costs rose 50 percent and ash burial 200 percent.

The centres reviewed showed an average burial cost of $4359. In Tauranga, it had increased from $5614 in 2025 to $8426. An ash burial had increased from $803 to $2425.

The maximum Work and Income Funeral Grant available to struggling families was $2697.43.

"Some really disproportionately high prices there," Funeral Directors Association chief executive Gillian Boyes said.

"It is up to councils to set their own rates. We appreciate that. Our point is that when you're making these massive increases, are you listening to funeral directors and families about what that means for the way that the family can celebrate someone's life and is it really supporting dignity in death when you're having such an enormous jump in one hit?

"It's clear central government is unlikely to increase the Work and Income Funeral Grant enough to cover even the average burial cost, so as the monopoly provider of deathcare infrastructure in many centres, we think councils should do more to support their communities. Every New Zealander deserves dignity in death."

Following the report's this week, the New Zealand Cemeteries and Crematoria Collective was backing the call for the Government to increase the funeral grant as rising costs put increasing pressure on grieving families.

Its chairperson Daniel Chrisp said all New Zealanders should be able to access a dignified farewell regardless of their financial circumstances.

"The cost of a basic burial has increased significantly in recent years. With burial plots in many parts of New Zealand now costing between $3500 and $4000, it is time for the WINZ Funeral Grant to be reviewed so it better reflects the real costs families are facing today."

At the same time, he said, cemetery and crematorium operators were facing their own financial challenges, often operating at a substantial loss, with councils absorbing a significant portion of the actual costs involved.

"Throughout the country, many councils are operating cemetery services with subsidy levels of between 30 and 60 percent in order to keep fees as affordable as possible for their communities," Chrisp said.

"Every New Zealander deserves a dignified farewell. The reality is that councils continue to subsidise these services because they recognise their importance to the community.

"The question many councils are now grappling with is whether cemeteries should operate primarily on a user-pays basis, or whether they are an essential community service that deserves ongoing public subsidy. Regardless of the model chosen, the actual costs must ultimately be met."

He said the collective was concerned about families struggling with the costs of funerals and burials, but said on the flipside that many councils were already making significant contributions to keep cemetery services affordable while balancing increasing operational costs and long-term financial sustainability.

Tauranga City Council's acting head of spaces and places Ross Hudson earlier said cemetery and cremation services were funded entirely through user fees and previously made a loss each year of about $500,000.

This fee increase, Hudson said, moved burial and ash burial fees closer to full cost to support the long-term sustainability of providing the services.

World.title: Police search home owned by well-known Wellington landlord Matthew Ryan
World.content:
A well-known Wellington landlord says a police search at his home is related to art he says he "legitimately purchased".

Police searched the Karaka Bays house on Friday morning.

Two unmarked police cars were parked outside the address, and officers in uniform were seen carrying the items away.

Matthew Ryan says there has "not been a business collapse - the companies are solvent". (File photo) DCM / supplied

Police confirmed they were conducting a preplanned search operation in Karaka Bays.

Ryan has owned more than 100 properties, and regularly spoken to the media about the housing market and property investment.

He had pleaded not guilty to charges including strangulation/suffocation, threatening to kill or cause grievous bodily harm, and unlawfully possessing a firearm.

Eight of his companies, which own numerous properties, appeared to have been placed into interim receivership by the High Court earlier this month.

Ryan said at the time he was appealing the order, and there had "not been a business collapse - the companies are solvent".

"This is a simple case of a former partner applying for an ex parte notice."

A car outside the Karaka Bays property. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

He told RNZ on Friday the search was not related to any receivership.

"It's related to some art that I've legitimately purchased and have a receipt for," he said in a text. "I believe I purchased it off the legal owner."

"I'm as certain as I can be. I've got no reason not to be helpful. This came out of the blue. I'm confident I've done nothing wrong."

World.title: Long-time Wellington party flat shut down by council
World.content:
End of an era as iconic Wellington flat closes Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Walking into 13 Garrett Street in the Wellington CBD, you're welcomed by a wallpaper of gig posters over concrete walls, a display of the home's legacy.

But no more posters will be added, as a complaint to Wellington City Council has forced the cancellation of all events, and the tenants will be exiting to make way for redevelopment.

The home, near the Cuba Street shops, has been the place for gigs, markets, poetry readings, movie nights and more since possibly the late '90s.

The three story building is set to be turned into offices on the upper floors, and a new venue space on the bottom.

The tenants of the home who will be leaving in November - all 16 of them - say the Capital is losing a space for community.

The Wellington City Council received a complaint alleging that the building had been hosting paid live events, which it did not have the permits for.

A pillar of music and arts scene

Flatmates Ollie Warren and Sarah Lee sit on their couch remembering their time hosting.

"It's become quite a pillar of what Wellington music and arts community can look like," Warren said.

A floor to ceiling shared wardrobe sits in the entrance hall, by the front room full of murals and speakers, along with mismatched vintage furniture.

A wooden stage stands at one end of the room, which while it looks peaceful in the daylight, comes alive at night.

In just the past four years, the flatmates said hundreds of people have performed.

In its history of performances, names like Mac Demarco pop up, Welly band Heavy Chest, and founder of music collective Eyegum, Joel Cosgrove who they say had his first gig there at 17.

"Garrett is a place for people to be prototyping and sharing things that aren't quite ready," Lee explained.

A wooden stage stands at one end of the Wellington flat's living room. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The flatmates said they made no income from the events, and any money from ticket sales went to the artists and organisers.

They said they always tried to operate events with safety in mind, and they respect the council trying to keep everyone safe.

"Obviously the council were going to catch up on us at one point," Warren said.

The group has had to cancel over a dozen events planned for this year as a result of the complaint.

Wellington City Council said it had set out its vision and partnership with the creative sector on supporting groups and artists, and providing access to new and under-utilised spaces to host events.

However, it said this support still needs to comply with building and planning regulations, for safety reasons.

The front room is full of murals and speakers and mismatched vintage furniture. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Music journalist Martyn Pepperell remembered going to the flat as a teenager in the late 90s.

He said the music changed with each group of tenants - from techno, drum and bass, electro punk, new rave, to indie dance.

Pepperell said people would team up and do multi-level shows, even on the roof.

A floor to ceiling shared wardrobe sits in the entrance hall. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He compared its closure to if the famous Cuba Street Bucket Fountain vanished.

"For some people this has just been part of the fabric of their life for decades."

Now, Pepperell said the building was at a crossroad moment, and Wellington would have to wait and see how the new venue fit into its history.

"In 10 years time, we may find that that's just another chapter in the bigger story of 13 Garrett Street."

Owners' plans

The owners of the property, Emily and William Broadmore, bought the building late last year with the plan to earthquake strengthen it for redevelopment.

They said the top half of the building will be turned into character offices, and the bottom half will be a venue.

The owners are working with DJ and promoter, Jack Parry, and architect and interior designer Allistar Cox, to develop the bottom floor of the building into an official venue.

The owners said they always knew the home was a party flat, but not that events were being ticketed and publicly advertised.

"This is not how we wanted the end of the era for them."

Flatmates Ollie Warren and Sarah Lee say the flat became a pillar of what the Wellington arts and music community can look like. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

While the owners said an end of the tenancy was always planned for earthquake strengthening and redevelopment, they said they had to begin this conversation sooner than anticipated because of the complaint.

"They always knew this day would come. It's just a real shame that it came as a result of a complaint from council."

With earthquake strengthening starting on the upper floors, the owners said it's possible that lower tenants - thrift shop Dirty Laundry and coffee spot Pour & Twist - could stay slightly longer.

Neighbours say the flat was never a problem

Speaking with neighbours, they say the party flat never bothered them.

Victoria Court Motor Lodge - a hotel next to the flat - said the noise was never an issue.

Owner Liam Wang said the noise didn't worry him, as the city was noisy regardless, and other music venues like The Rogue and Vagabond are close by.

However, he said if the home didn't have the right permits, it was fair for the council to shut it down.

Neighbour Dan Craig said he went to a gig at the flat 20 years ago, and felt it was a real shame it had been shut down.

"That's pretty rank bro."

He said it was part of the fabric of Wellington.

"It's like a little hidden secret, it's a shame."

Could the legacy continue?

While 13 Garrett Street itself is closing, the tenants hope the idea of it can continue at a new address.

The flatmates said they want to continue living in large numbers, and are looking for houses with six-plus bedrooms, where they could continue to host.

World.title: Māori father's fight for dedicated citizenship pathway continues after personal success
World.content:
Even after more than a year living in Aotearoa and having secured citizenship for himself and his three children, John Ruddock is still fighting to create a citizenship pathway for other overseas-born Māori, like him.

Ruddock's mother, Rhonda Bryers, was a singer known as 'The Voice of New Zealand' and later the 'Queen of the South Pacific'. He was born in Australia while she was touring, and raised mostly in Hawaii.

Ruddock (Ngāpuhi) grew up assuming citizenship would not be a problem for his own children, but when he returned with them to Aotearoa he found that as citizenship by descent is limited to one generation, there was no pathway for them.

Without citizenship his children could not enrol in school. He was raising them largely alone, feeding them on $30 a week.

"I just didn't know if people were going to come down the door and actually kick my kids or deport them, you know? It's just it was very scary and I just wouldn't wish any of that on my worst enemy.

"So I just feel there's got to be something that we can create, a tangata whenua pathway or whakapapa pathway, something. Because I don't have any family that's not buried in these soils."

Last year he took a claim to the Waitangi Tribunal, which recommended the Citizenship Act 1977 be amended to establish a tikanga pathway to citizenship that allows for hapū and iwi to assess whakapapa evidence and to extend citizenship by descent to two generations for Māori.

Ultimately Ruddock was able to secure citizenship for himself and his three children, but there has been no movement on a dedicated tangata whenua pathway to citizenship.

"The pathway that I did get... I mean, I don't really think it's considered a pathway. You know, I think I creaked open the door, which I think is the awesome part. It was on the news, and I feel that was important for a possibility of a pathway. But I do feel... we need some more done to prevent this from happening.

"And I feel, I don't think it's a huge threat to the population, to the government, to the economy. I just feel we're tangata whenua, and we have a unique thing having Te Tiriti, you know, and we are always and always will be tangata whenua."

Ruddock believed the problem he faced would only grow as more and more Māori were born to parents who were born in places like Australia and the United States.

"I'm sure a lot of people would love to bring their kids back home once they've, you know, established their life. And I just feel that there needs to be a pathway for that at least, you know?

"0.01 percent of the world's population are Māori and there's not going to be some huge stampede of Māori coming, but there should be at least a pathway set up for the future."

Keisha Castle-Hughes and John Ruddock. Supplied

In his claim to the Waitangi Tribunal, Ruddock was supported by Whale Rider actress Keisha Castle-Hughes, who was born in Australia and whose daughter was born in the United States.

"It was quite surprising that, you know, like the 'whale rider' is having this problem. She's beloved by everyone around the world."

Ruddock said he has had other Māori going through similar situations approach him, but many had given up and left Aotearoa.

Ruddock himself thought about leaving New Zealand.

"It's just going to keep happening, and the most stories I've heard is they've given up and left. So I decided that I'm not going to do that. And so I just stuck to my guns and, you know, I just put my kids first. I mean, that was my main focus, I'm just trying to raise my kids here at home."

Brooke van Velden. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

'No plans to review' - minister

Minister of Internal Affairs Brooke van Velden said she respected the findings of the Waitangi Tribunal.

"However, my position remains the same and I have no plans to review and open up the act.

"I have focused my efforts in this area on work to strengthen the citizenship by grant process with the introduction of a test from late 2027, and ensuring all applicants, no matter their race, receive more timely responses to their application.

"In October 2023, people were waiting an average of 180 days to get a decision on their citizenship by grant application. Now, the average wait time is 53 days."

'They're finding their identities': Whānau settling into life in Aotearoa

Ruddock said after a rocky year he was finally able to put his feet up and settle into his home in Wellington, and his children were flourishing.

"When we first came, I remember my kids said, 'I thought they said America's the land of the free - this is the land of the free. We can just run away, go play in the parks.'

"So, yeah, they love it. They're just getting settled in, finding their identities amongst their peers in school. It's quite a beautiful thing to watch as well.

"So I know this is, as a parent, this is what I wanted to be able to provide for them, which I couldn't in a foreign country."

He said his kids were "sucking up all the culture", including karakia and kapa hakam as well as embracing their Samoan heritage.

Ruddock thanked the Porirua Whānau Centre, which provided support while he was fighting to secure citizenship for his whānau.

"Being a single father of three, I don't really have time to venture out, you know? I don't really hang with people, I talk to kids all the time. So when basically the Whānau Centre, you know, they reached out to me when the news article went out and basically offered so much help.

"If anyone goes through that, you know, just stay strong. And, you know, in anything in life, just stay positive. And if you feel you're doing the right thing, then you probably are.

World.title: Watch: 'Cloud burst' hits Grey District, flooding homes and causing a slip
World.content:
About half-a-dozen homes flooded in the South Island overnight.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) crews responded to flooded homes in Greymouth, Cobden, Brunner and Runanga in the Grey District.

Southern shift manager Lyn Crosson said they also responded to a slip on the road in Cobden.

The scene in Cobden after overnight rain. Supplied / Jonathan Stark

Crosson said they were gearing up for more heavy rain and possible flooding this afternoon.

Cobden resident Jonathan Stark says his rain gauge shows more than 120 millimetres of rain fell in about three hours overnight.

"It was pretty wild weather. It started about three o'clock with heavy rain and then thunderstorms as well. We had 45 minutes of a proper downpour," Stark said.

"Our weather station, we checked this morning and it said we had 129 mills of rain in under three hours.

"We thought the water would have disappeared overnight like it normally does, but we woke up this morning to get ready to go to work and found what we found."

Water was still halfway up the tyres of his ute.

Supplied / Jonathan Stark

His garage was also still under water and he expected his spa pool would also be ruined.

Stark expected the damage to his property could cost a couple of thousand dollars.

He had never seen anything like Friday morning's downpour in his five years on the West Coast.

"I've never seen nothing major like this," Stark said.

"I've seen rain - it rains on the West Coast, but nothing so quick and furious."

His cat remained trapped under the house as they could not access it with the water still surrounding the property, but he was pleased his cat had survived the downpour.

"I can hear the cat crying out to get help but we just can't get to it," Stark said.

Surrounding streets were under water.

"It just happened so quickly," he said.

Supplied / Jonathan Stark

Char Stevens said she was still trapped in her Cobden home.

"We can't go anywhere - that's for sure. We're stuck," she said.

"It's come down from the bonnets of the cars to the tyres now. We're raised so the house is all right but when I waded out before to get wood it was basically up to my knees."

Stevens was woken by thunder early this morning, but it was not until she got out of bed later on that she realised her street looked like a river and water was up to the bonnets of cars.

"All I heard at 3am was the massive thunderstorm," she said.

"I went back to sleep and then my flatmate, when I got up, was like 'come outside'. We opened the door and we couldn't go any further because the water was right up there.

"When it got a bit lighter we could see that it was fully flooded. It's still flooded now but it looks like it's slowly receding. It's just crazy."

More to come

A heavy rain watch had been in place for the Westland Ranges from 8pm on Thursday until 3am on Friday, with heavy rain forecast to move northwards over the North Island on Friday.

Surface flooding in Greymouth, July 2026. Grey District Council

West Coast Emergency Management said on social media it was a "cloud burst style rain event".

"Please take care as first light arrives."

Images uploaded by Grey District Council showed surface flooding in Greymouth.

Surface flooding in Greymouth, July 2026. Grey District Council

Surface flooding in Greymouth, July 2026. Grey District Council

State Highway 7 was closed between Greymouth and Stillwater. The New Zealand Transport Agency advised road users to avoid the area or delay their journey if possible.

The council said parts of Wickes Street, Richmond Street, Bright Street, Barkley Place, Peel Street, and Sturge Street, all had high surface water, and there were reports of a tree down on Taylorville Road.

Heather Keats with details of this weekend’s cold snap Morning Report Download MP3 4m

MetService head of weather Heather Keats told Morning Report the heavy rain would head up the west of the country over the next couple of days.

"Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy," she explained.

"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.

"But then we're left with a very cold southerly flow. So we've got every type of weather coming over the next sort of 48 hours."

Localised clean-up

Grey District Mayor Tania Gibson. Supplied / Frank Film

Grey District Mayor Tania Gibson said the rain had eased for the moment, but more showers were expected later in the day.

"Our crews have been out since two o'clock this morning, and now that we're in the light of day, there's a lot of assessment going on, there's a lot of debris to clear, there's still road closures in the area and we're trying to find out who's been affected the most.

"But... some of those outer-lying suburbs have been affected and we had a lot of rain come through on the catchment on the hills, which has brought a lot of rain down into town and to those areas and which has brought a lot of debris down as well."

She said there would be a reasonably significant clean-up ahead.

"I was at home, but I was up because we had some poor little lambs in the paddock outside that were crying their hearts out. So, but we do have rain events quite often, but it's hard to assess until you start getting the reports because sometimes, nothing happens, but when they happen in those isolated areas, it's very quick.

World.title: US hits New Zealand with higher 12.5 percent tariff
World.content:
The US is set to impose new tariffs ranging from 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, including New Zealand, as the Trump administration looks to rebuild its tariff regime.

New Zealand and Australia face a 12.5 percent tariff, while major trading partners including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea were also targeted.

It comes after the US Supreme Court ruled the administration's previous so-called Liberation Day tariffs were illegal. The new levies replace the temporary Section 122 tariff imposed after that court decision, due to expire on 24 July.

US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer claimed the new tariffs were designed to combat imports made with forced labour - a claim previously rejected by New Zealand.

The new tariffs are set to come into effect from just after 4.01pm (New Zealand time) on Friday.

The US government's notice said New Zealand's tariff rate was based on USTR's findings from its investigation into New Zealand.

Trade policy consultant Charles Finny said the decision was not a surprise.

"This is exactly as we were anticipating," he said.

Finny said there was still uncertainty over how long the tariffs would remain in place, particularly if they were challenged in US courts.

"I think exporters should be planning on these 12 or 12.5 percent tariffs applying for many months," he said.

In a statement, Greer said: "President Trump recognises that decades of moral suasion have not eradicated forced labour from global supply chains.

"The United States has had a forced labour import ban for nearly a century, and rigourously enforces it; it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same."

The Trump administration agreed to impose lower 10 percent tariffs on countries it claimed had committed to impose a forced labour import prohibition. They included Argentina, Bangladesh, Canada, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Mexico, Pakistan and the UK.

Finny said the United States remained a good market for many exporters, but the higher tariff would make conditions tougher for some.

"For some exporters, it will be even tougher now with a 12.5 percent tariff, and they will be looking for new markets," he said.

World.title: Out of necessity is borne a unique and wholly Scottish opening ceremony
World.content:
The Glasgow Commonwealth Games was more or less forced inside.

The shortened preparation time meant it was simply easier to host most events in halls and exhibition centres that already existed, and a solid roof removes the many variables that Scotland's weather can introduce to proceedings.

It meant the opening ceremony, for the first time in history, would be held in an arena rather than a stadium. And what a blessing it turned out to be.

Australia emerged late in the athletes' parade, which was divided by regions as well as nations. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

If you've ever witnessed a rock band or pop star playing before a major football game, you'll know the energy is very rarely on point.

It's just too far, the noise dissipates and charismatic frontmen and global superstars are reduced to little more than carnival barkers, pleading with a distracted crowd to "put your hands up. Please."

On Thursday night in Glasgow, the crowd filed in as the perfect weather turned cool for the first time this week. Local DJ Hu Sane and radio presenters kept the crowd relatively entertained with the sort of pre-show antics you'd expect from a warm-up act.

The opening skit with cycling great Sir Chris Hoy, former Doctor Who star Sylvester McCoy and actor Greg McHugh served its purpose of delivering a few knowing chuckles and delivering King Charles III and Queen Camilla in a TARDIS.

King Charles III's arrival was the sort of thing we've come to expect from opening ceremonies. The rest of the show wasn't. (AP: Manish Swarup)

But from the opening strains of synth-heavy electro-folk band Valtos, it was clear this ceremony would feel different.

As the athletes entered the arena, projected on the screens wrapping around the upper decks were messages from local kids (or well-meaning and poorly read adults).

"I hope you win the game, good luck best wishes from Gulalai" "Good luck! I hope you enjoy Glasgow — our green place, you can do this!" "Have fun you can do it. I hope you do well be brave." "Good luck. Believe in yourself be proud of yourself. From Leah."

Nina Kennedy and Tim Hodge led the team into the arena. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Scotland is a nation that prides itself on being small but mighty. Fittingly, the smaller the team, the larger the cheer during the parade, with the loudest reserved for St Lucia.

The tiny Caribbean nation brought just three athletes to Glasgow and only the chef de mission marched, but she was welcomed like a Glaswegian local.

Then came the main attraction.

When in doubt, pipe. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Scotland's athletes danced their way to their seats accompanied by rapturous applause from the 14,000-strong crowd, before a cameo by Nessie, pipers and Outlander's Sam Heughan.

Then those supporters briefly turned into the stars of the show.

The same crowd that gleefully welcomed the current British monarch to Glasgow an hour earlier joined pipers and drummers in a stirring, reverberative rendition of Flower of Scotland, the national anthem about King of the Scots Robert the Bruce driving King Edward II's army back at the Battle of Bannockburn.

The pipes were indeed calling. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Fiji's noqu masu, New Zealand's haka, Samoa's siva tau (performed by the team as they emerged for the parade) can crack stone hearts and soak eyes that don't cry at funerals.

This was one of those moments.

The sounds of the pipes bouncing off the walls, the power of the drums rattling through the seats and the choral sensation cascading from the upper decks all ended up in the same place: deep in the bones of all those in attendance.

The size, shape and set-up of the venue made it feel like a more intimate performance than the sort of extravaganza intended for hundreds of millions of people to watch on TV.

There was a theme of gardens and nature throughout the ceremony. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It was enough to make everyone in the arena want to be Scottish, but most of all Commonwealth Sport president Donald Rukare.

"It's good to be back," he said.

The thanks to the 2014 hosts and ensuing elation from the Scottish crowd came with an undertone of side-eye to the slack left by Victoria's 2023 rug-pull.

Both Scotland and Australia pride themselves on punching above their weight, taking things in stride with good humour and getting on with the job.

There was a party atmosphere for the athletes' parade. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

But only one of those countries is putting on these Games. And there does seem to be a genuine feeling of pride in Glasgow for stepping into a tough situation, albeit with help from a few hundred million dollars from Victorian taxpayers.

During his speech, Rukare said he hoped the crowd would indulge him sporting a Wallace tartan kilt, reimagined in the colours of his native Uganda.

Indulge him? Saltires flew with the sort of fervour usually reserved for the athletes who will take centre stage for the next 10 days.

By the time King Charles officially declared the Games open, the whole event turned into a concert, courtesy of Callum Beattie, Tom Walker and KT Tunstall.

The lead-up to these Games has at times shown the hallmarks of a major global event pulled together under an intense time crunch, but the opening ceremony, aside perhaps from a few eisteddfod-level costumes, overcame that with a passion and spirit that was purely Scotland.

Rukare has spoken about making the Games fit for purpose, even if that means getting smaller in some ways, to remain relevant.

After this opening, it's hard to imagine going back.

World.title: Stage winner almost hits overzealous fan in gruelling Tour de France climb
World.content:
Ecuadorian rider Richard Carapaz timed his attack perfectly in the final climb to win the 18th stage of the Tour de France, while also surviving a near miss with a spectator.

It was the 33-year-old Carapaz's first stage win at this year's race and second overall. Leader Tadej Pogačar did not chase him down because Carapaz is not considered a threat to win the Tour and is in 10th spot.

"This is a wonderful victory," Carapaz said.

"I dedicate it to my family."

After moving ahead about 3 kilometres from the summit, Carapaz raced clear. He patted each side of his head as he approached the finish line, and was 45 seconds ahead of Swiss rider Mauro Schmid and American Matteo Jorgenson.

"It's been a special day. It took a lot of hard work," said Carapaz, who failed to win with a similar breakaway earlier in this year's race.

"This is the most rewarding thing for me, knowing that the work I put in has paid off."

Pogačar is chasing a third straight Tour title and fifth overall. The Slovenian star rolled over the line in a large group containing his closest rival, Remco Evenepoel, and Pogačar's UAE Emirates XRG teammate, Isaac Del Toro.

There was no change overall as Pogačar maintained his lead of 4 minutes, 32 seconds over the Belgian time trial star Evenepoel, the winner of two stages at this year's race, and 6:51 over the 22-year-old Mexican Del Toro in third overall.

The overnight stage was the first of three straight days of Alpine climbs.

The 185km trek featured an early Category 1 climb — the second-hardest category — up Côte d'Engins, before ending with a Category 1 ascent to the Orcières-Merlette ski station.

After going over Engins, Jorgenson was in a small group at the front. They were then joined by Carapaz, with Pogačar's yellow jersey group clearly hanging back.

"I think nobody would really commit," said Pogačar, who has won four stages at this year's race.

Carapaz's stage could have ended when he had a near miss with a fan standing in the road, but he swerved around him just in time.

Heading into the final climb up Orcières-Merlette, Jorgenson and Schmid could not respond when Carapaz, who won the 2019 Giro d'Italia, attacked.

"This final climb was tough and suited my strengths well," said Carapaz, whose other Tour stage win came in 2024.

"This was a hard-fought victory, but just as tough as the first one. It gets harder every year to win here."

The 19th stage ends with a HC climb (the hardest category) up L'Alpe d'Huez, an iconic Tour climb and among the most famed in cycling.

The 20th and penultimate stage is brutal and could be epic. It features three HC climbs — Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Galibier and Col de Sarenne — and one Category 1 climb up Col du Télégraphe, before a hilly finish to L'Alpe d'Huez.

The race ends on the Champs-Élysées in Paris on Sunday night AEST.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: History beckons as Stingers, Sharks surge into water polo semifinals
World.content:
It's been 26 years since Australia and the USA paved new ground for women's water polo, contesting the gold medal match at the Sydney Olympics.

Now, in the same pool used in those Games, the Stingers and the USA will meet once more, this time in a semifinal of the World Cup Finals.

"The moment's not lost on us," Australian skipper Bronte Halligan told ABC Sport.

"I hadn't made that connection yet, that the Aussie girls played the US in the final [at the Sydney 2000 Olympics], but now you've mentioned it, that is another thing.

"But no, it's not lost on us.

"Any game's an important game and a semi's a semi; you win, or you lose, and we're going to go in there and battle our little butts off and see what we can do, and then hopefully produce a really good result."

Australia's women's water polo team fought for the sport's inclusion in the Games, then won gold. (Getty Images: Martin Rose/Bongarts)

The Sydney Olympics water polo tournament was a groundbreaking one for the sport in so many ways.

For a start, it was the first to ever feature a women's competition, despite women competing at World Championships since 1986 and in World Cup competitions since 1979.

Australia's women were pivotal in getting water polo included, with player Liz Weekes threatening legal action if women weren't included and some 50 players protesting at Sydney Airport in 1997 when the president of World Aquatics, then known as FINA, arrived in the city.

Those players were vindicated and their dream realised, women finally permitted to play Olympic water polo — the oldest team sport at the Games.

Australia and the USA made it to the final of the six-team competition, playing out a thrilling final in front of 17,000 supporters at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre.

And it was the Stingers who came out on top, winning 4-3 after a last-second goal to Yvette Higgins.

A four-year-old Halligan attended those Games, although the now 29-year-old was not among the thousands who were there for that historic final.

The Stingers are leading the way into the semifinal. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

But now she and her Stingers teammates have an opportunity to repeat history.

And not just history from a quarter of a century ago either — these two teams met in the semifinal of the Olympics in Paris too, the Aussies winning 14-13 after a heart-stopping penalty shootout.

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

That victory saw the Stingers progress to the final, where they fell agonisingly short of a gold medal against Spain.

The USA and Australia have continued to cross paths though — it was against the USA that the Stingers had a pre-tournament training camp last week in Brisbane.

"We know them as a team. We know them as a squad," Halligan said.

"They're a bunch of phenomenal athletes; they're really tough opponents.

"We're lucky to have trained against them last week; we can kind of foresee what we're coming up against, but it's not going to be an easy game, and we've got to just stay united."

Bronte Halligan played her 200th match for Australia in the quarterfinal victory over Italy. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

To Halligan, who spent most of the 5am training sessions from the age of 14 at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre, this pool feels like home, which made the fact that she marked her 200th international appearance with a dramatic 15-14 win over Italy.

"It kind of all just fell into place," Halligan said.

"It became this really special moment here in Sydney, in a pool that I grew up training in and with my family and friends at a huge event in a World Cup quarterfinal.

"It just was kind of almost picture perfect.

"I just feel lucky that it all kind of fell into place and this is what happened."

Gabi Palm was named player of the match against Italy. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Halligan noted how special it was to see some of her former teammates and trailblazers in the stands — and that is exactly what the USA felt too.

The USA powered into the semifinal with a dominant 14-8 against China on Wednesday after meeting with some of their silver medallists from those 2000 Games.

"We heard from some of the players last night, and that was so amazing. Just taking us back, and learning our history," said 20-year-old USA driver Emily Ausmus, who scored four goals in that game.

"It was so cool to see the women before you that paved the path, and that got women's water polo into the Olympics.

"It's so cool that we're in the same venue; it's still so beautiful."

Emily Ausmus scored four goals for the USA in their quarterfinal victory. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Beautiful and set to be packed for another massive Australian-USA clash.

"It's so important to have all the friends and family here, and especially the Stingers alumni," Halligan said.

"They've paved the way for us and a bunch of them have played with us; I saw a bunch of my ex-teammates here in the stands, and they're so special because they all have touched our careers.

"We just feel fortunate to be able to play a big game like this and play it here in Sydney."

Sharks 'showed we belong', stun champions Spain

The Aussies are making a habit of shocking the world's best. (Supplied: World Aquatics)

On Thursday night, the Aussie Sharks also channelled the class of 2000, stunning reigning world champions Spain in a thrilling penalty shoot-out.

Australia were four goals down at one stage of the match, trailed 6-3 at quarter time, 16-13 at three-quarter time and 18-16 with 40 seconds to play.

However, the side fought back incredibly to level the scores late on at 18-18.

And, on a night of extraordinary drama at the Sydney Olympic pool, the Sharks had to equalise twice inside the final 10 seconds.

Marcus Berehulak, bandaged after being opened up by a stray Spanish fist in the first half, thought he had scored the leveller with six seconds to play, only for it to be taken off him by the referees for taking a free throw inside the six metres zone.

Marcus Berehulak scored what he thought was the equalising goal. (Supplied: World Aquatics)

As the parochial Sydney crowd booed the decision, the Aussies kept their heads as they were told to replay the final 7.9 seconds.

With the Sharks keeper up to create an extra man, Matthew Burns powered home the actual leveller at the near post with 1.1 seconds to play to set up penalties.

Substitute keeper Laurence Barker saved from Fran Valera in the shoot-out, while Australia slotted all five of their penalty shots to claim a 23-21 victory.

The victory was fitting for an Australian team that have embraced the underdog tag but, just as they did in Paris against Serbia, stunned the favourites with a never-say-die display of pure grit.

"Congratulations to Spain," player of the match Jacob Mercep, who led the Sharks with six goals, said.

"They had us in the first half, but we were able to come back.

"We were kind of manifesting this semifinal; we've been talking about it all winter.

"When it matters the most, we showed we belong."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Berehulak scored four, Matthew Byrnes — who slotted the final penalty — scored three, while veteran Blake Edwards added two.

"I got stitched up, and I'm glad I came back out there because that win was incredible … nothing like I've felt before," Berehulak said.

"Spain is a fantastic team, but I think we really stayed composed. We had a game plan that we stuck to, and we just kept chipping away.

"Having that crowd, and being able to deliver a performance against the current world champions — it tops my number one water polo memory of all time."

Captain Nathan Power, Charlie Negus and Nicolas Constantin Bicari all scored one each.

World.title: This is the AFL's most interesting Western Derby in a decade
World.content:
Fremantle is storming towards a historic AFL campaign.

Never has the club won more than 17 games during a regular season, and never has it finished a season with a higher percentage than it currently boasts.

Even in 2015, when Fremantle won those 17 games, drew one and finished top of the ladder, Ross Lyon's charges only had a percentage of 118.

The Dockers have won 16 games so far this season. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

This season, Justin Longmuir's side sits on 142 per cent with five games to play.

In tonight's Western Derby against West Coast, the Dockers could match their best-ever return and set up a comfortable run into finals.

A victory would see them remain at least three games clear at the top of the ladder with four matches to play, meaning they would need to win just one of their remaining games to clinch top spot.

Ross Lyon's Fremantle has a better percentage than the club's 2015 version that won 17 games. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

It's an enviable position, but after a barnstorming run of 14 wins in a row, recent weeks have shown sides are starting to get a handle on the Dockers.

Fremantle has lost four of its past five first halves, though it has gone on to win all bar one of those matches.

Quality talls the key for Freo Fremantle has lost its 14-game winning streak with a loss to GWS, but what are the keys for the Dockers to keep going and set up a tilt at their first flag? Cody Atkinson and Sean Lawson investigate.

It's something Longmuir is acutely aware needs monitoring, but otherwise there's little reason to panic.

His side boasts the stingiest defence in the league while also being the third-highest scoring.

The three-headed dragon of Jye Amiss, Josh Treacy and Patrick Voss has kicked 120 goals up forward.

The midfield is humming with or without Hayden Young, who has become something of the cream on a pretty spectacular cake.

Patrick Voss is part of a three-headed dragon for the Dockers up forward. (AAP: Michael Errey)

The premiership window isn't just open for Fremantle. It's been blown off its hinges.

Eagles on the up

West Coast shouldn't, on paper at least, pose much of a problem for the Dockers.

The Eagles have won just four games this year, and not since defeating a hapless Essendon back in May.

But that doesn't tell the whole story of coach Andrew McQualter's side.

In round eight, the Eagles returned from Melbourne after a 101-point belting by St Kilda.

West Coast lost to Fremantle by 56 points in April. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

In the three weeks prior, West Coast had been thrashed by Sydney, Geelong and the Dockers.

Things looked bleak for the long-suffering Eagles faithful who had entered the season hopeful their club's rebuild would start bearing fruit.

Indeed, the flowers are starting to bloom, and it seems the fruit isn't too far away.

West Coast has been improving in recent weeks, with results including a win against Essendon. (AAP: David Woodley)

West Coast may have only won two more games since that shellacking by the Saints, but it has been a lot more competitive.

In their opening eight rounds, the Eagles' average margin was minus 46 points, which included wins in rounds two and three.

Since then, that margin is just minus 11 points. They beat GWS and Essendon, lost to Port Adelaide by a goal and North Melbourne by a point.

They led at half-time against the Western Bulldogs and Brisbane.

Wins and losses don't tell the entire story of Andrew McQualter's Eagles this season. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Harley Reid has not dropped below 20 disposals since that loss to Saint Kilda in a sign he's finding consistency in his game, while Jake Waterman has kicked three or more goals in eight of his past 11 games.

McQualter has stated his side is hunting a "scalp" to crystallise its improvement. Fremantle would be the ideal trophy.

At Perth Stadium tonight, both the Dockers and Eagles have something to gain, but only one has a lot to lose.

World.title: 'Prehistoric' hurdles keep this club's women's program from thriving
World.content:
Macedon Football Netball Club president Ron Rutledge says his club does things a bit like Ted Lasso.

The "Lasso Way", inspired by the popular TV show, is a leadership style centred on kindness, personal growth and human connection, often over winning.

"Our number one thing is 'thank you' and our number two thing is 'please'," Rutledge tells ABC Sport.

"We're a very easy club to get on with … But we are in a desperate pitch now for our female participants."

The club is in the heart of the Macedon Ranges in central Victoria, about 60 kilometres north-west of Melbourne.

Ron Rutledge says the club has worked hard to grow its women's and girls' teams. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Founded in 1887 as an original member of the Riddell District Football League, its clubrooms contain cabinets filled with trophies won by generations of men's teams.

The latest additions are the two premiership trophies won by the senior women's side.

Six years ago, the club underwent a significant change when it established a women's team, followed by a girls' team.

"A lot of people before me worked very hard on getting a junior program going for females, particularly in the AFL sense. It's been a netball club for many years, and that has continued to grow and grow and grow," Rutledge says.

The senior women's team is again among the premiership favourites this season.

MFNC female participation keeps on growing. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But, like many long-standing clubs across the country, Macedon encountered a significant problem as female participation grew: its facilities were neither large enough nor suitable for the new women's and girls' teams.

The Cats' home ground, Tony Clarke Reserve, is also used by the local bowling, cricket and tennis clubs.

The football teams also train around the corner at JD Clifford Reserve during the week.

On Thursday nights, the youth boys, youth girls, senior men's and senior women's sides all train across the two grounds.

'Made for men'

Reigning senior women's club best and fairest winner Ruby Watts has played football since 2017, the year AFLW started.

Now 21, she played Auskick as a child but stopped after a year because she "didn't like playing with the boys", which was then the only option available.

She returned to the sport as a teenager when her local club, Gisborne Football Netball Club, established a girls' team. But she was forced to leave in 2024 when the club could no longer field a women's side.

Ruby Watts won the best and fairest last year. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

She joined Macedon with about six other players from Gisborne. The difference between the clubs' facilities was immediately noticeable.

"At Gisborne it was fine. Like, the facilities are perfect, they're clean, they're nice, but the ones here are a bit… they're just old and they're mainly made for men," Watts says.

"It's open urinals and just open showers, and it's just disgusting. There's one toilet with a door, so it's a big struggle.

"We have to use it after the men's teams, and it's not their fault. Like, they clean it nicely, but it's still disgusting. It just smells gross and it's not right. In 2026 we should be doing better, I reckon."

Women's players say the toilet situation in the change rooms isn't good enough. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Watts says the club does its best to make sure the women's side is included, but understands sometimes it is constrained by a lack of space.

At Thursday night selection dinners, for example, the women are encouraged to get their food first, while the men listen and cheer as the women's team is announced.

The club has also had several pride rounds this year for the women's competition, in which the shared space gets decorated with streamers and posters.

The away rooms for Macedon's home ground have just the one open showers room. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But during training beforehand, the women have only a small section of the oval to use if one is rained out.

"There is quadruple the amount of them than there is of us. It would be nice to get half of the ground, but we don't need it in comparison," she says.

The same imbalance means the men fill the clubroom on shared nights, while the women leave their belongings on nearby benches. By dinner, the men have showered and changed, while the women remain in their wet training clothes.

"You can't walk on the ground without your socks getting wet, like we don't have a locker to put our stuff in. A girl, a few weeks ago, lost all of her clothes, because there's nowhere safe to put them," Watts says.

Women's players have to leave their belongings on benches while they train. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

"She literally lost her jumper, her pants, like everything. And she still hasn't gotten her clothes back, just because we have no locker or nothing to put them in, nowhere safe.

"We put our clothes on the chairs and just along the fence and it gets nice and wet and dewy … Then the boys shower after training, but all of us girls have to go fully kitted, fully in our wet socks and everything.

"The boys have comfy jumpers and pants on because they don't care, they'll shower around anybody. We don't have a shower to get changed in. It's different for us."

MFNC has a successful women's program. But the players still have nowhere to get changed. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Eve Moait, 19, plays in the senior women's side and coaches the under-14 girls.

She loves the club and has embraced its Ted Lasso philosophy. A "Believe" sign hangs above the door to the home change rooms.

"My junior girls love it, they think it's hilarious … They think it's the thing that won them their first game because they all tapped it on the way out and truly believed it," Moait says.

Some of the younger players could not quite reach it.

"They were actually really good jumpers, but we had some really, really small girls and they'd lift each other up to tap it. They're so sweet."

There is a "BELIEVE" sign above the door at MFNC's change rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Before training, she gets changed in her car and then heads onto the ground.

She says the main club room is good, particularly since indoor artificial turf was installed, even if it's "terrible to clean as a coach".

"But then when we come to the toilet side, the girls just don't want to go in there," she says of her junior team.

"It's smelly because we come in on a Sunday after all the senior men have played the day before, and then all of the boys' teams have played the morning, so we come in during the afternoon at about one o'clock and it is disgusting.

" It smells, and there's grass, and there's underwear, and pee in the corner. It is so gross. "

The junior girls' team at Macedon Football Netball Club. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Moait often takes the junior players to a public toilet block 200 metres away, but says that can be difficult when she is responsible for all 18 members of the team.

"It's also a very awkward age for these girls," Moait says.

"We've noticed when they first come to the team, when they're at the very bottom age, so 11 or 12, they're typically fine. They'll go to the toilet, or try and avoid it if it's dirty, but it won't bother them as much.

"But when they hit the upper end and they start going into that time [puberty], they just shut off when it comes to the toilet, be like, 'nah, don't want to', and it's like I can't provide them with much better, so it's frustrating.

"There's no sanitary bin, it's dirty, and there's only one toilet there. It's not working for them, that's the problem."

MFNC train on cold and foggy Thursday nights. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The push for an upgrade

Rutledge has been lobbying the council and state government for help upgrading Tony Clarke Reserve, attracting visits from politicians across the political spectrum.

Macedon Ranges Shire Council has allocated $380,000 in its 2026–27 budget to upgrade the change rooms.

The away rooms at Macedon Football Netball Club. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The council's assets and operations director, Dom Testoni, told the ABC: "The proposed project, valued at approximately $650,000, would bring the facilities up to current standards and better support the needs of the growing number of participants using the reserve.

"While Council's recent application to the Victorian Government's Country Football Netball Program was unsuccessful, a number of funding avenues remain available.

"Council will submit a new application through the Victorian Government's Local Sports Infrastructure Program, which is currently open, and will continue to pursue other state and federal grant opportunities as they become available."

Macedon Football Netball Club home rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

But Macedon Ranges Shire Mayor Kate Kendall said that funding "falls a little bit short".

She described the facilities as "absolutely prehistoric" and in "such a dire state" that they deterred local girls and women from participating in sport.

"We look at inclusion and a lot of people talk about inclusion, but if we don't have the very basic needs met, where people can go to the toilet safely and privately, then it's just, you know, a poor tale," Kendall told ABC Sport.

MFNC president Ron Rutledge in the club's away rooms. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Macedon MP Mary-Anne Thomas told the ABC she had visited the club and it was clear the facilities were past their use-by date. She said she had pressed the council to find a short-term solution while it pursued grant funding.

Rutledge hopes portable change rooms can be installed while the club identifies a long-term solution.

Victorian Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said the situation demonstrated the consequences of cutting the Office for Women in Sport and Recreation from last year's state budget.

Girls players getting changed on the benches outside the football field. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

Purcell said the office was not merely symbolic and had provided important support to sporting clubs, particularly those with relatively new women and girls' teams.

"It's not enough to just say women can play and think everything is going to magically resolve overnight. It requires commitment and work from the government," she told ABC Sport.

"I think the big problem with women in sport, and what we confront now, is women worked really hard and clubs worked really hard to let women into the spaces, but letting women into the spaces doesn't necessarily mean that they feel welcome or supported, or that the facilities and access are there for them to feel comfortable and like they're taken seriously.

" We say women are welcome in sport. We have women's sporting teams, but we just don't have the access or the facilities to allow those teams and club cultures to thrive. "

Macedon senior women's team are going for the three-peat this year. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The Macedon way

Rutledge says he feels he is letting down the club's women's and girls' programs.

"I feel personally disappointed as president of the organisation. One of my commitments on the day that we had the election was that I want to make female participation one of our main goals," he says.

"We define outcomes not necessarily as premierships, but as participation and doing things for the community as well. We are a community club and we're very focused on letting the community judge us rather than us judging them.

"We've got a very powerful and energetic committee that works very closely with all parts of our operation… but we sit here tonight in a draconian position with our change rooms for our women."

Players say the culture at Macedon is different. (ABC: Danielle Bonica)

The women want better facilities and are not quiet about it. But they are not going anywhere.

Even after Gisborne re-established its women's team, players such as Watts decided they would rather make the longer drive to keep doing things "the Macedon way".

World.title: King Charles opens Glasgow 2026 during ceremony buoyed by Scottish pride
World.content:
Three years after the Victorian government pulled out as host, King Charles arrived in Glasgow via a time machine to help open the Commonwealth Games.

This year's Commonwealth Games in Glasgow is running on a bare-bones budget. Hence why the opening ceremony broke with tradition and was staged indoors at Glasgow's Hydro arena.

But the vibrant two-hour party was far from pared back.

And at a time when people have questioned the relevance of the Games after the Victorian government's shock withdrawal as host in 2023, the ceremony on Friday morning made the argument for with a modern "love letter to the Commonwealth".

"It was awesome," para swimming champion Tim Hodge beamed, having performed the new ceremonial role of baton-bearer for Australia.

" You wouldn't be able to tell whether they'd … thought of it in two years' time, or they'd spent 10 years intricately designing it. It was incredible. "

Australian flag-bearer Nina Kennedy also described the extravaganza as "awesome".

Nina Kennedy carries the flag as Australia enters the Hydro at the 2026 Commonwealth Games. (Getty)

While not exactly parachuting into the 2012 London Olympics opening ceremony with James Bond, King Charles and Queen Camilla kicked off these proceedings in style by arriving via the iconic Doctor Who time machine, the Tardis.

Able-bodied and para athletes from the 74 competing nations were then welcomed to a makeshift Glaswegian garden as electro-folk duo Valtos weaved Celtic influences into a contemporary dance and rap.

Rather than there being a single king's baton, nations were given their own to decorate and bring to the opening ceremony.

The batons were handcrafted in Glasgow from Scottish ash fallen in the city's parks, with each planted within the garden of the opening ceremony.

Spectre of Victorian Games that never were

The Australian athletes savoured their moment, briefly stalling proceedings as minders attempted to usher the huge contingent to seats as they waved and snapped selfies.

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

If ever there was an opening ceremony to savour, this was it. The past three years have been a roller-coaster for Australian athletes.

In another world, Kennedy and Hodge would have been leading their nation on home soil.

But Victoria's withdrawal as Games host was the last thing on the boisterous crowd's mind as Scotland's team strolled out, with the tartan-clad final nation in the procession given a standing ovation at a venue with few empty seats.

"[This is] a city built by people who believe that when something matters, you step forward," George Black, chair of the Glasgow 2026 organising committee, later roared on stage.

"When the future of these Games was uncertain, Glasgow didn't ask, 'Can we?'

"We asked, "When do we get started?'"

The end of the athletes' parade was followed by an appearance of Nessie the Loch Ness Monster, actor Sam Heughan of Outlander fame and bagpipers.

The opening ceremony then traversed through many facets of Glasgow. There was a flash mob under the Glasgow Central station clock, before dancing unicorns with traffic cones — for decades, regularly placed on an equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington — paid tribute to the city's underground club culture.

Actor Sam Heughan with Nessie during the opening ceremony for the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow (Getty: Jane Barlow)

A rousing rendition of the Proclaimers' anthem, I'm Gonna Be (500 Miles), was sung by Nina Nesbitt as the king's intercontinental baton relay finally came to an end.

Unlike the first time Glasgow hosted the Games in 2014, this year's 11-day event has just 10 sports and will be hosted at four pre-existing venues across an eight-mile corridor.

While doubt about the relevancy of the Games, which started as the British Empire Games in 1930, still remains, the Glasgow opening ceremony may have been enough to stir a feeling akin to seller's remorse.

World.title: Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026
World.content:
Has netball learned much since 2023? You be the judge.

The messy and drawn-out pay negotiations that dominated headlines during that World Cup year are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the sport.

The Diamonds are aiming to defend gold at the Commonwealth Games, and that mission starts on Saturday night in their opening match against Tonga at 8pm AEST. But the world number one team hit the court in Glasgow with uncertain futures.

The current Super Netball collective player agreement (CPA) expires on September 30, meaning all 88 players will be off contract. It is a chaotic way of doing things and leads to a mad scramble for everyone involved, with so many trying to secure opportunity at the same time.

Netball Australia surrenders, as players win long and bitter pay war Netball Australia has finally agreed to a modest revenue share partnership with its players, but how much have its brutal tactics throughout the pay negotiations damaged the game?

The 2027 signing window was supposed to open the Monday after the grand final on July 4. That has been delayed a month so the athletes can focus on their international duties while the terms of the next deal are worked through.

There are several sticking points that the national sporting organisation and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA) cannot agree on. More on that later.

It is important to note that ANPA provided a detailed submission late last year to try and get the ball rolling. Netball Australia wanted to wait and sort out its new broadcast agreement with Nine, which underwrites the majority of the costs of the CPA first. That was done in April.

Although from the sport's point of view, discussions are more respectful and constructive this time, with greater transparency of information shared amongst parties, the players are incredibly frustrated. And so are their agents, who argue they are unable to make meaningful progress on behalf of their talent.

There is no prohibition to hold non-binding conversations with your own club or another right now, yet a request to allow non-binding written offers while CPA talks take place was denied. The agents believe this would've freed up the system and given players more certainty.

Kathryn Deiulioi is the founder of Behind Your Brand, which manages several Diamonds athletes, including the Australian captain. (Image Supplied)

Kathryn Deiulio, the founder of Behind Your Brand, said it was her understanding that the Diamonds players did not ask the sport to push back the contracting window and wanted discussions to continue. There are concerns this kind of assumption could create a divide amongst the group, positioning some as more important than others.

"This misunderstanding creates the impression that they didn't consider the impact it could have on the remaining 60-70 players not playing at the Games," Deiulio told ABC Sport.

"It is our role to continue contract negotiations on their behalf, and it would have created an additional layer of complexity, given the time difference and the need to carefully manage communication with players so as not to distract them from their performance.

"However, ultimately, that is part of our role as agents and something we are equipped to manage … These are professional athletes who dedicate their lives to their sport, and they deserve the same level of security around employment expected in any other profession."

Australia won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. (Getty: Sue McKay)

Jace Bode is the chief executive of W Sports & Media, which works across a range of elite codes, such as cricket, Aussie Rules, football, golf and tennis.

"The fact that 80-plus athletes have once again been put in this position is incredibly disappointing and challenging to manage from our perspective," Bode told ABC Sport.

"We have the best netball competition in the world, and it is frustrating to watch these athletes continue to navigate uncertainty around their careers when it has so much potential."

This CPA will only be a 12-month deal, allowing Netball Australia to try and bring in more revenue from 2027 onwards with the free-to-air broadcast agreement and present a stronger offer. But both agents worry that without a longer CPA in place we may be right back here next year, ahead of a World Cup on home soil.

The Diamonds players have been in camp since Friday July 10. (Supplied: Netball Australia)

According to the new dates, contracts will open for clubs' own players from August 4-16. Non-binding written offers are permitted for all players during these 12 days. Then, from August 17-28, contracting officially opens for those looking to switch allegiances.

The agents argue this process favours those who intend to remain at their existing club, while placing players who may be looking elsewhere at a significant disadvantage. The time frame is also not ideal for those weighing up their options overseas, with the English Superleague contracting window already in full swing.

Complicating things further, in other sports it is normally the responsibility of the governing body to handle CPA talks with the players' association, but here the clubs appear to have taken greater control of the wheel.

All eight Super Netball franchises are likely to have competing ideas slowing progress further, and it is unclear if their vested interests will be prioritised over what is best for the sport as a whole.

Shimona Nelson represents Jamaica at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games. (Getty: Mark Kolbe)

The delay has wide-reaching implications beyond the Australian team at the Games.

In-form Melbourne Mavericks star Shimona Nelson had already flagged with Netball Jamaica that she would be unavailable for selection for Glasgow ahead of the Super Netball season. The goal shooter needs to get her tonsils removed and deal with a knee issue.

Although the Sunshine Girls did try and get her to change her mind, an appearance at the major tournament would be risky. Should she injure herself, with only one-year contracts being offered, where would that leave her?

It makes sense that Nelson has put herself first, considering the history of her career. After the Collingwood team disbanded, Nelson had to forge her way back into the league as a No.11 player with the Mavericks, working hard to return to a full-time contract the next season.

It is unfair that athletes are being forced to make these tricky decisions based on what is happening in Super Netball, and what is right for each of them is extremely individual.

Shimona Jok keeping an open mind as 11th player signing confirms she's eligible for Diamonds Super Netball import Shimona Jok was in the headlines after the Mavericks found a loophole to sign her as their 11th player. But now her eligibility for the Diamonds has been confirmed, would she ever go there?

There has been a rumour that Nelson isn't playing because she instead wants to represent the Diamonds at the next World Cup.

Nelson indeed plans to get her citizenship in September, purely to cement her status in a country she has lived in for almost 10 years and now classes as home.

At this point, there have been no discussions between the Australian camp or Shimona's about the possibility of her playing for the Diamonds.

So, what are some of the sticking points of the CPA talks?

Currently on the table is a 25 per cent pay increase for those on the minimum wage and a three per cent pay increase for everyone else.

This all sounds rosy until you do the numbers. Australia's consumer price index sits at four per cent. Once these changes are factored into the salary cap, with increased superannuation contributions and the rising cost of living, the take-home pay for many of the athletes could actually be worse off than they were this year. It may lead to a pay cut in real terms.

Former Thunderbird and Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the chief executive of the players' association. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Despite this, the sport will continue to restrict player opportunities to make extra cash in sponsorship deals. The cap for commercial arrangements with an existing team sponsor or partner is going to be raised to $50,000 but the agents want the cap removed entirely.

There are no monetary limits on a player's commercial agreements with third parties, but agents find the amount of compliance their talent must go through to get approval is unreasonable and leads to sponsors turning to athletes from other codes.

"When athletes are able to work with brands and authentically leverage their own platforms, they bring different eyeballs to the sport … This should be viewed as a positive, not a threat," Bode and Deiulio said.

"If netball does not evolve in this increasingly competitive female sports landscape, these limitations will have a broader impact on its growth and visibility."
